The choice depends on workload: consistency-first → leader-follower; write throughput + locality → multi-leader; partition tolerance + no leader → leaderless.
Replication lag (covered in the next card) is what makes the difference between synchronous and asynchronous replication visible to the application.

Leader-follower

  Writer --> Leader (log append)
                |
                +--> Follower 1 (apply log)
                +--> Follower 2 (apply log)

  reads: any replica (fast, may be stale) or leader (strong)
  failover: one follower is promoted
  write bottleneck: leader

Multi-leader

  Writer-EU --> Leader-EU --> Leader-US --> Follower-US
       |                        ^
       +------------------------+
         (bidirectional replication)

  two writers can conflict on the same row ->
    LWW (timestamp) | merge function | CRDT

Leaderless

  Client write (W replicas):  R1[X=1] R2[X=1] R3[  ]
  Client read  (R replicas):  R1[X=1] R2[X=1] R3[X=old]

  R + W > N  guarantees overlap
  N=3, W=2, R=2 -> strong-ish consistency
  conflict resolution: vector clocks (Dynamo) or LWW

Model comparison

  Model            Write bottleneck   Conflict handling   Failover      Example
  ---------------  -----------------  ------------------  ------------  -----------------
  Leader-follower  yes (leader)       none (single       election      PostgreSQL, MySQL,
                                       writer)                          MongoDB, Kafka
  Multi-leader     no                 application /       not needed    CouchDB, multi-DC
                                       CRDT / LWW                       systems
  Leaderless       no                 vector clocks /     no leader     Cassandra, DynamoDB,
                                       LWW                              Riak

Synchronous vs asynchronous replication

  sync:  leader waits for followers to acknowledge before replying
         -> no lag, lower write throughput, followers must be up

  async: leader acknowledges immediately, followers catch up later
         -> replication lag, higher throughput, tolerate follower loss

  semi-sync: leader waits for at least one follower -> balance

cards.title: Replication Lag and Read Consistency: Read-Your-Writes, Monotonic Reads, and Consistent Prefix
cards.summary:
Replication lag is the delay between a write being committed on the leader and being applied on a follower. It exists because most leader-follower systems use asynchronous replication: the leader acknowledges the write immediately, and followers catch up in the background. Under normal conditions lag is milliseconds, but under load, network slowness, a follower restart, or a follower that falls behind on a long-running transaction, lag can grow to seconds or minutes. The consequence is that reads served by a follower can return stale data — the client sees a state that does not include a write that already succeeded. This is not a bug; it is the direct consequence of asynchronous replication, and the application must design around it.

The most important read-consistency guarantees are the ones that describe what a single client (or a causally related group of clients) is guaranteed to see. Read-your-writes (also called read-after-write): after a client successfully writes a value, subsequent reads by the same client see that value or a later one. Without this guarantee, a user updates their profile, refreshes the page, and sees the old profile — the classic 'I just saved it, why is it gone?' bug. The usual fixes are: (1) route reads of data the client just wrote to the leader for a short window; (2) track the client's last write timestamp/version and wait until a replica has caught up past it; (3) read from the leader for a specific session (for example, a sticky session with a 'just modified' flag). The key insight is that this is a per-client guarantee — it does not require all replicas to be caught up, only that the client's own reads see its own writes.

Monotonic reads: if a client reads a value and then reads again, the second read does not go backwards in time. The classic violation: a client reads from a replica that is caught up to T=10, then reads from a different replica that is only caught up to T=5, and the value 'goes back' to an older state. The user experiences this as flickering or disappearing data. The fix is to bind a client to a single replica for the duration of a session, or to track the client's last-seen version and route reads to replicas that are at least that caught up. This is what 'sticky sessions' at the load balancer level provide, and what Cassandra's monotonic-read consistency level implies.

Consistent prefix: if a sequence of writes happens in some order, a reader sees those writes in the same order (even if not with the same timing). This matters most in systems where writes happen in a sequence — event logs, chat messages, social media posts — and the reader must not see message 3 before message 2. The fix is per-partition ordering (Kafka, Cassandra) or per-replica ordering guarantees, and it is the reason ordering is scoped to a partition or key rather than to the entire dataset.

These guarantees compose into causal consistency: the strongest consistency that is still available in a partitioned system without coordination. Causal consistency says that if a write happens before another (causally), all readers see them in that order; independent writes may be seen in any order. It gives read-your-writes, monotonic reads, and consistent prefix, all at once, and it does not require a global leader or a synchronous commit. This is why CouchDB, Cassandra (with some tuning), and MongoDB causal sessions offer it as a practical middle ground: stronger than eventual, weaker than linearizable, and achievable without paying the coordination cost of strong consistency.

The distributed-systems interview question is always the same: 'A user updates their data, refreshes, and sees the old value. How do you fix it without forcing all reads to the leader?' The answer is a per-client solution: track the write (a version, a timestamp, an LSN) and route or wait until the client's own read is guaranteed to see it. Options include: read-your-writes routing (write to the leader, read from the leader for a short window), a monotonic version check (send the version in a header and have the replica wait for it), or a client-side cache that holds the just-written value until the replica catches up. The worst answer is 'add more replicas' — that does not fix staleness, it increases the chance of hitting a stale one. The second-worst is 'switch to synchronous replication' — that works but is a sledgehammer that couples availability to replica health.

The interview-quality answer defines replication lag, names the three per-client guarantees (read-your-writes, monotonic reads, consistent prefix), explains causal consistency as the composition of all three, gives the concrete failure scenarios (update → refresh → see old; read replica A → read replica B → see older), and gives the concrete fixes (leader routing for own writes, version-based waiting, session binding). That demonstrates you understand replication as a consistency design space, not as a feature to turn on.
bullets: Replication lag is the delay between a write on the leader and its application on a follower — usually milliseconds, but grows under load, network slowness, or follower restart.
Read-your-writes: after a client writes, its subsequent reads see that value or later — violated by naive read-from-follower routing.
Monotonic reads: a client's second read does not go back in time — violated when switching between replicas at different catch-up points.
Consistent prefix: writes are seen in the order they occurred — matters for sequences, event logs, chat, feeds.
Causal consistency = all three at once; it is the strongest consistency achievable in a partitioned system without coordination, and is why CouchDB, MongoDB sessions, and tuned Cassandra offer it.

Fixes for read-your-writes: read from the leader for a short window after writes, track the last write version and wait for the replica to catch up, or bind the client to a single replica for its session.
'Add more replicas' and 'switch to synchronous' are both wrong answers — the first does not fix staleness, the second trades availability for consistency unnecessarily.
cards.code:
Read-your-writes violation

  t=0  client writes user.name = 'Alice' -> leader
  t=1  leader acknowledges
  t=2  client reads from follower
  t=3  follower hasn't applied the write yet -> returns 'old name'

  fix: route reads of own data to the leader for the next few seconds

Monotonic reads violation

  t=0  client reads from replica A (caught up to T=10) -> sees 'value V2'
  t=1  client reads from replica B (caught up to T=5)  -> sees 'value V1'

  fix: bind the client session to one replica, or
       track last-seen version and route to replicas >= that version

Consistent prefix violation

  t=0  write msg1
  t=1  write msg2
  t=2  write msg3
  t=3  reader sees msg1, msg3, msg2  (out of order across replicas)

  fix: single-partition ordering (Kafka, Cassandra clustering key)
       or read the whole log from one replica

Causal consistency (composition)

  write(a) -> write(b)    (b causally depends on a)
  all readers see a before b

  write(c)  write(d)      (independent)
  readers may see c-before-d or d-before-c

  offered by: CouchDB, Cassandra (with causal sessions),
              MongoDB causal sessions, Riak (with per-key)

Read routing strategies

  leader-only          strong but bottleneck
  follower round-robin may be stale
  session-bound        one replica per client -> monotonic
  version-aware        client sends last-seen version, replica
                       waits if behind
  leader-for-own-data  read leader for the client's own recent writes

cards.title: Partitioning and Sharding Strategies: Range, Hash, and Directory-Based
cards.summary:
Partitioning (also called sharding) splits a large dataset into smaller pieces that live on different machines. It is how a system scales beyond what a single machine can store or serve, and it is the mechanism that sits underneath every distributed database. There are two related but distinct concerns: how the data is divided into partitions, and how requests are routed to the right partition. Understanding the strategies for each, and the trade-offs between them, is what interviewers are probing when they ask 'how would you shard this?'

Range partitioning assigns each partition a contiguous range of the key space. Partition 1 holds keys A–F, partition 2 holds G–M, and so on. This is the model of a sorted index: range queries (WHERE created_at BETWEEN x AND y) hit only the partitions that overlap the range, which makes it efficient for time-series, logs, and any query that filters by a sorted field. The cost is hotspots: if the key is monotonically increasing (timestamps, auto-increment IDs, ObjectIds), all new writes go to the last partition while earlier partitions sit idle. The standard fixes are to shard by a compound key (region + timestamp) or to periodically rebalance, but neither fully eliminates the hotspot if the workload is genuinely time-ordered.

Hash partitioning applies a hash function to the key and uses the hash to decide the partition. The hash distributes keys uniformly across partitions, which eliminates hotspots for uniformly distributed keys. The cost is that range queries become scatter-gather — because a contiguous key range maps to a random set of partitions, a query for a range must hit every partition. This is why hash-sharded collections in MongoDB and hash-partitioned tables in Cassandra are good for equality lookups and write throughput but poor for range queries. Consistent hashing (covered in sys-hashing-1) is a refinement that makes adding and removing nodes cheaper: only ~1/N of keys move instead of almost all of them.

Directory-based partitioning maintains a lookup table that explicitly maps each key (or key range) to a partition. This is the most flexible model — you can move any key to any partition at any time by updating the directory, which is useful for tiered storage (hot data on fast shards, cold data on slow shards), for data residency (EU data on EU shards), and for rebalancing when a shard grows too large. The cost is that the directory is a central component: it must be highly available, it is on the critical path of every request (or must be aggressively cached), and it must stay consistent with the actual data placement. Directory-based partitioning is used by systems like HBase (via the .META. table), Bigtable, and custom sharding layers where the routing logic is application-defined.

A fourth strategy, sometimes called geo-partitioning or tag-based, partitions by an attribute rather than by the key's hash. For example, all rows with region='EU' go to the EU shard, all rows with region='US' go to the US shard, regardless of user ID. This is a special case of directory or range partitioning, and it is the standard answer for data residency and latency requirements — a query for an EU user never crosses the Atlantic to a US shard. The cost is that a single region's growth can outpace the others, so you need to be able to further shard within a region (a two-level scheme: region first, then hash or range within region).

Request routing is the second concern, and it is where most sharding implementations fail. The client needs to know which shard holds a given key. The three standard approaches are: (1) the client computes the shard from the key (hash or range function replicated on the client) — fast, but the sharding function is now part of the client's code, and changing it requires a coordinated rollout; (2) a routing tier (a proxy or gateway) computes the shard and forwards the request — simpler clients, but the routing tier is now on the critical path and must be highly available; (3) a coordination service (ZooKeeper, etcd, or the database's own config) that clients query for the shard map, with the map cached locally. Most production systems use a combination: a routing tier for external clients, client-side routing with a cached map for internal clients, and a coordination service to keep the map fresh.

The most important design constraint is the shard key. A good shard key has high cardinality (many distinct values), low frequency (no value dominates the data), and aligns with the query patterns (the queries must include the shard key to avoid scatter-gather). A bad shard key produces hotspots (monotonic keys), jumbo chunks (low cardinality), or scatter-gather queries (queries that do not include the key). This is the same lesson as the MongoDB sharding card, expressed at the distributed-systems level — sharding is not a database feature, it is a data-modeling decision, and the key is the whole design.

The interview-quality answer names the three strategies (range, hash, directory), explains what each is good for (range scans, uniform writes, flexible placement), calls out the hotspot and scatter-gather failure modes, describes the request-routing approaches (client-computed, routing tier, coordination service), and insists on the shard key as the design lever. It also references consistent hashing as a refinement rather than restating it — because that card exists. That demonstrates you understand partitioning as a layered design, not as a database flag.
bullets: Partitioning (sharding) splits a dataset across machines; the two design questions are how to divide the data and how to route requests.
Range partitioning: contiguous key ranges — great for range scans and time-series, but hotspots on monotonic keys.
Hash partitioning: hash the key to pick the partition — great for uniform write distribution and equality lookups, but range queries become scatter-gather.
Directory-based partitioning: a lookup table maps keys to partitions — most flexible (tiering, data residency, rebalancing), but the directory must be highly available and consistent.
Geo/tag partitioning: partition by an attribute (region, tenant) — good for data residency and latency, at the cost of unbalanced growth.
Request routing options: client-computed (fast, but the shard function is in client code), routing tier (proxy/gateway, on the critical path), coordination service (ZooKeeper/etcd, cached locally).
The shard key is the whole design: high cardinality, low frequency, aligned with query patterns — otherwise hotspots, jumbo chunks, or scatter-gather.
Consistent hashing (covered in sys-hashing-1) is a refinement that reduces key movement on scale in/out from O(N) to ~1/N.

Range partitioning

  P1: id 1..1M       P2: id 1M+1..2M     P3: id 2M+1..3M
  range scan:  WHERE id BETWEEN 1500000 AND 1800000  -> P2 only
  hotspot:    INSERT id = next  -> always P3

Hash partitioning

  partition = hash(key) % N     (or consistent hashing ring)
  equality:   WHERE key = 'abc' -> one partition
  range scan: WHERE key > 'm'   -> hits every partition (scatter-gather)
  hotspot:    none if keys are uniformly distributed

Directory-based partitioning

  partition_map = {
    'user:1..1000'   -> P1,
    'user:1001..5000'-> P2,
    'tenant:euro'    -> P3,
    'tenant:us'      -> P4
  }
  request -> lookup in map -> route to partition
  flexibility: can move any range to any partition (tiering, residency)
  cost: map must be HA + consistent with actual placement

Geo partitioning

  region='EU' -> EU shard
  region='US' -> US shard

  two-level scheme for scale:
    level 1: region
    level 2: hash(userId) within region

Request routing approaches

  client-computed
    partition = hash(key) % N       (or murmur2, or range lookup)
    + fast, no extra hop
    - sharding logic is part of client code, coordinated rollout

  routing tier
    client -> router -> shard
    + simple clients, logic centralized
    - router is on the critical path, must be HA

  coordination service
    client -> ZK/etcd -> shard map (cached locally)
    + flexible, single source of truth
    - extra hop on first lookup, cache invalidation complexity

Shard key decision tree

  Q: does the workload need range scans on the key?
     YES -> range partitioning, but watch for monotonic hotspots
     NO  -> hash partitioning

  Q: does the workload need data residency or tiering?
     YES -> directory / geo partitioning

  Q: what do queries filter on?
     if queries must include the shard key to avoid scatter-gather
     -> pick a key that the application can always provide

  Q: how uniform is the natural key?
     skewed -> salt (append hash suffix) or use a compound key

cards.title: Consistency Models: Linearizable, Sequential, Causal, Eventual, and What Each Guarantees
cards.summary:
A consistency model is a contract between the distributed system and the client about what values reads will observe. It is not a performance metric and not a binary choice — it is a spectrum from strongest (linearizable) to weakest (eventual), with several useful intermediate models. Every interview about distributed systems eventually lands here, because the choice of consistency model determines what the system can and cannot guarantee, and therefore what the application must handle.

Linearizable (also called strict or atomic) consistency is the strongest model. It says that the system behaves as if there is a single copy of the data, and every operation appears to take effect atomically at some point between its invocation and its response. If client A writes X=1 and receives an acknowledgment, and client B reads X afterward, B must see X=1 (or a later value). No client ever sees a value that is older than one already acknowledged to another client. Linearizability is expensive: it requires coordination (consensus or a single leader) on every operation, and it is what CAP-theorem 'CP' systems promise during a partition (they refuse operations rather than violate linearizability). PostgreSQL with synchronous replication, etcd, ZooKeeper, and Google Spanner offer linearizable reads and writes.

Sequential consistency is slightly weaker. It says that operations appear to execute in some total order that is consistent with the order each client issued them, but that total order does not need to match real time across clients. Two clients can disagree about whether A's write or B's write happened first, as long as each client's own operations appear in the order they issued them. This is the model that multiprocessor memory often provides, and it is the model of systems that assign a global sequence number but do not require the sequence to respect wall-clock ordering. It is rarely what application developers actually want, because it does not guarantee real-time ordering.

Causal consistency is the strongest model that is still available in a partitioned system without coordination. It says that operations that are causally related (one happened-before another through the client's observation or through message passing) must be seen by all clients in that order, and operations that are concurrent (no causal relationship) may be seen in any order. This captures the intuitively important guarantees: you cannot see a reply before the message it replies to, you cannot see a delete before the insert that made the record exist, you cannot see an update before the read that produced it. Causal consistency gives read-your-writes, monotonic reads, and consistent prefix (from the replication lag card), all at once. It is achievable with vector clocks or dependency tracking, without the coordination cost of linearizability. CouchDB, MongoDB causal sessions, and Cassandra's lightweight transactions (via Paxos) with proper configuration approach it.

Eventual consistency is the weakest model. It says only that if no new writes occur, all replicas eventually converge to the same value. It says nothing about when, and nothing about what a client sees in the meantime. Eventual consistency is what you get from asynchronous replication with no ordering guarantees, and it is what most large-scale systems actually provide for non-critical data (social feeds, view counts, recommendations). It is not a defect — it is a deliberate choice to prioritize availability and latency over immediate agreement. The interview trap is to call it 'weak' dismissively; the correct answer acknowledges that it is the only model you can have at scale without coordination, and that most data does not need anything stronger.

The models form a hierarchy of guarantees, and each stronger level implies all weaker ones. Linearizable implies sequential, causal, and eventual. Sequential implies eventual (but does not necessarily imply causal in all formalizations). Causal implies eventual. The practical decision is: what does the application need to see? If the answer is 'the latest value, always,' you need linearizable and you will pay for it in latency and availability during partitions. If the answer is 'my own writes, and never going backwards,' causal consistency is enough and much cheaper. If the answer is 'eventually correct is fine for this data,' eventual consistency is the right choice and is the only one that scales without coordination. Naming the data per model — critical financial data needs linearizable, user-facing profile reads need causal, view counts and feeds can be eventual — is what separates a strong answer.

The interview-quality answer names the four models with the intuitive guarantee each provides (real-time single-copy for linearizable; total order per client for sequential; happens-before preserved for causal; eventual convergence for eventual), states the strictness hierarchy, ties each to a real system (Spanner/etcd for linearizable, MongoDB sessions for causal, Cassandra/Dynamo for eventual), and emphasizes that the choice is per-data not per-system. It also connects to CAP and PACELC — linearizable is what CP systems promise, eventual is what AP systems offer, and PACELC describes the latency-vs-consistency trade-off when there is no partition. That demonstrates you understand consistency as a design decision, not a label.
bullets: Consistency models form a hierarchy: linearizable ⊃ sequential ⊃ causal ⊃ eventual — stronger implies weaker.
Linearizable: behaves like a single copy of the data; every operation appears atomic and respects real time; requires coordination; offered by Spanner, etcd, ZooKeeper, PostgreSQL sync replication.
Sequential: a global total order consistent with each client's own operation order, but not necessarily with real time — rarely what applications want.

Causal: causally related operations are seen in order, concurrent ones may be seen in any order; gives read-your-writes, monotonic reads, and consistent prefix; achievable without coordination (vector clocks or dependency tracking).
Eventual: without new writes, replicas eventually converge — says nothing about timing or intermediate states; the only model that scales without coordination.
The choice is per-data, not per-system: financial data → linearizable; user-facing reads and session state → causal; view counts, feeds, recommendations → eventual.
CAP: linearizable is what 'CP' systems promise during partitions; eventual is what 'AP' systems offer. PACELC describes the latency-vs-consistency trade-off even without partitions.
cards.code:
Model guarantees (informal)

  Linearizable   "the system behaves like a single-copy register"
                 real-time ordering across clients

  Sequential     "some global order, consistent with each client's
                 own order"
                 total order across clients (but may not match real time)

  Causal         "causally related operations are seen in order"
                 concurrent operations may appear in any order

  Eventual       "replicas eventually converge"
                 no timing, no ordering, no intermediate guarantees

Hierarchy

  linearizable ⊃ sequential ⊃ causal ⊃ eventual

Per-client guarantees implied by causal

  read-your-writes    see your own writes or later
  monotonic reads     never go backwards in time
  consistent prefix   see writes in causal order

Practical mapping (data -> model)

  payments, ledger, inventory   -> linearizable
  user profile, session state   -> causal (read-your-writes + monotonic)
  feed, view count, recs        -> eventual
  auth tokens, rate limiter     -> linearizable or quorum

CAP connection

  CP systems (Spanner, etcd)   -> linearizable (refuse under partition)
  AP systems (Cassandra, Dynamo)-> eventual (serve under partition)

  PACELC: even with no partition (E), you still trade latency (L)
  vs consistency (C). Synchronous replication = strong but slow.
  Async replication = fast but eventual.

Anti-pattern

  "strong everywhere" -> pays coordination cost on reads that don't need it
  "eventual everywhere" -> user sees stale data after own writes
  -> the right answer is per-data, not per-system

cards.title: Clock Skew and Logical Clocks: Why Timestamps Lie and What Lamport and Vector Clocks Fix
cards.summary:
In a single machine, you can ask 'what time is it?' and get an answer that is consistent across all your threads. In a distributed system, every machine has its own physical clock, and those clocks disagree. Clock skew is the difference between two machines' clocks, and it is nonzero even with NTP (Network Time Protocol): NTP typically keeps machines within tens of milliseconds of each other, but under load, network congestion, or VM migration, the skew can grow to seconds. This matters because many distributed algorithms use timestamps to decide ordering — 'this write is newer, it wins' — and if the clocks disagree, the ordering is wrong. The most dangerous consequence is that two writes with the same logical time, one from a fast clock and one from a slow clock, can be resolved incorrectly, silently losing one of the writes.

A concrete example. Client A writes X=1 at t=100 on a server whose clock is 5 seconds fast (actual real time = 95). Client B writes X=2 at t=98 on a server whose clock is 1 second slow (actual real time = 99). Last-write-wins compares timestamps: 100 > 98, so A's write wins — but B's write actually happened later in real time. The system has discarded the more recent write. This is why last-write-wins (LWW) conflict resolution is dangerous for correctness-critical data: it assumes clocks are synchronized well enough that the latest timestamp really is the latest, and that assumption is often false.

Lamport clocks (also called logical clocks) solve the ordering problem without requiring synchronized physical clocks. They work as follows: each node maintains a counter. On any local event (a send, a receive, or a local action), the counter is incremented. When a node receives a message, it sets its counter to max(local, message_counter) + 1. This produces a total order of events that respects causality: if event A happens-before event B (through message passing or because A and B are on the same node), then the Lamport timestamp of A is less than the Lamport timestamp of B. The reverse is not guaranteed: A's timestamp < B's timestamp does not imply A happened-before B — they could be concurrent. Lamport clocks are used to establish a consistent total order in replicated state machines (each operation gets a Lamport timestamp, and the state machine applies operations in timestamp order), and in distributed systems like Cassandra, which uses a variant of Lamport clocks for conflict resolution in some contexts.

Vector clocks solve the concurrency-detection problem that Lamport clocks cannot. Each node maintains a vector of counters, one per node in the system. On a local event, the node increments its own counter. On receiving a message with a vector from another node, it increments its own counter and takes the pointwise maximum with the received vector. Now two events can be compared: event A happened-before event B if and only if A's vector is less than or equal to B's vector in every component and strictly less in at least one. If neither is less than the other, the events are concurrent — and the system knows it, instead of arbitrarily picking one. This is what allows systems like DynamoDB and Riak to detect conflicting writes and either surface them to the application or merge them (for CRDTs), rather than silently discarding one. The cost of vector clocks is size: a vector grows with the number of nodes, so in a large system the metadata can grow to become larger than the data. Production systems use bounded vector clocks (only track the most recent N nodes) or hash-based alternatives, at the cost of some precision.

Hybrid Logical Clocks (HLC) are the modern compromise, used by CockroachDB and others. HLC combines physical time with a logical counter: the timestamp is a pair (physical_time, logical_counter). When the system needs to order events, it uses the pair; if physical time has not moved forward, the logical counter increments to keep the ordering consistent with causality. This gives causal ordering (like Lamport clocks) while still approximating real time (like physical clocks), and it keeps the timestamp size constant. HLC is what allows CockroachDB to offer serializable transactions with a physical-time-based clock that is corrected for skew — it is the practical answer for systems that need both causal ordering and something that looks like wall-clock time.

Google's TrueTime is the extreme end of the spectrum: instead of trying to eliminate clock skew, TrueTime embraces it by exposing uncertainty intervals. Every timestamp is a range [earliest, latest], and the API guarantees that the true time is somewhere in the range. Spanner uses this to implement linearizability: it waits out the uncertainty interval before committing (the commit-wait step), so no later transaction can have a timestamp that is actually earlier. TrueTime requires specialized hardware (GPS receivers and atomic clocks in every datacenter), which is why Spanner's approach is not broadly reproducible. The interview-quality answer should mention TrueTime to show breadth but not recommend it as a general solution — the practical answer for most systems is HLC or logical clocks plus application-level tolerance.

The interview-quality answer distinguishes physical clock skew from logical ordering, explains why LWW is dangerous when clocks disagree, describes Lamport clocks (total order, respects causality, cannot detect concurrency) and vector clocks (detects concurrency, at the cost of metadata size), names HLC as the modern compromise and TrueTime as the specialized solution, and states the practical rule: for correctness-critical ordering, use logical clocks or HLC; for time-based TTLs and dashboards, physical clocks are fine. That demonstrates you understand the clock problem as an ordering problem, not just as a time-sync problem.
bullets: Clock skew is the difference between two machines' physical clocks — nonzero even with NTP, and seconds under load, network issues, or VM migration.
Last-write-wins with physical timestamps is dangerous: a fast-clock write can beat a genuinely later write, silently losing data.
Lamport clocks: a per-node counter incremented on every event, updated on receive via max + 1; produces a total order that respects causality but cannot distinguish concurrent events.
Vector clocks: a per-node vector of counters; can detect whether one event happened-before another, or whether they are concurrent — at the cost of metadata growing with node count.
Hybrid Logical Clocks (HLC) combine physical time with a logical counter; give causal ordering with bounded metadata; used by CockroachDB.
TrueTime (Spanner) exposes clock uncertainty intervals and waits them out to achieve linearizability, at the cost of specialized hardware (GPS + atomic clocks).
Rule of thumb: causal/ordering correctness → logical or hybrid clocks; TTLs, dashboards, analytics → physical clocks are fine.

Physical clocks are not a total order

  Server A (clock +5s)  write X=1 at t=100
  Server B (clock -1s)  write X=2 at t=98

  LWW: 100 > 98 -> A wins
  Reality: B was later -> B should have won
  -> write X=2 silently lost

Lamport clock

  Each node has counter c.
  local event:      c = c + 1
  send:             c = c + 1, send message with (c)
  receive (m):      c = max(c, m.c) + 1

  Guarantee: A happens-before B  =>  A.lamport < B.lamport
  Not:       A.lamport < B.lamport  =>  A happens-before B (could be concurrent)

  Use: total order of events for a replicated state machine
       (apply operations in Lamport order)

Vector clock

  Each node has a vector V[i] (one counter per node).
  local event:      V[i] = V[i] + 1
  receive (m, Vm):  V[j] = max(V[j], Vm[j]) for all j
                    V[i] = V[i] + 1

  compare(A, B):
    A happens-before B   if A <= B (all components) and A < B in at least one
    B happens-before A   symmetric
    otherwise             concurrent

  Use: detect conflicting writes (Dynamo, Riak)
       -> application merges or picks (not blindly LWW)

  Cost: vector size grows with nodes
        production systems bound it (track last N nodes)

Hybrid Logical Clock (HLC)

  timestamp = (physical_time, logical_counter)
  - if physical time advanced, logical resets to 0
  - otherwise logical increments
  - receive: keep physical max, bump logical to stay > any seen

  gives causal ordering + approximates wall clock
  bounded size (two numbers)
  used by CockroachDB

TrueTime (Spanner)

  API returns [earliest, latest] -- guaranteed true time is within
  - commit-wait: sleep until earliest > max seen timestamp
  - requires GPS + atomic clocks per datacenter
  - not reproducible on commodity infra

cards.title: Consensus: Raft, Paxos, Quorum, and Leader Election in Plain Terms
cards.summary:
Consensus is the problem of getting multiple machines to agree on a single value or a single sequence of values, even when some machines fail and the network is unreliable. It sounds simple, but it is the hardest problem in distributed systems, because you cannot trust anything: messages can be delayed, reordered, or lost; machines can pause (GC, VM migration) and wake up believing something false; clocks disagree; and there is no way to distinguish a slow node from a dead one. Consensus is the primitive that makes strong consistency possible — linearizable reads, leader election, distributed locks, atomic transactions across machines, and configuration changes all require consensus under the hood. If you understand consensus, the rest of distributed systems becomes architecture; if you do not, you are memorizing tools.

Paxos (Leslie Lamport, 1989) was the first practical consensus algorithm, and it is the theoretical foundation of nearly every system in production. The basic Paxos protocol works in two phases: a proposer asks a quorum of acceptors to promise not to accept any lower-numbered proposal (phase 1), then sends the actual value with that proposal number (phase 2). If a majority of acceptors agree, the value is chosen. Multi-Paxos extends this to a sequence of decisions (a replicated log), which is what real systems need. The problem with Paxos is that it is famously difficult to understand and even more difficult to implement correctly; Google's Chubby paper and Raft's authors both acknowledge that Paxos has been the source of decades of confusion, and many production systems that claim to use Paxos actually use variations or alternate algorithms.

Raft (Diego Ongaro and John Ousterhout, 2014) was designed explicitly as an understandable alternative to Paxos, and it has become the consensus algorithm of choice for most new systems. Raft decomposes consensus into three relatively independent subproblems: leader election, log replication, and safety. A Raft cluster has a leader and followers, and time is divided into terms (a monotonically increasing integer). Each term begins with an election: a follower whose election timeout expires becomes a candidate, increments the term, requests votes, and needs a majority to win. Once a leader is elected, it accepts client requests, appends them to its log, and replicates them to followers; a log entry is committed once a majority of nodes have it. If the leader crashes, a new election begins, and the node with the most up-to-date log is the only one that can win — this is the safety rule that prevents losing committed entries. Raft is what etcd, Consul, CockroachDB, TiKV, and many others use.

Quorum is the central mechanism of every consensus algorithm. A quorum is a majority of nodes: for N nodes, a quorum is floor(N/2) + 1. The rule is that any two quorums must overlap, which is what guarantees that a new leader can see all committed decisions (it talks to a majority, and any majority overlaps with the majority that committed the previous entry). This is also why consensus requires an odd number of nodes: with 3 nodes, you can tolerate 1 failure; with 5, you can tolerate 2; with 4, you can still only tolerate 1 (a majority of 4 is 3, so 2 failures leave 2 nodes, which is not a majority). The formula is that 2F + 1 nodes tolerate F failures. This is why production consensus clusters are always odd-sized and typically 3 or 5 nodes.

The trade-off is latency and availability during partitions. Consensus requires a majority to be reachable for every decision, so a network partition that splits the cluster into minority and majority sides leaves the minority unable to make progress — this is the correct behavior (the minority cannot commit new decisions), but it means the minority side is unavailable for consensus-dependent operations. Latency is also higher than non-consensus operations because a decision requires a round trip to a majority; this is why etcd and ZooKeeper are used for critical metadata, not for user-facing high-throughput data. The rule is: use consensus where correctness is essential (config, locks, leader election, critical metadata), and use other mechanisms (replication with quorum reads and writes, or eventual consistency) where throughput and latency matter more.

The interview-quality answer names the problem (agreement despite failures), explains Paxos as the theoretical foundation and Raft as the practical, understandable alternative, describes Raft's three parts (election, replication, safety), explains quorum and the 2F+1 rule, and states the trade-off (latency and unavailability on the minority side during partitions). It also names real systems (etcd, Consul, ZooKeeper/ZAB, Spanner) and ties consensus back to why strong consistency is expensive. That demonstrates you understand consensus as the foundation of distributed correctness, not as an algorithm to memorize.
bullets: Consensus is getting multiple nodes to agree on a value or sequence despite failures — the foundation of linearizability, leader election, distributed locks, and configuration management.
Paxos is the theoretical foundation but famously hard to implement; Raft was designed as an understandable alternative and is the algorithm in most new systems.
Raft decomposes into leader election, log replication, and safety; time is divided into terms; the node with the most up-to-date log wins an election.
Quorum is floor(N/2) + 1; any two quorums overlap, so a new leader always sees committed entries — this is why 2F + 1 nodes tolerate F failures.
Consensus clusters are odd-sized (3 or 5) because even sizes do not improve fault tolerance and just add latency.
The trade-off: a minority side of a partition cannot make progress — this is correct (no split-brain) but means consensus operations are unavailable to the minority.
Real systems: etcd and Consul (Raft), ZooKeeper (ZAB, Paxos-family), CockroachDB and TiKV (Raft), Spanner (Paxos variants with TrueTime).
cards.code:
Consensus requirements

  agreement:      all correct nodes decide the same value
  validity:       the decided value was proposed by some node
  termination:    all correct nodes eventually decide
  integrity:      a node decides at most once

Paxos (basic)

  Phase 1 (prepare):
    proposer -> acceptors: 'prepare(n)'
    acceptor responds: 'promise not to accept < n'

  Phase 2 (accept):
    proposer -> acceptors: 'accept(n, value)'
    majority accept -> value is chosen

Raft (simplified)

  States:  Follower  <->  Candidate  ->  Leader

  Term increments on every election.

  Election:
    follower's election timeout expires -> becomes candidate
    -> increment term, vote for self, request votes
    -> majority vote -> becomes leader

  Replication:
    client -> leader appends to log
    leader -> followers replicate
    committed when majority has the entry

  Safety:
    only the candidate with the most up-to-date log can win
    -> committed entries are never lost

Quorum math

  N=3: majority=2, tolerates 1 failure
  N=5: majority=3, tolerates 2 failures
  N=4: majority=3, tolerates 1 failure (same as N=3, worse latency)

  -> use odd sizes; 3 or 5 in production

Partition behavior

  Cluster: A, B, C, D, E
  Partition: [A, B]  vs  [C, D, E]

  [C, D, E] has majority (3 of 5) -> can elect leader, commit
  [A, B]   has minority (2 of 5) -> cannot commit, becomes unavailable

  -> correct: the minority cannot diverge from the majority

Real systems

  etcd, Consul            Raft
  ZooKeeper               ZAB (Paxos-family)
  CockroachDB, TiKV       Raft
  Spanner                 Paxos + TrueTime
  Kafka KRaft             Raft (metadata only)

cards.title: Distributed Locks: Redis, Redlock, ZooKeeper, and Why TTL Locks Are Not Correctness Tools
cards.summary:
A distributed lock provides mutual exclusion across processes and machines — only one client can hold the lock at a time, and other clients wait or fail. In a single JVM, synchronized and ReentrantLock do this for threads in one process. In a distributed system, the lock must be enforced by an external service that all clients consult, and that service itself must be correct despite failures. This is a deceptively hard problem, and the gap between 'mostly works' and 'correct' is where most production incidents live.

The simplest implementation is a Redis lock: SET key value NX PX timeout. The NX makes the SET succeed only if the key does not exist (atomic mutual exclusion), and the PX sets an expiration so the lock is released if the holder dies without releasing it. This works for many cases and is what most teams start with. The release requires care: you must only delete the lock if you are still the holder, which requires an atomic compare-and-delete — the standard implementation is a Lua script that checks the value before deleting. Without that check, a client whose lock already expired can delete a lock that another client has just acquired, breaking mutual exclusion.

Redlock is Redis's attempt to make the Redis lock more robust by using multiple independent Redis nodes. The client tries to acquire the lock on a majority of nodes (for example, 3 of 5) within a bounded time, and considers the lock acquired only if a majority succeeds. This was intended to survive the failure of a minority of Redis nodes. However, Redlock has been sharply criticized — most prominently by Martin Kleppmann — on the grounds that it is unsafe for correctness because it relies on timing assumptions that distributed systems cannot guarantee. The core argument: a client can hold the lock, pause (GC, VM migration, network stall) for longer than the TTL, wake up believing it still holds the lock, and proceed to modify shared state, while another client has legitimately acquired the lock. TTL-based locks cannot guarantee safety under arbitrary pauses, no matter how many Redis nodes you use.

The alternative is consensus-based locks in ZooKeeper or etcd. ZooKeeper's lock uses sequential ephemeral nodes: each client creates an ephemeral sequential node under a lock path, and the client with the lowest sequence number holds the lock; others watch the node just below theirs and acquire when it is deleted. If the client crashes, its session expires and the ephemeral node is deleted automatically — no TTL race, because the session lifecycle is managed by the consensus system. etcd's lock uses leases: a lease has a TTL, but the lease is kept alive by the client, and the lock is tied to the lease; a crashed client stops renewing, the lease expires, and the lock is released. Crucially, both ZooKeeper and etcd run on consensus (ZAB or Raft), so the lock service itself is linearizable — the lock state is consistent across nodes.

Even consensus-based locks have the pause problem, which is why production systems pair locks with fencing tokens (covered in the next card). A lock alone, no matter how correct the lock service, cannot prevent a paused client from acting on stale lock ownership. The resource being protected must reject operations from clients whose lock ownership is no longer current — typically by requiring a monotonically increasing token with every operation and rejecting any token lower than the highest it has seen. The lock guarantees 'at most one client tries to acquire'; the fencing token guarantees 'only the current owner can actually modify'.

The practical guidance is: use a Redis lock for performance optimization (avoiding duplicate work when two workers might run the same job) where a rare duplicate is acceptable. Use a ZooKeeper or etcd lock, plus fencing tokens, for correctness-critical mutual exclusion (leader election, exclusive resource access, critical section over shared state). Never rely on a plain TTL lock for anything where a double-execution would cause data corruption. The interview trap is to recommend Redlock as the answer to 'how do you do distributed locks?' — the strong answer acknowledges its limitations and points to consensus-based locks with fencing.

The interview-quality answer distinguishes performance locks (Redis, tolerate rare duplicates) from correctness locks (ZooKeeper/etcd, plus fencing), explains the TTL race and why Redlock does not solve it, describes the ZooKeeper sequential ephemeral node pattern and the etcd lease pattern, and insists on fencing tokens for correctness. That demonstrates you understand distributed locks as a hard problem, not as a Redis command.
bullets: A distributed lock provides mutual exclusion across processes; it requires an external service that all clients consult and that survives failures.
Redis SET key value NX PX: atomic acquire with TTL; release must use compare-and-delete (Lua script) to avoid deleting another client's lock.
Redlock (multi-node Redis) was designed for robustness but relies on timing assumptions; a paused client can wake up believing it holds the lock after TTL expiry, causing a double-execution.
ZooKeeper locks: sequential ephemeral nodes; lowest sequence number holds; session expiration cleans up a crashed client automatically.
etcd locks: leases with TTL, kept alive by the client; the lock is tied to the lease; session expiry releases the lock.
Consensus-based locks (ZK, etcd) are linearizable at the lock service — but they still cannot prevent a paused client from acting on stale ownership.
Fencing tokens close the pause gap: every lock acquisition gets a monotonic token, and the resource rejects any operation with a token lower than the highest it has seen.
Use Redis locks for performance (rare duplicates acceptable); use ZK/etcd + fencing for correctness (mutual exclusion that must not fail).
cards.code:
Redis lock (acquire)

  SET lock:resource:42 <client-id> NX PX 30000
  -- NX: succeed only if absent (mutual exclusion)
  -- PX: expire in 30s (crash safety)

Redis lock (release -- must be atomic)

  -- BROKEN: DEL if the lock expired and another client holds it
  DEL lock:resource:42

  -- CORRECT: compare-and-delete via Lua
  if redis.call('GET', KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then
    return redis.call('DEL', KEYS[1])
  else
    return 0
  end

Redlock (multi-node)

  1. get current time t0
  2. try SET NX PX on N independent Redis nodes (e.g. 5)
  3. success if majority (e.g. 3) acquired
     AND total time < TTL
  4. release: DEL on every node

  Critique (Kleppmann): a client can pause longer than TTL
  and wake up believing it holds the lock -> double execution.
  Multi-node does not fix the timing assumption.

ZooKeeper lock (sequential ephemeral nodes)

  /locks/myresource/lock-0000000001  <- holder
  /locks/myresource/lock-0000000002  <- waiting, watches 0001
  /locks/myresource/lock-0000000003  <- waiting, watches 0002

  acquire: create ephemeral sequential node, check if lowest
  release: delete node (or session expires -> auto-delete)
  -> no TTL race; ZK session lifecycle handles crashed clients

etcd lock (lease)

  lease = client.grantLease(ttl=30s)     -- auto-renewed
  client.put("/lock/42", value, lease)
  if etcd.compareAndSwap("/lock/42", ...)
    -> acquired
  release: etcd.delete("/lock/42", lease)
  crash -> lease not renewed -> expires -> lock released

Fencing token (required for correctness)

  acquire lock -> lock service returns monotonically increasing token
  every write to the resource carries the token
  resource remembers highest token seen
  reject any write whose token < highest seen

  -> even if client A pauses past TTL and wakes up, its
     stale token is rejected by the resource

Guidance

  Redis lock         performance (rare duplicate acceptable)
                     e.g. avoid duplicate cron runs

  ZK/etcd + fencing  correctness (must not double-execute)
                     e.g. leader election, exclusive resource

  plain TTL lock     NEVER for correctness

cards.title: Fencing Tokens and Split-Brain: Why a Paused Client Can Corrupt Your Data
cards.summary:
Split-brain is the condition where two nodes in a cluster both believe they are the leader (or both hold a lock) and both try to act as though they are authoritative. The classic scenario: a network partition splits a cluster into two halves, and each half elects a leader because each can reach a majority of its own side (in a two-node split, each side thinks it is half of the cluster). Both leaders accept writes, both produce divergent state, and when the partition heals, there is no way to reconcile without losing data. Split-brain is the failure mode that quorum-based systems exist to prevent — a leader can only be elected by a majority, and a majority exists on at most one side of a partition, so at most one leader can emerge. Quorum is the prevention; fencing tokens are the containment for when prevention fails.

The harder split-brain case is not a network partition but a pause. A client acquires a lock, starts an operation, and then pauses — for a garbage collection stop-the-world, a VM migration, or a long network stall. The lock has a TTL and expires while the client is paused. Another client acquires the lock and starts the same operation. Then the paused client wakes up, still believing it holds the lock, and proceeds to write — now two clients are writing to the same resource, one of them legitimately (the new lock holder) and one stale (the old holder). The stale client has no idea it has lost the lock because it never observed the expiry. No amount of correct locking prevents this, because the pause is not observable to the client.

Fencing tokens solve the pause case. The lock service assigns a monotonically increasing token to every lock acquisition — token 1 to the first client, token 2 to the second, token 3 to the third, and so on. Every write to the protected resource must carry the token. The resource (the storage system, the database, the file server) remembers the highest token it has ever seen and rejects any write whose token is lower than that. When the stale client wakes up and writes with token 1, the resource — which has already seen token 2 from the new lock holder — rejects token 1 as stale. The stale client's write is refused, and the correct client's write proceeds. The token turns a silent corruption into a visible error, which the client can retry (after reacquiring the lock) instead of silently double-executing.

Real systems use fencing tokens in many forms. HDFS NameNode High Availability uses a fencing mechanism when failing over from the active to the standby — the standby fences the old active (typically by killing it or revoking its access to the shared storage) before taking over, so the old active cannot continue writing. Kafka uses a leader epoch: every time a new partition leader is elected, the epoch increments, and followers and consumers reject data with an older epoch. Cassandra's lightweight transactions use Paxos with timestamps, which effectively serves as a monotonic ordering. Every consensus-based system has some form of monotonic sequence or epoch that plays the fencing role — the pattern is so fundamental that it is often assumed rather than named.

The implementation rules for fencing tokens: (1) the token must be monotonically increasing across all lock acquisitions, not per-client; (2) the resource must check the token on every write, not just on the first; (3) the check must be atomic with the write (a conditional update that fails if the token is stale); (4) the token must be part of the write request, not stored separately, so the check cannot be skipped; (5) the token must be durable — a resource restart that forgets the highest token can re-accept stale writes. These rules are why fencing is not just 'add a number to the request' — it changes the semantics of every write to the protected resource, and the resource must cooperate.

The interview-quality answer distinguishes split-brain from pause-induced staleness (partition vs GC/VM pause), explains why quorum prevents split-brain but cannot prevent pause, describes the fencing token mechanism (monotonic token + resource-side rejection of stale tokens), gives real examples (HDFS NameNode HA, Kafka leader epoch), and states the implementation rules (monotonic, checked on every write, atomic with the write, durable). That demonstrates you understand correctness as a layered problem — quorum, locks, and fencing together, not any one alone.
bullets: Split-brain: two nodes believe they are leader (or two clients believe they hold the lock) and both act authoritatively, producing divergent state.
Quorum prevents partition-induced split-brain — a leader needs a majority, and a majority exists on at most one side of a partition.

Pause-induced staleness is harder: a client can pause past its lock TTL, wake up, and write while another client legitimately holds the lock — no lock service can prevent this because the pause is not observable.
Fencing tokens close the pause gap: the lock service assigns a monotonically increasing token per acquisition, and the resource rejects any write whose token is lower than the highest it has seen.
Implementation rules: monotonic across all acquisitions, checked on every write, atomic with the write, durable across resource restarts.
Real examples: HDFS NameNode HA fencing, Kafka leader epoch, Cassandra lightweight transaction timestamps, etcd revisions.
Fencing turns silent corruption into a visible error — the stale client's write is rejected and it retries after reacquiring the lock.
cards.code:
Split-brain from partition (prevented by quorum)

  5-node cluster partitioned into [A, B] and [C, D, E]
  [C, D, E] has majority -> elects leader L1
  [A, B]    has minority -> cannot elect -> becomes unavailable

  Only one leader exists -> no split-brain

Split-brain from pause (NOT prevented by locks alone)

  t=0    Client 1 acquires lock (TTL=30s)
  t=1    Client 1 starts write, pauses (GC / VM migration)
  t=31   lock expires
  t=32   Client 2 acquires lock, starts write
  t=60   Client 1 wakes up, still believes it holds the lock
         writes stale data -> corruption

Fencing tokens (prevention via resource-side check)

  t=0   Client 1 acquires lock -> token=1
  t=1   Client 1 writes with token=1 -> resource accepts
  t=31  lock expires
  t=32  Client 2 acquires lock -> token=2
  t=33  Client 2 writes with token=2 -> resource records 2
  t=60  Client 1 wakes up, writes with token=1
        -> resource has seen 2, rejects 1 as stale

Resource-side check (atomic conditional write)

  UPDATE shared_state
     SET value = :new, last_token = :token
   WHERE last_token < :token

  -- zero rows updated -> stale token -> reject

Implementation rules

  1. monotonic token across all acquisitions (not per-client)
  2. checked on every write
  3. atomic with the write (conditional update)
  4. token in the request (not stored separately)
  5. durable (survives resource restart)

Real systems

  HDFS NameNode HA   standby fences old active before takeover
  Kafka              leader epoch increments on every election;
                     followers reject older epochs
  Cassandra          LWT timestamps act as monotonic ordering
  etcd               revisions are monotonic and checked
  ZooKeeper          zxid is monotonic; clients can check it

cards.title: CAP and PACELC in Depth: Precise Definitions, Common Misconceptions, and How to Actually Use Them
cards.summary:
The CAP theorem (Brewer 2000, proved by Gilbert and Lynch 2002) is the most cited and most misunderstood result in distributed systems. It says that a distributed data store cannot simultaneously guarantee Consistency, Availability, and Partition tolerance. The precise definitions matter: Consistency in CAP means linearizability (the system behaves as if there is one copy of the data, and every operation appears atomic and real-time ordered), Availability means that every request to a non-failing node returns a non-error response (it does not promise the response is the latest value — that is what consistency promises), and Partition tolerance means the system continues to operate despite arbitrary message loss between nodes. CAP applies only when a partition actually happens; without a partition, you can have both consistency and availability.

The most common misconception is that 'CA' is a real category — that is, systems that choose Consistency and Availability and somehow avoid Partition tolerance. This is wrong for any distributed system, because network partitions are not optional: they happen (cable cuts, switch failures, network congestion, VM pauses). The moment a system runs on more than one machine, partition tolerance is a requirement, not a choice. The real choice during a partition is CP (refuse operations on the minority side to preserve consistency) versus AP (serve operations on both sides and reconcile later, accepting inconsistency). Calling a system 'CA' is either describing a single-node system (which is not distributed and therefore not covered by CAP) or misunderstanding CAP.

The second misconception is that CAP is a binary choice — that a system is either CP or AP. In reality, consistency is a spectrum (linearizable, sequential, causal, eventual), and availability is also a spectrum (always available, available on the majority, available for reads but not writes). Most systems make different choices for different operations: MongoDB is CP for a majority-committed read and AP for a read with a lower read concern; Cassandra is tunable — per-operation consistency levels determine whether it behaves more like CP (QUORUM/ALL) or AP (ONE). The 'CP or AP' framing is a simplification that works in interviews but not in production design.

The third misconception is that CAP tells you which system to choose. It does not — CAP describes a trade-off during partitions, but most of the time there is no partition, and the trade-off that matters in the common case is latency versus consistency. This is what PACELC (Daniel Abadi, 2012) captures: if there is a Partition (P), choose Availability or Consistency (A or C); Else (E), choose Latency or Consistency (L or C). The 'Else' branch is the key insight: even with no partition, strong consistency requires coordination (synchronous replication, quorum reads), which adds latency; and low latency requires weaker consistency. PACELC makes the trade-off explicit in the normal case, which is where systems spend 99% of their time.

Real system classifications under PACELC make the taxonomy concrete. DynamoDB (and Cassandra in AP configuration) is PA/EL — available during partitions, low latency in the normal case, eventual consistency. Spanner (and CockroachDB in its default mode) is PC/EC — consistent during partitions (majority side), high latency in the normal case (commit-wait, cross-region coordination). MongoDB is PA/EC by default — available during partitions, consistent in the normal case (reads from the primary). Each choice is a business decision, not a technology quality: a banking ledger chooses PC/EC and accepts higher latency; a social feed chooses PA/EL and accepts eventual consistency.

The practical use of CAP and PACELC is to force the question 'what does this operation actually need?' For each piece of data and each operation, ask: can it tolerate a stale read (eventual consistency)? Can it tolerate being unavailable during a partition (CP)? Can it tolerate added latency for stronger consistency (EC)? The answer is per-operation, not per-system — a single application can have a linearizable ledger, a causally consistent profile store, and an eventually consistent analytics cache, all in the same system, each chosen for its data's actual requirements. The strongest interview answers treat CAP and PACELC as tools for asking that question, not as labels for picking a database.

The interview-quality answer distinguishes the precise CAP definitions (linearizability, non-error response, partition tolerance is mandatory), states that CA does not exist in distributed systems, explains that CP and AP are spectra rather than categories, introduces PACELC as the 'normal case' extension, gives real system classifications (DynamoDB PA/EL, Spanner PC/EC, MongoDB PA/EC), and insists that the choice is per-operation and driven by business requirements. That demonstrates you understand the theorem as a design tool, not as trivia.
bullets: CAP: Consistency = linearizability, Availability = every request to a non-failing node returns a non-error response (not necessarily the latest), Partition tolerance = the system continues under message loss.
CAP applies only during a partition; without a partition, both consistency and availability are achievable.
CA does not exist for distributed systems — partition tolerance is mandatory once you run on more than one machine.
CP vs AP are not binary categories: consistency and availability are spectra, and systems often make different choices per operation.
PACELC extends CAP: if Partition, choose Availability or Consistency; Else, choose Latency or Consistency — the normal-case trade-off that CAP omits.
Real classifications: DynamoDB PA/EL, Spanner PC/EC, MongoDB PA/EC, Cassandra tunable (between PA/EL and PC/EC per operation).
The choice is per-data and per-operation, driven by business requirements — a single application can have linearizable, causal, and eventual data at once.
cards.code:
CAP precise definitions

  Consistency (C)     linearizability: every operation appears atomic
                      and real-time ordered, as if one copy exists

  Availability (A)    every request to a NON-FAILING node returns
                      a non-error response (does NOT promise freshness)

  Partition (P)       arbitrary message loss between nodes

  CA is not a category for distributed systems
  -> P is mandatory; the choice is CP vs AP during partitions

Misconceptions

  1. 'CA exists'                -- no, P is mandatory if you are distributed
  2. 'CP or AP is binary'       -- consistency and availability are spectra
  3. 'CAP picks a database'     -- CAP describes partition behavior only
                                   (and there is often no partition)

PACELC

  If Partition:      Availability vs Consistency   (A or C)
  Else:              Latency vs Consistency        (L or C)

System classifications

  DynamoDB            PA/EL  available on partition, low latency,
                             eventual consistency

  Cassandra           PA/EL  by default; tunable per-op
                             (QUORUM/ALL pushes toward PC/EC)

  Spanner             PC/EC  consistent on partition (majority),
                             higher latency (commit-wait, cross-region)

  CockroachDB         PC/EC  by default; can trade latency for
                             consistency with follower reads

  MongoDB (default)   PA/EC  available on partition,
                             reads from primary -> consistent normal case

  Redis (single-node) not distributed -> not covered

Per-operation decision framework

  Q: can this operation tolerate stale reads?
     YES -> eventual consistency (PA/EL)
     NO  -> continue

  Q: can this operation be unavailable during a partition?
     YES -> CP is acceptable (refuse on minority)
     NO  -> AP is required (serve both sides, reconcile)

  Q: can this operation tolerate extra latency for consistency?
     YES -> synchronous replication / quorum reads (EC)
     NO  -> async replication, bounded staleness (EL)

Typical application

  payments, ledger          -> PC/EC (Spanner, CockroachDB, sync PostgreSQL)
  user profile, session     -> causal consistency (MongoDB sessions, CosmosDB)
  feed, view count, recs    -> PA/EL (DynamoDB, Cassandra ONE)
  config, locks, leader     -> PC/EC (etcd, ZooKeeper)

  one application, multiple consistency levels per data type

cards.title: Idempotency and Exactly-Once: Why Exactly-Once Is a Lie and Effectively-Once Is the Real Goal
cards.summary:
Exactly-once delivery is a phrase used by almost every messaging system, and it is almost always misleading. In a distributed system with unreliable networks and crash-prone nodes, exactly-once delivery in the literal sense — each message is delivered to the consumer exactly one time, never zero, never two — is impossible. The reason is fundamental: the sender cannot distinguish a message that was lost in transit from a message that was delivered but whose acknowledgment was lost. The classic thought experiment: the producer sends a message, the consumer processes it, the consumer's acknowledgment is lost, the producer's retry timer fires, and the producer sends the message again. The consumer has now processed it twice. No protocol can prevent this without infinite retries (which risk duplication) or an oracle that knows whether delivery happened (which does not exist).

What messaging systems actually provide is one of three delivery guarantees, and each is a trade-off. At-most-once: the message is sent once and never retried, so it may be lost but never duplicated. At-least-once: the message is retried until acknowledged, so it is never lost but may be duplicated. Exactly-once: a specific, narrow guarantee that the message is processed once within the scope of the messaging system itself (Kafka transactions, for example), but which does not extend across external systems. The honest framing is that exactly-once at the application level — the effect happens once and only once across all systems involved — is not a delivery guarantee. It is a guarantee you build by combining at-least-once delivery with idempotent processing. The industry term for this is effectively-once.

Idempotency is the property that performing an operation multiple times has the same effect as performing it once. It is the consumer's responsibility, not the messaging system's. There are several patterns, and the right one depends on the data and the operations. Naturally idempotent operations: setting a value to a specific state (UPDATE status = 'SHIPPED' WHERE id = 42) is idempotent regardless of how many times it runs. Non-idempotent operations that can be made idempotent: incrementing a counter can be made idempotent by storing the last-processed event ID and skipping duplicates; inserting a row can be made idempotent by using an INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING with a unique constraint on the idempotency key. The idempotency key must be stable across retries — a business key (orderId + eventType) or a UUID generated at the origin — and must not be derived from the delivery (topic-partition-offset changes across replays and cluster moves).

The standard implementation pattern is the deduplication table (often called an inbox table). In the same database transaction that applies the domain change, insert the idempotency key into a table with a unique constraint on that key. If the insert succeeds, the domain change is applied; if it fails with a duplicate-key error, the message has already been processed and the consumer returns success without applying the change again. This makes the domain effect and the dedup record atomic — either both happen or neither does. The table needs a TTL that covers the maximum redelivery window, which can be days if dead-letter queues are replayed, so the TTL should be generous (weeks or months, not minutes).

For operations that call external systems (payment providers, email services, third-party APIs), the local dedup table only protects the local database. The external call must also be idempotent — the standard pattern is to pass the same idempotency key to the external system, which returns the original result on retry instead of performing the operation again. Stripe accepts an Idempotency-Key header; the payment processor returns the original charge response when the same key is used twice. Email providers typically deduplicate by message-id. If the external system has no idempotency mechanism, the operation cannot be made fully idempotent and must be either made naturally idempotent (upsert instead of insert) or wrapped in a saga with a compensation. This is why 'exactly-once' is always scoped: exactly-once within Kafka, exactly-once within a single database, but effectively-once across the whole system requires design at every layer.

The interview-quality answer distinguishes delivery guarantees (at-most-once, at-least-once, and the narrow exactly-once of Kafka transactions) from processing guarantees (effectively-once via idempotency), explains why exactly-once delivery is impossible in the general case (the lost-acknowledgment problem), describes the idempotency patterns (naturally idempotent operations, unique constraints, dedup tables), insists on stable idempotency keys (business keys or origin-generated UUIDs, never topic-partition-offset), and covers external systems with their own idempotency keys. The strongest answers say clearly that 'exactly-once' is a marketing term when applied to end-to-end delivery, and that the real engineering discipline is at-least-once + idempotent consumers.
bullets: Exactly-once delivery in the literal sense is impossible in a distributed system — the lost-acknowledgment problem means the sender cannot distinguish a lost message from a lost ack.
Delivery guarantees: at-most-once (may lose, never duplicates), at-least-once (never loses, may duplicate), exactly-once (only within the messaging system, not across external systems).
Effectively-once = at-least-once delivery + idempotent processing — this is the real goal, and it is a design discipline, not a system setting.
Idempotency patterns: naturally idempotent operations (set-to-state), unique constraints with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, deduplication tables (inbox).
The idempotency key must be stable across retries (business key or origin UUID), never topic-partition-offset — offsets change across replays and cluster moves.
The dedup record must be written in the same transaction as the domain effect, or a crash between the two reopens the duplicate window.
External systems need their own idempotency keys (Stripe Idempotency-Key, email message-id); the local inbox only protects the local database.
The dedup table TTL must cover the maximum redelivery window, including DLQ replay, which can be days or weeks.
cards.code:
The lost-acknowledgment problem

  Producer          Broker          Consumer
  send(msg)   ->    store(msg)  ->  process(msg)
                                              |
                                              v
                                      ack lost in network
                    <-- retry timer fires
  send(msg)   ->    store(msg)  ->  process(msg)   <- DUPLICATE

  -> at-least-once; duplicates are the price of not losing

Delivery guarantees

  at-most-once    send once, no retry -> may lose, no duplicates
  at-least-once   send until acked    -> no loss, may duplicate
  exactly-once    only within the messaging system
                  (Kafka transactions, read_committed consumers)
                  does NOT extend to external databases/APIs

Idempotent consumer (inbox table)

  BEGIN;
    INSERT INTO inbox(event_id) VALUES (:eventId)
      ON CONFLICT (event_id) DO NOTHING;      -- 0 rows if duplicate

    if (rowsInserted == 1) {
        applyDomainChange(event);              -- only on first processing
    }
  COMMIT;
  consumer.commitSync();

Naturally idempotent operations

  UPDATE orders SET status = 'SHIPPED' WHERE id = 42;
  -- running this 1 or 100 times leaves the same state

Non-idempotent made idempotent

  -- BAD: running twice increments twice
  UPDATE counters SET value = value + 1 WHERE id = 42;

  -- GOOD: dedup guard before the increment
  INSERT INTO inbox(event_id) VALUES (:eventId) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING;
  if (rowsInserted == 1)
      UPDATE counters SET value = value + 1 WHERE id = 42;

External system (Stripe)

  stripeClient.charge(amount, RequestOptions.builder()
      .setIdempotencyKey(eventId)       -- origin-generated UUID
      .build());
  -- retry with the same key -> returns the original charge, no duplicate

Bad idempotency keys

  topic + partition + offset   -- changes across replays, cluster moves
  timestamp                    -- not unique, not stable
  random on each attempt       -- every retry looks like a new event

Good idempotency keys

  origin-generated eventId (UUID v4)  -- stable across retries
  business key (orderId + operation)  -- stable, semantic

The three layers of effectively-once

  1. delivery      at-least-once (broker retries)
  2. local effect  inbox / unique constraint (dedup)
  3. external call provider idempotency key (dedup at the third party)

cards.title: Multi-Region Architecture: Active-Active vs Active-Passive, RTO/RPO, and Conflict Resolution
cards.summary:
A multi-region architecture runs a system in more than one geographic region (US-East, EU-West, AP-South) to achieve one or more of: disaster recovery (survive the loss of a region), latency (serve users from a nearby region), or regulatory compliance (data residency). The choice between active-passive and active-active, and the RTO/RPO targets that drive it, is one of the most consequential architecture decisions a team makes, and interviewers test it because it exposes whether a candidate can balance availability, latency, cost, and correctness.

RTO (Recovery Time Objective) is the maximum acceptable time to restore service after a failure — how long the system can be down. RPO (Recovery Point Objective) is the maximum acceptable data loss measured in time — how much recent data can be lost. These are business decisions, not technical ones, and they drive the entire architecture. An RTO of 4 hours and an RPO of 15 minutes (typical for non-critical internal services) permit a passive-standby region with periodic backups. An RTO of 5 minutes and an RPO of near-zero (typical for payments, health, or auth) require a hot standby or active-active, with synchronous or near-synchronous replication. Confusing RTO and RPO is a common interview mistake — RTO is about time to restore, RPO is about data loss, and they have different architectural implications.

Active-passive (also called warm standby or pilot light) keeps a full deployment in a second region, but traffic goes only to the primary region. Data is replicated from primary to secondary (synchronous for low RPO, asynchronous for lower latency and higher throughput). During normal operation, the secondary serves no traffic — it exists to take over if the primary fails. The failover can be manual (an operator triggers it after confirming the primary is dead) or automated (a health checker triggers it after a threshold). The advantages are simplicity, cost (the secondary can be smaller), and no write conflicts (all writes go to the primary). The disadvantages are failover time (minutes to tens of minutes for DNS, database promotion, and cache warmup), capacity during failover (the secondary must be sized for the full load, or the system degrades), and the risk of split-brain if the primary is alive but unreachable and both regions try to be primary.

Active-active runs deployments in both regions and sends traffic to both, with each region serving a slice of users (sharded by geography or by user hash) or both regions serving all users (with cross-region replication of all data). The advantages are lower latency (each user talks to a nearby region), zero-downtime failover (if one region dies, the other absorbs the load, sometimes with a temporary capacity shortfall), and continuous availability during regional failures. The disadvantages are significant. Data becomes a multi-region consistency problem: if both regions accept writes to the same data, conflicts occur and must be resolved (covered in the replication models card — LWW, CRDTs, merge functions).
