Replication between regions adds latency to writes (synchronous cross-region replication is slow) or accepts staleness (asynchronous replication). Capacity planning is harder — each region must be sized for the share of load it handles plus a failover surge. Cost is roughly double because both regions run at full capacity.

The choice between active-passive and active-active follows from the RTO/RPO and the workload. Active-passive is the right default for most systems — it is simpler, cheaper, and covers the disaster-recovery requirement (loss of a region). Active-active is justified when the RTO requirement is very low (sub-minute), the workload needs geographic latency reduction, or the business cannot tolerate any regional downtime. For a payment system, active-active with a strongly consistent primary region per shard is common (each shard has a primary region, and users are routed to their shard's primary for writes); for a social feed, active-active with eventual consistency and conflict resolution is common. For an internal admin tool, active-passive with an hours-long RTO is entirely appropriate.

Conflict resolution is the hard problem of active-active, and it deserves explicit treatment. The options are: last-write-wins (simple but loses one of the conflicting writes and depends on clock sync), custom merge (the application defines a merge function — for example, taking the maximum of two numbers or merging two address objects field by field), conflict-free replicated data types (CRDTs — data structures like counters, sets, and sequences that are mathematically designed to merge without loss), and partition-by-key (route all writes for a key to one region so conflicts cannot occur — effectively sharded active-active). Partition-by-key is the pragmatic answer for most systems: it gives you active-active availability (each region can serve its own shard even when the other is down) without write-write conflicts, at the cost of a routing layer that maps users to their home region. The interview trap is to propose active-active without naming the conflict problem — the strong answer always includes how conflicts are prevented or resolved.

The interview-quality answer defines RTO and RPO precisely, distinguishes active-passive (simpler, cheaper, failover time) from active-active (lower latency, zero-downtime failover, but multi-region consistency and conflict resolution), ties the choice to RTO/RPO and workload requirements, and insists on naming conflict resolution for active-active (LWW, CRDTs, merge functions, partition-by-key). That demonstrates you understand multi-region as a trade-off space, not as a checkbox.
bullets: RTO = max acceptable time to restore service; RPO = max acceptable data loss in time; both are business decisions that drive the architecture.
Active-passive (warm standby): full deployment in a second region, traffic only to the primary; simple and cheaper, but failover takes minutes and requires the secondary to absorb full load.
Active-active: both regions serve traffic; lower latency and near-zero failover, but multi-region consistency and conflict resolution become mandatory.
Active-active conflict resolution: LWW (simple, lossy), custom merge functions, CRDTs (mathematically safe, complex), or partition-by-key (route per-key writes to one region — pragmatic default).
Partition-by-key is the common production pattern: active-active availability without write-write conflicts, at the cost of a routing layer.
Cross-region replication is synchronous (low RPO, high latency) or asynchronous (low latency, bounded staleness); the choice follows from the RPO.
The choice follows RTO/RPO: payments and auth need near-zero RPO/RTO (active-active or hot standby); internal tools can tolerate hours (active-passive with backups).
cards.code:
RTO / RPO

  RTO = max acceptable downtime (time to restore)
  RPO = max acceptable data loss (time window)

  Example targets:
    internal admin tool   RTO=4h   RPO=15m   -> active-passive + backups
    e-commerce catalog    RTO=30m  RPO=5m    -> warm standby
    payments, auth        RTO=1m   RPO=0     -> active-active or hot standby

Active-passive (warm standby)

  Users -> [ Region A: primary ]  --async/sync repl-->  [ Region B: standby ]

  - traffic only to A
  - B sized for full load (or degraded)
  - failover: DNS cutover + DB promote + cache warmup
  - failover time: minutes to tens of minutes

Active-active

  Users -> [ Region A ]  <--replication-->  [ Region B ]
  (users sharded by geography, or all regions serve all users)

  - both serve traffic -> lower latency, zero downtime on regional failure
  - multi-region write conflicts -> must resolve
  - cost roughly doubles

Active-active conflict resolution

  LWW (last-write-wins)
    - simple
    - loses one write, depends on clock sync
    - safe only for low-value data (view counts)

  Custom merge
    - application-defined (max of two numbers, field-wise merge)
    - needs a rule for every field

  CRDT (conflict-free replicated data types)
    - G-Counter, PN-Counter, OR-Set, LWW-Register, RGA (sequence)
    - mathematically merge without loss
    - complex to model and implement

  Partition-by-key (pragmatic default)
    - all writes for a key go to one home region
    - no write-write conflicts
    - routing layer maps user -> home region
    - failover: promote the secondary for that shard

Replication across regions

  synchronous     RPO ~ 0, latency includes round trip to remote region
  asynchronous    low write latency, bounded staleness (RPO > 0)

  typical: async replication + partition-by-key for active-active
           sync replication inside a region for strong local consistency

cards.title: Failure Detectors and Gossip Protocols: How Nodes Learn Who Is Alive Without a Central Authority
cards.summary:
In a distributed system, there is no oracle that tells you which nodes are alive and which are dead. A node can be slow (GC, VM migration, network congestion) or actually dead, and from the perspective of another node, the two are indistinguishable — both look like a timeout. This is the fundamental problem of failure detection: you cannot distinguish a slow node from a dead one, so you either wait longer (detecting failures slowly) or detect faster (and accept false positives). Every failure detector makes this trade-off, and understanding it is what interviewers are probing when they ask about gossip, heartbeats, and cluster membership.

The simplest failure detector is the heartbeat: each node periodically sends a ping to every other node, and if a node misses N heartbeats within a timeout, it is declared failed. This is simple but has two problems. First, it scales poorly — O(N²) messages for N nodes, because every node pings every other node. Second, the timeout is a fixed threshold, so it cannot adapt to varying network conditions: too short and you get false positives under load, too long and you detect real failures slowly. Fixed heartbeats are used by small clusters (Redis Sentinel, etcd with a few nodes) but do not scale to hundreds or thousands of nodes.

SWIM (Scalable Weakly-consistent Infection-style Membership, used by HashiCorp Consul and Cassandra) is the standard protocol for scalable membership. It combines two ideas. First, instead of every node pinging every other node, each node periodically picks a random subset of peers and pings them — this reduces message load to O(N log N) or even O(N) depending on the parameters. Second, when a node needs to ping a peer, it does so indirectly through k other nodes; if the direct ping times out but the indirect pings succeed, the peer is alive (the direct link may be congested) — this reduces false positives without increasing timeouts. When a node is declared suspect (not confirmed dead), the suspicion is broadcast to other nodes, which ping the suspect directly before agreeing to mark it dead. This 'suspect → confirm → dead' flow is what makes SWIM robust under transient network issues.

Gossip protocols (epidemic protocols) are how the membership information propagates across a large cluster without a central coordinator. The model is biological: each node periodically selects a random peer and exchanges state — the full membership list, versions, or a delta. Over time, information spreads exponentially, like an epidemic, reaching every node in O(log N) rounds. Gossip is eventually consistent by design: two nodes may temporarily disagree about whether a peer is alive, but they converge. The cost is that there is no authoritative answer at any instant — the cluster has a probabilistic view of membership, not a guaranteed one.

The combination of SWIM (for efficient failure detection) and gossip (for propagating the resulting membership changes) is what makes large clusters practical. Cassandra uses a variant of SWIM plus gossip to maintain cluster membership and share metadata (schema versions, token ownership, node states). Consul uses SWIM (via the Serf library) to maintain the gossip pool and detect failures. Akka Cluster uses a similar approach for its membership protocol. The interview point is that these systems do not rely on a central coordinator (which would be a single point of failure) and do not use O(N²) heartbeats (which do not scale) — they use randomized protocols with probabilistic guarantees, and they accept that the membership view is eventually consistent.

Phi accrual failure detectors are a related concept worth naming. Instead of a binary alive/dead decision, a phi accrual detector computes a continuous suspicion level (φ) based on the observed distribution of heartbeat intervals. Applications set a threshold: if φ exceeds it, the node is treated as suspect. Higher φ means more suspicious. This lets applications make the alive/dead decision at the point where it matters (for example, a load balancer might tolerate higher φ before marking a node down than a database replica would). Cassandra uses phi accrual as part of its failure detection. The value is that it decouples the detection mechanism (the observed timing distribution) from the decision threshold (application-specific), which is more flexible than a fixed timeout.

The trade-off that runs through all of these protocols is sensitivity vs stability. A sensitive detector (short timeout) catches real failures quickly but produces false positives under transient slowness, causing unnecessary failovers, rebalances, and cascading load shifts. A stable detector (long timeout) avoids false positives but detects real failures slowly, prolonging the outage. The right balance depends on the cost of a false positive (a failover is expensive) vs the cost of a slow detection (downtime is expensive). The interview-quality answer names the problem (slow vs dead are indistinguishable), describes heartbeats and their O(N²) scaling issue, explains SWIM (random peer selection, indirect probes, suspect-then-confirm), explains gossip for propagation, mentions phi accrual for adaptive thresholds, and states the sensitivity-vs-stability trade-off. That demonstrates you understand cluster membership as a probabilistic problem, not a solved one.
bullets: Slow and dead are indistinguishable from the outside — every failure detector trades detection speed against false positives.
Naive heartbeats are O(N²) messages and use fixed timeouts that cannot adapt to network conditions — fine for small clusters, not for large ones.
SWIM (Consul, Cassandra): random peer selection (O(N log N) or less), indirect probes through k peers to reduce false positives, suspect-then-confirm flow before declaring a node dead.
Gossip protocols propagate membership information by having each node periodically exchange state with a random peer — spreads in O(log N) rounds, eventually consistent.
SWIM + gossip is the standard scalable membership stack — no central coordinator, no O(N²) heartbeats, probabilistic guarantees.
Phi accrual failure detectors compute a continuous suspicion level from observed heartbeat intervals; applications choose the threshold, decoupling detection from decision.
The trade-off is sensitivity (fast detection, false positives under load) vs stability (fewer false positives, slow detection of real failures).
cards.code:
Naive heartbeats

  Every node pings every other node every T seconds.
  N=100 nodes -> 100 * 99 = 9,900 pings per interval (O(N^2))
  fixed timeout -> cannot adapt to network conditions

SWIM protocol (simplified)

  Each node periodically:
    1. pick a random peer P
    2. direct ping P
    3. if no ack in timeout, ask k other nodes to ping P indirectly
    4. if indirect pings fail too, mark P as SUSPECT (not dead)
    5. gossip SUSPECT(P, inc=1)
    6. if P is still SUSPECT after timeout, mark DEAD and gossip DEAD
    7. if P acks at any point, mark ALIVE and gossip ALIVE

  message complexity: O(N log N) or less
  false positives: reduced by indirect probes

Gossip propagation

  Node A knows: membership = {A, B, C, D, E}
  Node A picks random peer (say C) and exchanges state
  C merges the new state (version-based)
  Next round, C gossips to D, D to A, ...
  -> converges in O(log N) rounds

  eventually consistent: two nodes may temporarily disagree

Phi accrual failure detector

  Collect heartbeat intervals -> estimate distribution
  phi(t) = -log10( P(later than t since last heartbeat) )

  phi = 1   ~ 10% suspicion
  phi = 8   ~ very high suspicion
  phi = 12+ ~ almost certainly dead

  Application chooses threshold:
    load balancer    high threshold (tolerate slow nodes)
    database replica low threshold (failover sooner)

Cassandra's combination

  - SWIM variant for failure detection
  - phi accrual for suspicion level
  - gossip for membership, schema version, token ownership, node state
  - no central coordinator

Trade-off

  sensitivity  high -> fast detection, false positives, failover churn
  stability    high -> fewer false positives, slow detection, longer outage

  choose based on the cost of failover vs the cost of downtime

cards.title: Java Memory Model and happens-before: Why Your Threads See Stale Values
cards.summary:
The Java Memory Model (JMM) is a specification that defines what values a thread is allowed to observe when it reads a variable written by another thread. It exists because modern CPUs and JIT compilers aggressively reorder and cache memory accesses for performance. Without a memory model, a program could behave differently on different hardware, and no one could reason about concurrent code. The JMM says: absent a happens-before relationship between a write and a read, the read may observe the write, may not, and may observe a value that never existed in source code (a torn read or a reordered result). This is the single most important concept in Java concurrency, and it is the reason volatile, synchronized, and every concurrency utility exists.

The happens-before relationship is the JMM's ordering rule. If action A happens-before action B, then every memory write that A performed is guaranteed to be visible to B, and A appears to execute before B in a single-threaded view. The JMM defines several rules that create happens-before edges. Program order: within a single thread, each action happens-before every later action in that thread (a thread always sees its own writes). Monitor lock: a release of a monitor (leaving a synchronized block) happens-before every subsequent acquisition of the same monitor. Volatile: a write to a volatile field happens-before every subsequent read of that same field. Thread start: thread.start() happens-before every action in the started thread. Thread join: every action in a thread happens-before thread.join() returns. Transitivity: if A happens-before B and B happens-before C, then A happens-before C. Final field semantics (JMM guarantee for final fields): correct construction of an object publishes its final fields safely to any thread that observes the reference. Interruption and concurrent collection semantics add further edges. These rules are the vocabulary you need for every concurrency reasoning task.

A concrete example shows why happens-before matters. Thread A writes x = 1 and flag = true (in that order, non-volatile). Thread B reads flag and, if it is true, reads x. On some hardware and JIT configurations, B could observe flag = true but x = 0, because the writes were reordered or because the cache was not flushed. If flag is volatile, then A's write to flag happens-before B's read of flag, which happens-before B's read of x, so B is guaranteed to see x = 1. If both are accessed inside synchronized blocks on the same monitor, the monitor release/acquire creates the same edge. Without either, there is no guarantee, and the program is buggy even if it works on your laptop.

Atomicity is separate from visibility and ordering. The JMM guarantees that reads and writes of 32-bit primitives (int, float) and references are atomic, but reads and writes of 64-bit primitives (long, double) were historically allowed to be torn (split into two 32-bit halves) unless the field is volatile. In modern Java on 64-bit JVMs, long and double are atomic in practice, but the JLS still requires volatile or AtomicLong for the guarantee. Compound operations (count++) are never atomic regardless of field size — they are read-modify-write sequences that require synchronization or atomics. The interview trap is to say 'int is atomic, so count++ is safe' — it is not, because atomicity of the read and the write does not make the read-add-write a single atomic step.

The most important practical rule is: whenever two threads access a shared mutable field, and at least one of them writes, there must be a happens-before edge between the write and every subsequent read. This is established by volatile, synchronized, atomic classes, or the higher-level utilities (locks, concurrent collections, executors, futures). If you cannot name the happens-before edge for a piece of shared state, the code is racy — even if it passes tests. This is why the JMM is often described as a contract for how to write correct concurrent code: it tells you exactly which synchronization primitives create which guarantees, and anything else is undefined behavior.

The interview-quality answer names the JMM as a specification, explains happens-before with the volatile and synchronized examples, distinguishes visibility from atomicity (count++ is not atomic even with volatile int), lists the main happens-before rules (program order, monitor, volatile, start, join, transitivity, final fields), and states the practical rule: for every shared mutable field, name the happens-before edge or assume the code is broken. That demonstrates you can reason about concurrency from first principles, not from folklore.
bullets: The Java Memory Model defines what values a thread may observe from another thread's writes — absent a happens-before edge, the read may see anything, including a value that never existed in source.
Happens-before rules: program order (within a thread), monitor release/acquire, volatile write/read, thread start, thread join, transitivity, and final-field publication.
Volatile and synchronized both create happens-before edges: a volatile write happens-before a subsequent volatile read of the same field; releasing a monitor happens-before acquiring it.
Atomicity is separate from visibility: int and reference reads/writes are atomic; long and double are only guaranteed atomic if volatile or via AtomicLong/AtomicDouble.
Compound operations (count++) are never atomic, even on volatile ints — they are read-modify-write sequences that need synchronization or atomics.
The practical rule: for every shared mutable field with at least one writer, name the happens-before edge — otherwise the code is racy regardless of tests.
The JMM is why concurrency bugs are hardware- and JIT-dependent — code that works on your laptop can fail in production.

cards.title: Locks in Java: ReentrantLock, ReadWriteLock, and StampedLock
cards.summary:
synchronized is the original Java locking primitive: it is simple, reentrant, and automatic (the lock is released even when an exception is thrown). But it has real limitations: the lock is not interruptible once a thread is waiting on it, there is no way to try to acquire it without blocking, there is no fairness option, and there is no way to have more than one condition variable per lock. ReentrantLock was introduced in Java 5 to address all of these, and it is the right tool when you need any of its features. When you do not need them, synchronized is still simpler and often faster under high contention because of JVM-level optimizations (biased locking in older JVMs, escape analysis, and the fact that the JIT understands synchronized deeply).

ReentrantLock is a mutual-exclusion lock with the same reentrancy as synchronized: the thread holding the lock can acquire it again without deadlocking, and it must release it the same number of times. Its extra capabilities are: tryLock() (non-blocking acquisition, returns true/false immediately), tryLock(timeout, unit) (bounded wait), lockInterruptibly() (acquisition can be interrupted by Thread.interrupt), fairness (a fair ReentrantLock gives the lock to the longest-waiting thread in FIFO order, preventing starvation at the cost of throughput), and multiple Condition variables (each Condition is a separate wait/notify queue, allowing producer/consumer patterns to notify only the relevant waiters). The critical discipline with ReentrantLock is that the release must be in a finally block — unlike synchronized, a thrown exception will not release the lock automatically, and the thread will hold it forever, deadlocking the rest of the system.

ReadWriteLock (with ReentrantReadWriteLock as the standard implementation) allows many readers to hold the lock simultaneously, while a writer gets exclusive access. The rule is: multiple readers OR one writer, never both. This is a huge win for read-heavy workloads where the shared data changes rarely (a configuration cache, an in-memory index, a routing table) — instead of serializing every read, the lock lets reads proceed in parallel and only blocks for writes. The implementation supports reentrancy, a fairness option, and lock downgrading (acquire write lock, then acquire read lock, then release write lock — you still hold the read lock). It does NOT support lock upgrading: you cannot acquire a read lock and then acquire a write lock in the same thread, because two readers each trying to upgrade would deadlock. The other important detail is that a fair ReadWriteLock is much slower than an unfair one, and unfair is the default. Write starvation is possible under unfair mode if reads constantly outnumber writes, which is why some applications prefer StampedLock or a plain ReentrantLock when reads are extremely fast.

StampedLock (Java 8+) is a further refinement with three modes: write lock (exclusive), read lock (shared), and optimistic read (no lock at all). The optimistic read works by returning a version stamp; the reader reads the data without locking, then validates the stamp at the end. If the stamp is unchanged, the read is consistent; if it changed (a writer intervened), the reader falls back to a read lock and re-reads. This is called optimistic concurrency, and it is dramatically faster for read-mostly workloads because it avoids the cost of acquiring the lock in the common case. The critical constraint is that optimistic reads are only safe if the data they read is immutable once published or if validation detects every mutation — reading multiple fields without a lock is fine only if they are all validated by the stamp. StampedLock is not reentrant (a thread that holds a write lock cannot re-acquire it — it will deadlock), and its lock objects must never be used as fields of a shared data structure without care. It is the right tool when profiling shows ReadWriteLock is the bottleneck and reads dominate writes; otherwise ReadWriteLock is simpler.

The decision between them: use synchronized for simple cases with low contention (it is simplest and cannot leak a lock via a missed finally). Use ReentrantLock when you need tryLock, lockInterruptibly, fairness, or multiple Conditions. Use ReadWriteLock when reads dominate writes and the read path is fast enough that the extra lock overhead is worth it. Use StampedLock when reads dominate writes and profiling shows the read lock is the bottleneck — StampedLock is the fastest under these conditions but has the most restrictive rules. Never default to the more complex tool: the right question is not which is fastest in a microbenchmark but which is correct for the workload and simple enough to get right.

A separate but related concern is deadlock avoidance. Lock ordering is the standard technique: establish a global ordering for all locks and always acquire them in that order. If two threads each need A and B, both acquire A first then B — no cycle, no deadlock. The alternative is tryLock with a timeout: acquire A, try to acquire B with a timeout, and if it fails, release A and retry. This is harder to reason about but works when lock ordering is impractical. Detecting deadlock in production is done with jstack (which shows 'Found one Java-level deadlock' with the threads, the locks, and the wait chains) or with JMX's ThreadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads(). Prevention is always better than detection, and lock ordering is the single most effective prevention.

The interview-quality answer names ReentrantLock's advantages over synchronized (tryLock, interruptible, fair, multiple conditions), describes ReadWriteLock's concurrent readers / exclusive writer model and its upgrade limitation, explains StampedLock's optimistic reads and validation stamp, gives the selection criteria (simplicity vs features vs read-heavy performance), and insists on lock ordering for deadlock avoidance. That demonstrates you can reason about concurrency tools, not just use them.
bullets: synchronized: simplest, reentrant, auto-released on exception; lacks tryLock, interruptibility, fairness, and multiple conditions.
ReentrantLock: adds tryLock / tryLock(timeout) / lockInterruptibly / fairness / multiple Conditions; requires release in a finally block or the lock leaks forever.

ReadWriteLock: many readers OR one writer; great for read-heavy, rarely-written data; no lock upgrade (reader -> writer deadlocks), supports lock downgrade (writer -> reader); fair mode is much slower.

StampedLock: write, read, and optimistic read; optimistic reads validate a stamp and fall back to a read lock if the stamp changed; not reentrant; fastest for read-mostly workloads where profiling shows the read lock is the bottleneck.
Selection: synchronized for simple low-contention; ReentrantLock for its extra features; ReadWriteLock for read-heavy data; StampedLock for profiling-driven read-mostly optimization.
Deadlock avoidance: establish a global lock ordering and always acquire in that order; tryLock-with-timeout is the fallback when ordering is impractical.
Diagnose deadlocks with jstack ('Found one Java-level deadlock') or ThreadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads().

cards.title: Atomics and CAS: AtomicInteger, LongAdder, the ABA Problem, and False Sharing
cards.summary:
Atomic classes (java.util.concurrent.atomic) provide lock-free, thread-safe operations on single variables by relying on the CPU's compare-and-swap (CAS) instruction. CAS is a hardware primitive that takes three values — a memory location, an expected value, and a new value — and atomically performs: if the current value at the location equals the expected value, replace it with the new value and return true; otherwise return false. The whole operation is a single instruction (CMPXCHG on x86), so no lock is needed, and the operation is both atomic and visible. Every atomic class and every lock-free data structure in the JDK is built on CAS.

AtomicInteger (and AtomicLong, AtomicBoolean, AtomicReference) provides methods like get(), set(), incrementAndGet(), getAndIncrement(), compareAndSet(expected, new), and updateAndGet(function). Under the hood, each is a small loop: read the current value, compute the new value, try CAS; if CAS fails, re-read and retry. This is called the CAS loop, and it is the reason atomics are fast under low contention (one successful CAS) but can spin under high contention (many threads repeatedly failing CAS and retrying). The updateAndGet method takes a lambda and applies it inside the CAS loop; since Java 8, the lambda is applied multiple times if CAS fails, so the lambda must be side-effect-free and idempotent. This is a subtle trap — a side-effecting lambda (logging, incrementing another counter) will produce wrong results because it runs on every retry.

LongAdder and LongAccumulator (Java 8) are alternatives to AtomicLong designed for high write contention. The problem with AtomicLong is that all threads CAS the same memory location, so under high contention the CAS loop spins heavily, and the cache line containing the value bounces between cores. LongAdder fixes this by internally maintaining an array of cells (one per core, roughly), where each thread updates its own cell (striped counting). When a reader calls sum(), it adds up all the cells. Writes scale linearly with the number of cores because threads do not contend on the same location. The trade-off is that sum() is not a moment-in-time snapshot — it is a fuzzy value that may include updates from other threads that happened after the call started. For metrics and counters where approximate values are acceptable, LongAdder is dramatically faster than AtomicLong under load. For a counter where exact ordering matters (a sequence number), AtomicLong is the right choice.

The ABA problem is a subtle hazard of CAS that catches even experienced developers. It happens when a value changes from A to B to A between a thread's read and its CAS. The CAS sees A, thinks nothing changed, and succeeds — but the state has actually changed twice in the meantime. The classic example is a lock-free stack: thread 1 reads the top node A, plans to pop A by CAS-ing top from A to A.next. Meanwhile, thread 2 pops A, pops A.next, pushes A back, and A.next now points to a different node. Thread 1's CAS sees top == A (still true) and succeeds, but now top points to the wrong next node — the stack is corrupted. The fix is to attach a version counter to the reference: AtomicStampedReference<T> pairs the value with an integer stamp, and CAS succeeds only if both the value and the stamp match. Any A-to-B-to-A transition increments the stamp, so the CAS correctly fails. The alternative is AtomicMarkableReference<T>, which pairs the value with a boolean mark for cases where a single bit of state is enough.

False sharing is a performance hazard that appears in striped counters and lock-free data structures. Modern CPUs do not access individual bytes; they operate on cache lines (64 bytes on x86). If two threads update two different variables that happen to reside on the same cache line, the CPU's cache coherence protocol must invalidate and reload the line on every write — even though the threads never touch the same variable. This is called false sharing, and it can degrade throughput by an order of magnitude. The fix is padding: ensure that variables updated by different threads are at least 64 bytes apart, typically by adding unused long fields between them. LongAdder and other JDK internals already do this internally. On Java 8+, the @sun.misc.Contended annotation (or @jdk.internal.vm.annotation.Contended) instructs the JVM to pad the annotated field automatically, but it requires the -XX:-RestrictContended flag in some configurations. The interview point is that false sharing is invisible to profiling tools unless you know to look for it — the code looks correct and the locks are fine, but throughput is mysteriously poor.

The practical decision: use AtomicInteger/AtomicLong for single-variable atomic operations with low-to-moderate contention. Use LongAdder/LongAccumulator for high-contention counters where approximate values are acceptable. Use AtomicReference with AtomicStampedReference when ABA is a concern (lock-free data structures with reuse of nodes). Use explicit locks or synchronizers when the invariant spans multiple variables — atomics only give per-variable atomicity, not multi-variable atomicity. And be aware of false sharing when writing striped or lock-free code; if throughput does not scale with cores, padding is the likely fix.

The interview-quality answer explains CAS, distinguishes AtomicLong from LongAdder (contention and approximation trade-off), explains the ABA problem and AtomicStampedReference as the fix, and covers false sharing and padding. That demonstrates you understand lock-free programming at a deep level, not just the API surface.
bullets: CAS (compare-and-swap) is a hardware instruction: set a value only if it equals an expected value, atomically; it is the foundation of every atomic class and every lock-free structure.
Atomics use CAS loops: read, compute, CAS, retry on failure. Under low contention they succeed in one iteration; under high contention they spin.
Atomic updateAndGet runs the lambda on every retry — the lambda must be side-effect-free, or results are wrong.
LongAdder / LongAccumulator stripe updates across cells to avoid contention on a single location; sum() is approximate (a fuzzy snapshot), and writes scale with cores.
Use AtomicLong for exact counters (sequence numbers); use LongAdder for high-contention metrics where approximate is acceptable.

ABA problem: a value changes A → B → A between read and CAS, so CAS sees an unchanged value and succeeds on stale assumptions; AtomicStampedReference adds a monotonic stamp that increments on every change and makes CAS fail correctly.

False sharing: two variables on the same 64-byte cache line are invalidated on every write even when threads touch different variables; fix with padding or @Contended, and check it when throughput does not scale with cores.

cards.title: Concurrent Collections: ConcurrentHashMap, CopyOnWriteArrayList, and the BlockingQueue Family
cards.summary:
The java.util.concurrent package provides thread-safe collections that are safer and faster than wrapping a standard collection in synchronized. Each one is designed for a specific access pattern, and picking the wrong one is a common source of both bugs and performance problems. The mental model is: thread-safe does not mean any-access-safe — ConcurrentHashMap is thread-safe for concurrent reads and writes but not for compound operations unless you use its atomic methods; CopyOnWriteArrayList is thread-safe for reads but writes copy the entire array; BlockingQueues are designed for producer-consumer patterns with built-in blocking.

ConcurrentHashMap (covered in depth in java-hashmap-1) is a hash map that allows concurrent reads and writes without a single global lock. In JDK 8+ it uses per-bucket locking and CAS for empty buckets, giving excellent concurrency for independent keys. The critical rule is that its individual operations are thread-safe, but compound operations are not: get-then-put is a race even if each method call is atomic. The fix is to use the atomic compound methods: putIfAbsent, computeIfAbsent, compute, computeIfPresent, merge, replace(key, old, new). These methods hold the bucket lock for the duration of the mapping function, so the whole read-compute-write is atomic. The other critical rule: computeIfAbsent's mapping function must not modify the map or perform long-running work while holding the bucket lock — it can block other writers to the same bucket, and if it modifies the map you get undefined behavior (and in JDK 8, potential infinite loops on some paths).

CopyOnWriteArrayList (and CopyOnWriteArraySet) is designed for read-heavy, write-rare workloads where iteration far outnumbers modification. Every mutation (add, remove, set) creates a new copy of the underlying array, so readers see a stable snapshot and never need to lock. Iterators are snapshot-based: they never throw ConcurrentModificationException, and they iterate over the array as it existed when the iterator was created — even if new elements are added or removed during iteration, the iterator sees the original state. The cost is that writes are O(n) (copy the whole array) and memory-heavy (old arrays are held until their readers finish). This makes CopyOnWriteArrayList a bad choice for write-heavy lists, large lists, or long-lived iterators, and an excellent choice for listener lists, observer registries, and small configuration collections that change rarely. The rule of thumb: if writes are more than a tiny fraction of reads, use something else.

The BlockingQueue family is the foundation of producer-consumer patterns. A BlockingQueue is a queue with two blocking operations: put(E) blocks when the queue is full, and take() blocks when the queue is empty. The variants differ in their capacity and ordering. ArrayBlockingQueue: bounded, FIFO, backed by an array, supports an optional fairness flag; the standard choice for fixed-capacity producer-consumer (bounded is essential for backpressure — an unbounded queue hides overload until it becomes OutOfMemoryError). LinkedBlockingQueue: optionally bounded (default is Integer.MAX_VALUE, which is effectively unbounded — a trap), FIFO, linked nodes; higher throughput than ArrayBlockingQueue in some workloads but the unbounded default is dangerous. SynchronousQueue: a handoff queue with no capacity, where a put blocks until a matching take arrives and vice versa; used by Executors.newCachedThreadPool and useful for handing off work directly between two threads without buffering. PriorityBlockingQueue: unbounded, ordered by a comparator or natural ordering; used when tasks must be processed by priority, not arrival time. DelayQueue: unbounded, elements become available only after their delay has elapsed; used for scheduling (retries with backoff, session expiry, rate limiter buckets). LinkedTransferQueue: unbounded, with both blocking and non-blocking transfer semantics; used in high-performance producer-consumer where the producer can wait for the consumer to take the element directly.

The deque variants — BlockingDeque, LinkedBlockingDeque, ConcurrentLinkedDeque — add double-ended operations (putFirst, putLast, takeFirst, takeLast) and are used for work-stealing patterns and bidirectional queues. ConcurrentLinkedQueue and ConcurrentLinkedDeque are non-blocking (lock-free) and do not block when empty or full; you poll and get null, or you check and act. They are used when you need a queue but do not want blocking behavior (for example, in lock-free algorithms and certain event-loop patterns).

Other members of the package are worth knowing. ConcurrentSkipListMap and ConcurrentSkipListSet are sorted concurrent collections (skip-list-based, O(log n) operations); they are used when you need a concurrent sorted map — for example, an ordered index that must be updated concurrently. ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet() is a common way to get a concurrent set with weak iteration semantics; it is often a better choice than ConcurrentSkipListSet when you do not need ordering. CopyOnWriteArrayList is the only 'copy-on-write' collection in the package, and its constraints are discussed above.

The interview-quality answer distinguishes thread-safety of individual operations from compound atomicity (computeIfAbsent vs get-then-put), names CopyOnWriteArrayList's read-heavy snapshot semantics and its write cost, describes the BlockingQueue variants with their use cases (ArrayBlockingQueue for bounded backpressure, LinkedBlockingQueue's unbounded trap, SynchronousQueue for direct handoff, PriorityBlockingQueue for priority, DelayQueue for scheduled work), and warns about the traps (unbounded queues as a form of hidden overload, iterators of CopyOnWriteArrayList being snapshots rather than live views). That demonstrates you can pick the right collection for the access pattern, not just the one whose name starts with Concurrent.
bullets: java.util.concurrent collections are each designed for a specific access pattern — thread-safe does not mean safe for every usage.
ConcurrentHashMap: per-bucket locking + CAS; individual operations are atomic, but get-then-put is a race; use putIfAbsent, computeIfAbsent, compute, merge for atomic compound operations.
computeIfAbsent's function must be side-effect-free and fast — it runs under the bucket lock and can block other writers.

CopyOnWriteArrayList: every write copies the array (O(n)), readers see a stable snapshot, iterators never throw ConcurrentModificationException; ideal for listener/observer lists, bad for write-heavy or large lists.

BlockingQueue variants: ArrayBlockingQueue (bounded, FIFO, backpressure), LinkedBlockingQueue (bounded or unbounded — unbounded default hides overload), SynchronousQueue (no capacity, direct handoff), PriorityBlockingQueue (priority order), DelayQueue (scheduled availability), LinkedTransferQueue (high-perf handoff).
ConcurrentLinkedQueue / ConcurrentLinkedDeque: non-blocking (lock-free) queues — poll returns null instead of blocking; used in lock-free algorithms.
ConcurrentSkipListMap / ConcurrentSkipListSet: sorted concurrent collections for ordered indexes; ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet() for a fast concurrent set.
Unbounded queues (LinkedBlockingQueue default) hide overload until OutOfMemoryError — prefer bounded queues for backpressure.

cards.title: ForkJoinPool and Parallel Streams: Work-Stealing, Common Pool Hazards, and When Not to Parallelize
cards.summary:
ForkJoinPool (Java 7) is a specialized thread pool designed for divide-and-conquer workloads. Its distinguishing feature is work-stealing: each worker thread has its own double-ended queue (deque) of tasks, and when a worker runs out of its own tasks, it steals from the tail of another worker's deque (taking the oldest, largest tasks) while the owner continues taking from the head (newest, smallest tasks). This balanced distribution keeps all cores busy without a central scheduler and without hot spots on a single queue. ForkJoinTasks submit sub-tasks via fork() (which pushes them onto the worker's deque) and wait for results via join(); when a worker calls join(), instead of blocking idle it may steal other work, so the pool stays saturated even under recursive decomposition.

A RecursiveTask<V> is a ForkJoinTask that returns a value; a RecursiveAction is one that does not. The pattern is: if the problem is small enough (below a threshold), solve it directly; otherwise split it into two or more sub-tasks, fork them, and join their results. The threshold matters — too large and the recursion does not have enough parallelism; too small and the fork/join overhead dominates. The recommended starting point is roughly 10,000 to 100,000 basic operations per leaf task, but the right value depends on the cost per operation and should be tuned with a profiler. In practice, most parallel decomposition ends up close to the leaf size at which the work per leaf is a few microseconds — enough to amortize the fork/join cost but small enough to exploit all cores.

Parallel streams (Java 8) are a much easier front end to the same machinery. list.parallelStream() splits the source (if it is efficiently splittable — ArrayList, arrays, and ranges are; LinkedList and iterators are not) and runs the pipeline on the common ForkJoinPool. The common pool is a shared, JVM-wide pool sized to Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors() - 1. This shared nature is the source of most parallel-stream disasters: a parallel stream that performs blocking IO (an HTTP call, a database query, a file read) occupies one of the common-pool threads for the duration of the block, and since the pool has only N-1 threads, a handful of such tasks can starve the entire JVM of common-pool capacity. The fix is never to run blocking work on the common pool — use a dedicated ForkJoinPool for blocking parallel work, or better, do not use parallel streams for blocking IO at all (use virtual threads or an async executor instead).

The splittability of the source matters more than most developers realize. ArrayList, arrays, IntStream.range, and ConcurrentSkipListMap have efficient spliterators that divide evenly. LinkedList, Stream.iterate, and BufferedReader.lines have poor spliterators (iteration is O(n) per split, or the source does not support random access), so parallelStream on them often performs worse than sequential. The reduction operations must also be safe: collect with a combiner that does not depend on encounter order, use concurrent collectors for unordered streams, and be wary of forEach if the ordering matters (parallelStream().forEach does not guarantee order; forEachOrdered does, but at a cost).

When to use ForkJoinPool or parallel streams: pure CPU-bound work on large, splittable data with no IO, no locks, and no shared mutable state. Classic cases are numeric computations (summing a large array, matrix operations), bulk transformations, and search problems. When not to use them: IO-bound work (the common-pool starvation trap), small collections (the overhead exceeds the benefit), work with synchronization or shared mutable state (contention kills the benefit), work where the reduction is order-dependent, and anywhere the latency budget matters (parallel streams optimize throughput, not per-element latency). The decision is simple: if the work is CPU-bound and the data is large and splittable, parallel streams are a one-line win; otherwise, use explicit async (CompletableFuture, virtual threads) or keep it sequential.

The interview-quality answer explains work-stealing (per-worker deques, steal from tail, owner takes from head), the RecursiveTask pattern (leaf threshold, fork/join), parallel streams as a front end to the common pool, the common-pool starvation trap for blocking IO, splittability of sources, and the decision criteria (CPU-bound, large, splittable, no IO). That demonstrates you understand parallel execution as a throughput tool with specific preconditions, not as a universal speedup.
bullets: ForkJoinPool uses work-stealing: each worker has its own deque, and idle workers steal the oldest tasks from other workers' deques; join() can steal instead of blocking, keeping the pool saturated.
RecursiveTask<V> returns a value, RecursiveAction does not; split below a leaf threshold, fork sub-tasks, join results.
Parallel streams use the shared common ForkJoinPool (N-1 threads); they split the source and process in parallel with the same fork/join machinery.
Common-pool starvation is the main hazard: blocking IO on a common-pool thread starves the JVM; use a dedicated pool or async/virtual threads for IO.
Splittability matters: ArrayList, arrays, and ranges split well; LinkedList, Stream.iterate, and BufferedReader.lines do not — parallel often loses to sequential.
Use parallel streams for CPU-bound, large, splittable data with no IO, no locks, no shared mutable state, and order-independent reductions.
Avoid parallel streams for IO-bound work, small collections, synchronization-heavy work, order-dependent reductions, or latency-sensitive code.

cards.title: Deadlock, Livelock, Starvation, and wait/notify: The Four Ways Threads Stop Making Progress
cards.summary:
Concurrent programs can fail to make progress in four distinct ways, and distinguishing them in an interview is a strong signal. Deadlock: two or more threads are blocked forever, each waiting for a resource held by another, forming a cycle. Livelock: threads are not blocked — they are actively running — but they keep responding to each other in a way that prevents progress (like two people stepping aside to let the other pass, repeatedly). Starvation: one or more threads are perpetually denied access to a resource because other threads are always preferred (for example, an unfair lock where a high-priority thread always wins). And the classic wait/notify bugs: missing notifications, lost wakeups, and spurious wakeups. Each has distinct symptoms and distinct fixes.

Deadlock requires four simultaneous conditions, known as the Coffman conditions: mutual exclusion (resources are held exclusively), hold-and-wait (a thread holds one resource and waits for another), no preemption (resources cannot be forcibly taken away), and circular wait (a cycle of threads each waiting for the next). Breaking any one condition prevents deadlock. The practical fix in application code is to break circular wait via lock ordering: establish a global ordering on all locks (for example, by account ID) and always acquire them in that order. The alternative is to break hold-and-wait via tryLock with a timeout: acquire the first lock, try to acquire the second with a timeout, and if it fails, release the first and retry. Detecting deadlock in production is done with jstack (which prints 'Found one Java-level deadlock' with the threads and the lock chain) or with ThreadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads(). Detection is for diagnosis; prevention is the goal.

Livelock is trickier because the CPU is busy — a thread dump shows RUNNABLE threads, not BLOCKED ones — but no work is completed. The classic example is two threads using tryLock with retry: thread A holds lock 1 and tries to get lock 2, thread B holds lock 2 and tries to get lock 1, both fail, both release their locks, both retry — forever. The fix is to add randomized backoff between retries (so the two threads do not keep colliding in lock-step), or to switch to lock ordering, which eliminates the cycle entirely. The symptom in production is high CPU with no throughput — an important distinction from deadlock, which shows low CPU and idle threads.

Starvation happens when a thread never gets scheduled or never gets a lock because other threads are always prioritized. Unfair locks (ReentrantLock default, synchronized, ReadWriteLock default) can starve a thread if the lock is constantly reacquired by other threads. Thread priorities can starve low-priority threads on platforms that honor them (most modern JVMs do not, but the risk remains conceptually). A thread pool with a LIFO or priority queue can starve long-running tasks if short tasks keep arriving. The fix is fairness (fair ReentrantLock, fair ReadWriteLock — at a throughput cost), bounded queues that apply backpressure instead of letting short tasks crowd out long ones, and avoiding thread priorities as a scheduling tool. Fair locks are roughly 5-10x slower than unfair ones in microbenchmarks, which is why fairness is opt-in and should be reserved for cases where starvation is a real risk.

The wait/notify primitives have three classic bugs. First, waiting without a loop: Object.wait() can return spuriously (without a notify), and the correct pattern is `while (!condition) wait();` — always re-check the condition after waking, never use `if`. Second, lost wakeups: if the notifier calls notify() before the waiter calls wait(), the notification is lost (wait does not remember it), so the waiter blocks forever unless there is a timeout or a condition check. The correct pattern is to hold the lock while changing the condition and while calling notify, so the state change and the notification are atomic. Third, notifyAll vs notify: notify() wakes one arbitrary waiter, which can be the wrong one (a reader when a writer is needed), producing a lost wakeup for the intended thread. notifyAll() wakes everyone and is the safe default; notify() is a micro-optimization that is easy to get wrong. The modern answer is to use java.util.concurrent primitives (BlockingQueue, CountDownLatch, Condition) rather than raw wait/notify — they get all of this right.

The interview-quality answer distinguishes the four failure modes by their symptoms (deadlock: BLOCKED threads, low CPU; livelock: RUNNABLE threads, high CPU, no throughput; starvation: some threads never run; wait/notify: missed or spurious wakeups), names the Coffman conditions and lock ordering as the primary prevention, insists on the while-loop pattern for wait and on notifyAll as the safe default, and recommends java.util.concurrent primitives over raw wait/notify. That demonstrates you can diagnose and prevent concurrency progress failures, not just describe them.
bullets: Deadlock: threads block forever waiting on each other's resources (BLOCKED, low CPU); requires mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, and circular wait — break any one to prevent it.
Lock ordering is the primary deadlock prevention: acquire locks in a global, consistent order so a cycle cannot form.
Livelock: threads are RUNNABLE but keep retrying and never progress (high CPU, no throughput); fix with randomized backoff or lock ordering.
Starvation: a thread never gets the resource because others are always preferred; fix with fair locks (at a throughput cost), bounded queues, and no reliance on thread priority.
wait() can return spuriously and notifications can be lost; always wait in a `while (!condition) wait();` loop, and hold the lock while changing the condition and calling notify.
Use notifyAll() as the safe default — notify() can wake the wrong waiter and lose the intended wakeup.
Prefer java.util.concurrent primitives (BlockingQueue, CountDownLatch, Condition) over raw wait/notify — they handle these pitfalls correctly.

cards.title: Virtual Threads in Java 21: Cheap Blocking, Pinning, and What They Change
cards.summary:
Virtual threads (finalized in Java 21, previewed since 19) are JVM-managed threads that are far cheaper than platform threads. A platform thread maps 1:1 to an operating-system thread, so creating one costs a kernel call, a stack allocation (typically 512 KB to 1 MB), and OS scheduler pressure — which is why a typical JVM can sustain a few thousand platform threads but not millions. A virtual thread is a lightweight object managed by the JVM: it starts with a small heap-allocated stack that grows as needed, and it is scheduled by the JVM onto a small pool of carrier platform threads (one per CPU core, by default in ForkJoinPool). The JVM can park a virtual thread (for example, when it blocks on IO) without holding the carrier thread — the carrier moves on to run another virtual thread. This means a JVM can have millions of virtual threads alive with only a few dozen carrier threads, and blocking IO stops being expensive.

The core insight is that blocking IO is what makes traditional thread pools expensive. A servlet thread handling a request that waits 100 ms for a database call is idle for 100 ms but occupies an OS thread the whole time, so a service needs one thread per concurrent request, and platform threads cap that at a few thousand. Virtual threads break this cost model: the thread that is waiting is unmounted from the carrier, so the carrier serves other requests. A service can now spawn one virtual thread per request and write plain, blocking code — no reactive gymnastics, no callbacks, no CompletableFuture chains — while still handling tens of thousands of concurrent requests. This is the primary use case: IO-bound concurrent work, especially request-per-task patterns in web servers, gRPC services, database clients, and message consumers.

The critical caveat is pinning. A virtual thread cannot be unmounted from its carrier in two situations: when it is executing inside a synchronized block or method (Java 21 and earlier — Java 24 removes this limitation via JEP 491), and when it is executing a native method or a blocking JNI call. While pinned, the virtual thread holds the carrier thread, so blocking inside synchronized means the carrier blocks and cannot serve other virtual threads. A workload with heavy synchronized usage and long blocking calls inside synchronized is the worst case for virtual threads — it degrades to platform-thread behavior and can even starve the carrier pool. The fixes are to replace synchronized with ReentrantLock in hot paths (ReentrantLock.park does not pin), to keep blocking calls out of synchronized blocks, and to use JFR (jdk.VirtualThreadPinned) or the -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads flag to detect pinning in development. On Java 24+, synchronized no longer pins, which removes the biggest real-world obstacle, but older versions still require the discipline.

The second caveat is that virtual threads are not a general performance improvement for CPU-bound work. If the task is pure computation, a virtual thread runs on its carrier just like a platform thread, and spawning millions of them wastes memory without any benefit. Virtual threads solve the blocking-IO cost problem, not the parallelism problem — for CPU-bound work, a bounded platform-thread pool sized to the CPU count remains correct. The third caveat is that virtual threads do not pool. A pool of virtual threads would be a contradiction — the point is that they are cheap to create, so you create a new one per task (Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()). Pooling platform threads amortizes the creation cost; creating virtual threads is already cheap, so pooling them adds overhead without benefit.

ThreadLocal is another interaction to be aware of. ThreadLocal was designed for platform threads, which are typically long-lived and pooled — so a ThreadLocal set on a platform thread persists across tasks, and forgetting to remove it causes the classic leak. Virtual threads are created per task and discarded, so a ThreadLocal set on a virtual thread is garbage-collected with the virtual thread — no leak, but also no reuse, so the same ThreadLocal is not visible to subsequent tasks. This means ThreadLocal-based context propagation (for example, Spring's RequestContextHolder, MDC) still works within one virtual thread, but you cannot rely on it being inherited or transferred. For structured context propagation across virtual threads, Java 21 introduced ScopedValue (preview) as the intended replacement, and MDC still needs explicit propagation across async boundaries.

Adoption guidance: use virtual threads where the bottleneck is IO concurrency (HTTP clients, database queries, file operations, message consumers) and the code is synchronous. Keep bounded platform-thread pools for CPU-bound work. Replace synchronized with ReentrantLock in paths that block inside the lock. Use structured concurrency (covered in the next card) for coordinating multiple virtual-thread tasks. Avoid using virtual threads with thread pools or with code that relies on thread pinning semantics (JNI, native code). The migration is usually a one-line change in Spring Boot 3.2+ (spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true) or an executor choice — the code stays the same, and the JVM takes care of the rest.

The interview-quality answer explains the cheap-thread cost model (heap stack, carrier threads, unmounting on block), the IO-bound use case, the pinning problem (synchronized and native calls) and its fixes, the fact that virtual threads do not help CPU-bound work and should not be pooled, and the ThreadLocal interaction. That demonstrates you understand virtual threads as an IO concurrency tool, not as a universal improvement.
bullets: Virtual threads are JVM-managed threads with heap-allocated stacks, scheduled onto a small pool of carrier platform threads; they unmount on blocking IO, so millions can exist with a few dozen carriers.
The primary use case is IO-bound concurrent work: one virtual thread per request, plain blocking code, tens of thousands of concurrent requests.

Pinning: a virtual thread cannot unmount inside synchronized (Java 21 and earlier) or in native/JNI calls, so blocking there holds a carrier; fix by replacing synchronized with ReentrantLock in blocking paths (Java 24 removes the synchronized pinning).
Virtual threads do not help CPU-bound work — carrier threads are still finite; use bounded platform-thread pools for CPU-bound tasks.
Do not pool virtual threads — they are cheap to create per task; Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() is the standard.
ThreadLocal on a virtual thread does not leak (the virtual thread is discarded with the task) but also is not reused across tasks; use ScopedValue for structured context propagation.
Spring Boot 3.2+ enables virtual threads with spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true.

cards.title: ThreadLocal Leaks, MDC Propagation, and ScopedValue: Context in the Modern JVM
cards.summary:
ThreadLocal is the JVM's mechanism for per-thread state — each thread has its own map of ThreadLocal instances to values, so a ThreadLocal set in one thread is invisible to another. It was designed for a world of pooled, long-lived platform threads, where the same thread serves many tasks and context must be reset between them. That design assumption drives both its value and its failure modes. The value: in a request-per-thread server (Tomcat with platform threads), the request context (user, tenant, trace ID) can live in a ThreadLocal for the duration of the request. The failure modes: leaks when remove is not called, and broken propagation across threads that are not the request thread.

The leak is covered in detail in java-threadlocal-1 and is worth a one-line recap: a ThreadLocalMap entry holds a weak reference to the ThreadLocal key but a strong reference to the value; on a pooled thread, if the ThreadLocal key is garbage-collected but the entry survives, the value stays reachable and leaks. On a long-lived thread pool, this accumulates. The fix is always calling remove in a finally block after the work, and preferring lifecycle-managed frameworks (Spring's RequestContextHolder, MDC cleanup) that do this automatically.

MDC (Mapped Diagnostic Context) in SLF4J and Logback is built on ThreadLocal: you call MDC.put('traceId', ...) to attach context to log lines, and the logging framework reads the MDC map when formatting each line. This works beautifully within one thread, and fails completely across threads. If you submit work to a thread pool (Executors, @Async, a message consumer), the worker thread has an empty MDC — the trace ID, tenant ID, and user ID do not appear in its log lines. Worse, if the worker thread is pooled and the previous task left stale MDC entries, you get context bleeding across requests (user A's tenant in user B's logs), which is a subtle correctness and privacy bug. The standard fixes are: (1) capture the MDC map in the submitting thread and set it in the worker, then clear it; (2) use a task-decorating executor (Spring's TaskDecorator, or a custom wrapper) that propagates the context automatically; (3) use a distributed tracing framework (Micrometer Tracing, OpenTelemetry) that propagates trace context via headers and associates it with the current span on every thread, independent of MDC. The third option is what most modern Spring Boot applications should do — MDC is a manual discipline, tracing is automatic.

Virtual threads change the leak calculus but not the propagation problem. A virtual thread is created per task and discarded, so a ThreadLocal set inside it is garbage-collected with the virtual thread — no leak. But there is also no reuse, so a ThreadLocal set by a parent task is not visible to a child virtual thread, and MDC context does not transfer. The propagation problem remains exactly as it was with platform-thread pools, and it is the reason the JDK introduced ScopedValue (preview in 21, maturing in later versions) as the intended replacement for ThreadLocal in async code.

ScopedValue is a newer mechanism for immutable, bounded-lifetime context sharing. The model is: ScopedValue.where(KEY, value).run(() -> work()) — within the run block (and any threads the work spawns, if they are structured), KEY.get() returns value; outside the block, it is not set. It is immutable (no set after binding), the value is automatically cleared when the scope exits (no leaks, no cleanup discipline), and it is designed to be inherited by child tasks in structured concurrency. ScopedValue is not a drop-in replacement for ThreadLocal in all cases (it is not mutable, and it requires the run/call structure), but it is the correct tool for request context, tenant context, and trace context in modern async code. The catch: as of Java 21 it is a preview API, not yet enabled by default, so production adoption requires the appropriate JVM flags and a willingness to migrate when it is finalized.

The practical guidance in an interview: for existing Spring Boot applications, rely on RequestContextHolder (Spring's built-in ThreadLocal) within the request thread, propagate MDC explicitly across thread boundaries (TaskDecorator, MDC.getCopyOfContextMap + MDC.setContextMap), and use a tracing framework (Micrometer Tracing + OpenTelemetry) for distributed trace context. For new code, prefer ScopedValue when it is available, or explicit context objects passed as parameters when the code is already async. Never rely on ThreadLocal inheritance across threads — it does not happen automatically for a reason, and the workarounds are fragile.

The interview-quality answer recaps the ThreadLocal leak and the remove-in-finally fix, explains MDC's ThreadLocal basis and its cross-thread failure (missing context, stale bleeding), names the propagation fixes (TaskDecorator, explicit MDC copy, tracing framework), introduces ScopedValue as the immutable, scoped, inherited-by-design alternative, and states the practical migration guidance. That demonstrates you have actually propagated context across async boundaries, not just used MDC in a single-threaded request.
bullets: ThreadLocal is per-thread state on a ThreadLocalMap; on pooled platform threads, failing to call remove leaks the value (weak key, strong value).
MDC (SLF4J/Logback) is built on ThreadLocal: it works within a thread and fails across thread boundaries — worker threads see no MDC, or worse, stale context from a previous task.

Propagation fixes: capture the MDC map and set it in the worker, use a TaskDecorator or task wrapper, or rely on a tracing framework (Micrometer Tracing + OpenTelemetry) that associates trace context via headers.
Virtual threads eliminate the ThreadLocal leak (per-task lifetime) but not the propagation problem — a child virtual thread does not inherit the parent's ThreadLocal.
ScopedValue (Java 21 preview) is the intended replacement: immutable, bounded by a run/call scope, automatically cleared, and inherited by structured child tasks.
For new code: prefer ScopedValue when available, or explicit context objects passed as parameters; never rely on ThreadLocal inheritance across threads.
For existing Spring Boot: RequestContextHolder within the request thread, explicit MDC propagation across boundaries, and a tracing framework for distributed trace context.

cards.title: Coordination Primitives and Backpressure: CountDownLatch, CyclicBarrier, Semaphore, Structured Concurrency
cards.summary:
The java.util.concurrent package includes several coordination primitives beyond locks and queues, each solving a specific shape of multi-thread coordination. CountDownLatch: a one-shot barrier that lets one or more threads wait until a set of operations completes — a thread calls await() and blocks until the internal count reaches zero, while other threads call countDown() when they finish. It is the standard tool for 'wait for N services to respond, then aggregate', 'wait for startup tasks to complete before opening the server', and 'wait for N workers to finish before moving to the next phase'. It is one-shot: once the count reaches zero, it stays at zero, and you cannot reset it (use CyclicBarrier for that).

CyclicBarrier is the reusable barrier: N threads call await() and block until all N arrive, then all proceed, and the barrier resets for the next round. It is used for iterative algorithms where a group of threads must synchronize at the end of each iteration (parallel simulations, grid computations, multi-phase processing), and for test harnesses that need to launch N threads at exactly the same moment. The constructor can take a barrier action that runs once per round (in the last thread to arrive) — useful for merging per-thread results between phases. The reset() method breaks the current barrier and lets you reuse it, but threads already waiting on it receive a BrokenBarrierException.

Semaphore is the generalized permit-based lock: it holds a fixed number of permits, and each acquire() takes one while release() returns one. It is used for rate limiting (bounded concurrent access to a shared resource — for example, at most 10 concurrent calls to an external API), resource pools (at most N connections), and backpressure (the queue of waiting threads is the natural pressure signal). Unlike a lock, it is not tied to ownership — any thread can release, which is what makes it suitable for permit-style coordination. A fair Semaphore (fairness=true) gives permits in FIFO order, at a throughput cost. The main trap is that a semaphore must be released in a finally block (or the permits leak and the limit slowly reduces to zero), and that a semaphore with a permit count of 1 is not a lock (it does not provide ownership or reentrancy — using it where a lock is needed produces subtle bugs).

Backpressure is the broader concept these primitives serve. When a producer is faster than a consumer, the system has three options: buffer (unbounded queues, which hide overload until OOM), block (bounded queues and blocking puts, which applies pressure back to the producer), or shed (reject with an error, for example HTTP 429 or a 503 with Retry-After). Every production system needs at least one of these, and the strongest systems use all three: bounded queues to apply backpressure, fast failure (429/503) when the queue is full, and circuit breakers so the consumer does not keep retrying a failing dependency. The critical failure mode of ignoring backpressure is the queue growing unbounded — the symptom is not a slow request but a JVM crash with OutOfMemoryError after minutes of overload, which is much worse than a fast 503.

Structured concurrency (Java 21 preview) is the modern coordination model for multiple related tasks. Instead of spawning threads and forgetting about them, structured concurrency ties the lifetime of child tasks to the parent scope: try (var scope = new StructuredTaskScope.ShutdownOnFailure()) { scope.fork(taskA); scope.fork(taskB); scope.join(); scope.throwIfFailed(); /* use results */ }. If any child fails (ShutdownOnFailure) or succeeds (ShutdownOnSuccess), the scope cancels the rest and returns — no orphaned threads, no leaks, no 'fire and forget' tasks still running after the request returns. It also propagates context (ScopedValue) to children, and the scope's structure makes cancellation and error handling predictable. The two common policies are ShutdownOnFailure (fan-out all-of semantics, cancel siblings on first failure) and ShutdownOnSuccess (any-of semantics, cancel siblings on first success). This is the model Spring Boot 3.2+ uses internally for virtual-thread request handling, and it is what most new async code should adopt as the API stabilizes.

The interview-quality answer names CountDownLatch (one-shot wait for N completions), CyclicBarrier (reusable barrier with optional barrier action), Semaphore (permit-based limit, rate limiting, resource pools), explains that Semaphore must be released in finally and is not a lock, describes backpressure (buffer, block, shed, and why unbounded queues are the wrong default), and introduces structured concurrency (scoped child lifetimes, ShutdownOnFailure / ShutdownOnSuccess, context propagation, no orphaned threads). That demonstrates you understand coordination as a layered stack, from primitive synchronization to structured task scopes.
bullets: CountDownLatch: one-shot barrier; await() blocks until count reaches zero; countDown() from workers; cannot be reset.
CyclicBarrier: reusable barrier; N threads await() until all arrive; optional barrier action per round; reset() breaks the current round.
Semaphore: N permits; acquire/release for rate limiting, resource pools, and backpressure; must be released in finally; not a lock (no ownership, no reentrancy).
Backpressure options: buffer (unbounded — dangerous), block (bounded queue + blocking put), shed (429/503). Production systems typically use all three.
Ignoring backpressure shows up as OutOfMemoryError after minutes of overload, not as slow requests — bounded queues turn it into a fast rejection instead.
Structured concurrency (Java 21 preview): StructuredTaskScope ties child task lifetimes to the parent scope; ShutdownOnFailure / ShutdownOnSuccess cancel siblings; no orphaned threads.
Structured concurrency propagates context (ScopedValue) to children — the correct pattern for fan-out/fan-in with cancellation.

cards.title: Runtime Memory Areas Deep Dive: Heap Subdivision, Metaspace vs PermGen, Off-Heap, and OOM Flavors
cards.summary:
This card goes deeper than java-jvm-1, which covers the basics of Heap, Stack, and Metaspace. Here the focus is the internal subdivision, the historical PermGen transition, off-heap memory, and the distinct OutOfMemoryError flavors that each area produces. Knowing which OOM you are seeing is the first step to diagnosing it, and interviewers test this because it separates someone who has read the docs from someone who has triaged a heap dump at 3 a.m.

The heap is subdivided by the generational collector. In the default collectors, it is split into a Young Generation (Eden plus two Survivor spaces, S0 and S1) and an Old Generation (Tenured). New objects are allocated in Eden; a minor GC copies survivors to a survivor space, and objects that survive enough minor GCs are promoted to Old. G1 rearranges this into equal-sized regions that are dynamically labeled Eden, Survivor, Old, or Humongous (for objects larger than half a region, typically 1 MB with 2 MB regions). ZGC uses a similar region-based layout with colored pointers to enable concurrent relocation. The heap is always the source of the classic OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space — it means too many live objects, not too many allocations (the GC can handle allocation rate; it cannot handle retention). The fix is to find what is retaining memory (a leak, an unbounded cache, a collection growing without bound), not just to increase the heap.

Metaspace replaced PermGen in Java 8. PermGen was a fixed-size region of the Java heap that held class metadata and was notoriously too small — the famous OutOfMemoryError: PermGen space happened on every hot redeploy in older application servers. Metaspace moves class metadata to native memory, outside the heap, and grows dynamically by default (bounded only by available native memory, or by -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize if set). The OOM flavor is OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace. The common causes are: too many classes loaded (a runaway bytecode generator, a dynamic proxy cache, a scripting engine compiling expressions on every request), a classloader leak (a class cannot be unloaded until its defining classloader is garbage-collected), or a too-small MaxMetaspaceSize. Increasing the limit is a workaround, not a fix — the right answer is to find what is loading classes and why they are not being unloaded.

Direct and off-heap memory is allocated outside the Java heap and outside Metaspace, in native memory. The three main sources are: (1) NIO direct buffers — ByteBuffer.allocateDirect(n) allocates native memory whose address is passed to the OS for I/O without a copy; (2) memory-mapped files (FileChannel.map) — the OS page cache is mapped into the process address space; (3) native code allocations via JNI (Netty's pooled direct buffers, RocksDB, compression libraries, database drivers). Off-heap memory is not garbage-collected automatically — it is freed only when the DirectByteBuffer is collected (via a Cleaner) or when the JNI code explicitly frees it, so leaks show up as process RSS growth that the JVM heap does not explain. The OOM flavor is OutOfMemoryError: Direct buffer memory (when -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize is exceeded) or the process being killed by the OS OOM killer (when native memory exceeds the container limit). Diagnosis requires native memory tracking (-XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary plus jcmd VM.native_memory) and process-level RSS monitoring, not heap dumps — the leak is invisible to a heap dump.

There are two more OOM flavors worth knowing. GC overhead limit exceeded: the JVM is spending more than 98% of its time in GC and reclaiming less than 2% of the heap — the heap is nearly full of live objects, and the GC is thrashing. The fix is the same as Java heap space (find the retention), or disabling the check with -XX:-UseGCOverheadLimit (which just delays the inevitable). Unable to create new native thread: the JVM cannot create an OS thread, because the process has hit a thread limit (ulimit -u on Linux, the cgroup pids.max, or simply too many threads with too-large stacks). This is not a memory OOM in the JVM sense — it is an OS limit — and the fix is fewer threads (thread pool instead of thread-per-request, or virtual threads). StackOverflowError is different still: it is not an OutOfMemoryError at all — the per-thread stack is exhausted, typically by deep recursion, and the fix is to increase -Xss or (better) restructure the recursion.

The practical diagnosis framework: read the OOM message carefully (the flavor tells you the area), then check whether the heap is full of live objects (jmap -histo, a heap dump, or GC logs showing low reclaimed percentage), whether Metaspace is growing (jcmd VM.metaspace or the Metaspace OOM itself), or whether native memory is growing (process RSS vs heap size, NMT, jcmd VM.native_memory summary). Each area has a different tool, and the tool is the fastest path to the root cause. The interview-quality answer names the subdivision (Eden/Survivor/Old or G1 regions), explains the Metaspace transition (PermGen was a fixed heap region; Metaspace is dynamic native memory), covers direct and off-heap memory (NIO, Netty, JNI, memory-mapped files) and why it is invisible to heap dumps, and lists the OOM flavors with their diagnoses. That demonstrates you can triage a memory incident, not just recite the memory model.
bullets: Heap is split into Young (Eden + two Survivors) and Old under generational collectors; G1 uses regions labeled Eden/Survivor/Old/Humongous; the OOM is java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space (live objects, not allocation rate).

Metaspace (Java 8+) holds class metadata in native memory and grows dynamically (bounded by MaxMetaspaceSize); it replaced PermGen, which was a fixed heap region that produced the infamous PermGen OOM on every redeploy.
Metaspace OOM means too many loaded classes or a classloader leak — a class cannot be unloaded until its defining classloader is garbage-collected.

Direct/off-heap memory (NIO direct buffers, memory-mapped files, Netty pooled buffers, JNI) is outside the heap and Metaspace, is not garbage-collected by the heap GC, and shows up as process RSS growth that heap dumps cannot explain.

OOM flavors: Java heap space (retention), Metaspace (class loading), Direct buffer memory (MaxDirectMemorySize), GC overhead limit exceeded (GC thrashing), unable to create new native thread (OS thread limits).
StackOverflowError is a per-thread stack exhaustion (usually deep recursion), not a heap OOM — fix the recursion or increase -Xss.
Diagnosis: read the OOM message, then use the matching tool — heap dump or jmap -histo for heap, jcmd VM.metaspace for Metaspace, NMT and RSS monitoring for off-heap.
cards.code:
