Memory areas and their OOMs

  Area                     Content                     OOM flavor
  -----------------------  --------------------------  -------------------------------
  Young Gen (Eden/S0/S1)   new objects                 java.lang.OutOfMemoryError:
  Old Gen (Tenured)        long-lived objects          Java heap space
  Metaspace (native)       class metadata, bytecode    java.lang.OutOfMemoryError:
                                                       Metaspace
  Direct / off-heap        NIO direct buffers,         java.lang.OutOfMemoryError:
                           memory-mapped files, JNI    Direct buffer memory
  Per-thread stack         method frames, locals       StackOverflowError
                                                       (not an OutOfMemoryError)
  OS threads               java.lang.Thread            OutOfMemoryError:
                                                       unable to create new native thread

Heap subdivisions

  Default generational:
    Young = Eden + S0 + S1    (minor GC copies survivors)
    Old   = Tenured            (major/full GC)

  G1 regions (equal-sized, dynamically labeled):
    [Eden][Eden][Surv][Old][Old][Humongous][...]
    Humongous = object > half a region (~1 MB with 2 MB regions)

  ZGC regions:
    similar layout, colored pointers, concurrent relocation

PermGen -> Metaspace (Java 8)

  PermGen (<= Java 7): fixed region of Java heap, class metadata
    -> OutOfMemoryError: PermGen space on hot redeploys
    -> -XX:MaxPermSize to size (still ran out)

  Metaspace (Java 8+): native memory, dynamic, default unbounded
    -> -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=256m to bound
    -> OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace when class loading outpaces unloading

Off-heap memory sources

  ByteBuffer.allocateDirect(n)     -- native memory, freed when buffer GC'd
  FileChannel.map(...)             -- memory-mapped file (OS page cache)
  Netty PooledByteBufAllocator     -- pooled direct buffers
  JNI libraries                    -- allocate/free via native code
  RocksDB, compression libraries   -- native off-heap caches

  -> not visible in heap dumps
  -> check: process RSS - (heap used + metaspace + thread stacks)
  -> tools: -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary, jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary

OOM diagnosis cheat sheet

  Java heap space
    jmap -histo:live <pid>          -- top classes by instance count
    jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump /tmp/x.hprof
    look for: large collections, caches without eviction, request state

  Metaspace
    jcmd <pid> VM.metaspace
    look for: dynamic proxy classes, scripting engines, classloader leaks

  Direct buffer memory
    -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=<n>     -- explicit bound (default = max heap)
    jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary
    look for: NIO/Netty buffer leaks

  GC overhead limit exceeded
    GC logs showing > 98% time in GC, < 2% reclaimed
    -> same root cause as Java heap space (retention)

  unable to create new native thread
    ulimit -u, cgroup pids.max, thread count vs stack size
    -> thread pool or virtual threads, not thread-per-request

  StackOverflowError
    -Xss (per-thread stack size)
    -> usually deep recursion; fix the algorithm, not the flag

cards.title: JIT Compilation: C1, C2, Tiered, Deoptimization, Escape Analysis, and Safepoints
cards.summary:
The JVM does not run bytecode directly — it interprets it first, then compiles hot methods to native machine code at runtime. This is the just-in-time compiler, and it is why Java can approach C++ performance despite starting from bytecode. The compilation pipeline has two compilers with different goals and different trade-offs, and understanding their interaction explains most JVM performance behavior interviewers probe.

C1 (the client compiler) compiles quickly with moderate optimization. It is designed for startup: a method that runs a few times gets compiled to decent machine code in milliseconds, so applications reach steady state fast. C2 (the server compiler) compiles slowly with aggressive optimization: inlining, escape analysis, loop unrolling, lock elision, speculative optimizations based on observed types, and hundreds of others. C2 produces much faster code but takes longer to compile, and it uses more memory. Historically, you chose between C1 and C2 with -client or -server; since Java 8, tiered compilation is the default and uses both: level 0 is the interpreter, levels 1-3 are C1 with increasing amounts of profiling, and level 4 is C2. A hot method is first compiled by C1 (fast startup), then recompiled by C2 once it is clearly hot (fast steady state). This combination gives both fast startup and high peak throughput.

Hot method detection is driven by two counters. The invocation counter counts how many times a method is called; when it exceeds a threshold, the method becomes eligible for compilation. The backedge counter counts loop iterations; a hot loop inside a cold method can trigger compilation of the enclosing method, which is why a method called once but running a million-iteration loop still gets compiled. The thresholds are tuned by the JVM and can be inspected with -XX:+PrintCompilation (which prints each compilation as it happens) or JFR's jdk.Compilation events.

Deoptimization is the JVM's escape hatch for speculative optimizations. C2 compiles based on assumptions — for example, that a virtual call site has only ever seen one concrete type, so it can inline the method directly (a monomorphic call). If a new type appears at that call site, the assumption is violated, and the compiled code cannot run — the JVM must deoptimize, discard the optimized code, and fall back to the interpreter or a less-specialized version. The mechanism is an uncommon trap: the compiled code checks the assumption at runtime, and if it fails, jumps to a slow path that triggers deoptimization. The event shows up in JFR as jdk.Deoptimization with a reason (uncommon trap, class hierarchy change, made not entrant). Frequent deoptimization is a performance problem because the code is re-interpreted and re-compiled, and it often indicates a polymorphic call site that the JIT keeps trying to specialize.

Escape analysis is the C2 optimization that determines whether an object can escape its allocating method or thread. If the object never escapes, the compiler can apply scalar replacement (breaking the object into its individual fields, allocated in registers or on the stack instead of the heap), lock elision (removing synchronized blocks on objects that are provably thread-local), and stack allocation (if the object fits and does not escape, it can live on the stack). These optimizations reduce allocation and GC pressure invisibly, and they are why microbenchmarks often report zero allocations for code that clearly allocates in source. They can also be disabled (-XX:-DoEscapeAnalysis) to see the difference, and they explain surprising behavior (for example, a large object that never escapes does not trigger a GC).

Safepoints are the mechanism the JVM uses to pause threads for operations that require a consistent view of the world. Most JVM operations that require stopping the world — garbage collection, deoptimization, biased locking revocation (in older JVMs), JFR sampling, thread dumps — are performed at safepoints. Between safepoints, a thread runs freely, but at every safepoint check, it asks the JVM whether a global pause is pending, and if so, parks. The JVM inserts safepoint checks at specific points: method returns, loop backedges (in counted loops), and other places the compiler can schedule them. The key insight is that a thread can only be paused at a safepoint, so the JVM must wait for every thread to reach one before the world stops. This is time-to-safepoint (TTSP), and it is separate from the pause duration itself: even a 1 ms GC pause can take 500 ms of wall time if some thread is running a long counted loop with no safepoint check. TTSP is why you sometimes see GC pause times that do not match the observed latency, and why loops with many iterations without safepoint checks can hurt latency. The fix is to add safepoint checks in hot loops (-XX:+UseCountedLoopSafepoints, default on in modern JVMs) or to avoid long-running counted loops in latency-sensitive code.

The interview-quality answer explains tiered compilation (C1 for startup, C2 for peak, both under the default tiered model), deoptimization and uncommon traps (speculative optimizations that fail), escape analysis (scalar replacement, lock elision, stack allocation), and the safepoint problem (threads must reach a check, and TTSP is separate from pause duration). That demonstrates you understand the JIT as a system with trade-offs, not as a black box labeled fast.
bullets: JIT: interpreter first, C1 (client, fast compile, moderate optimization) for startup, C2 (server, slow compile, aggressive optimization) for peak — tiered compilation (default since Java 8) uses both.
Hot detection uses invocation and backedge counters; a hot loop can trigger compilation of the enclosing method even if called once.

Deoptimization: C2 compiles on assumptions (monomorphic call sites, class hierarchy stability); when an assumption fails, an uncommon trap triggers deoptimization, and the method falls back to the interpreter or a less-optimized version.
Escape analysis enables scalar replacement (fields in registers/stack), lock elision (removing locks on provably-local objects), and stack allocation — invisible allocation reduction in hot code.
Safepoints are the JVM's global pause points (GC, deoptimization, JFR sampling, thread dumps); a thread can only pause at a safepoint check.
Time-to-safepoint (TTSP) is separate from pause duration — a long counted loop without safepoint checks delays every thread from pausing.
Diagnostics: -XX:+PrintCompilation for compilation events, JFR jdk.Compilation and jdk.Deoptimization, -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions for JIT internals.
cards.code:
Tiered compilation levels

  Level 0   interpreter
  Level 1-3 C1 with increasing profiling
  Level 4   C2 (aggressive optimization)

  Hot path: interpreted -> C1 compiled -> C2 compiled

Compilation flags (for diagnosis)

  -XX:+PrintCompilation
    -> prints each compilation (method, level, inlined size)

  -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions -XX:+PrintInlining
    -> prints which call sites were inlined and why

  -XX:-DoEscapeAnalysis
    -> disables escape analysis (to see its effect)

  -XX:CompileThreshold=<n>
    -> invocation count threshold (tiered usually handles this)

  -XX:+UseCountedLoopSafepoints   (default on modern JVMs)
    -> inserts safepoint checks in counted loops

Deoptimization reasons (JFR jdk.Deoptimization)

  uncommon_trap            -- a compiled assumption failed
  class_check              -- a class hierarchy change broke an assumption
  null_check               -- a null check failed in speculative code
  made_not_entrant         -- a class was redefined (JVMTI hotswap)

  -> frequent deopt -> re-interpret, re-compile, often a polymorphic
     call site that the JIT keeps trying to specialize

Escape analysis example

  // Source: allocates a Point object
  public int distanceSquared(int x, int y) {
      Point p = new Point(x, y);   // escapes? no -- p never leaves the method
      return p.x * p.x + p.y * p.y;
  }

  // C2 with escape analysis: scalar replacement
  //   -> allocates nothing on the heap; uses registers for p.x and p.y
  //   -> jmap -histo shows no Point instances from this method

  // Source: escapes
  public Point makePoint(int x, int y) {
      return new Point(x, y);      // escapes to caller -> real allocation
  }

Safepoint mechanics

  Every thread runs between safepoint checks.
  At each check, the thread asks: is a global pause pending?
  If yes -> park until the pause ends.

  Common safepoints:
    - GC (all STW phases)
    - deoptimization
    - biased locking revocation (older JVMs)
    - JFR sampling
    - thread dumps, heap dumps
    - code cache cleanup

  Time to safepoint (TTSP):
    the JVM must wait for every thread to reach a safepoint
    -> a long counted loop without a check delays every thread
    -> a 1 ms GC can cost 500 ms of wall time if TTSP is 500 ms

  Observability:
    -Xlog:safepoint=info
    JFR jdk.SafepointBegin / jdk.SafepointEnd

cards.title: Class Loading: Bootstrap, Platform, Application Loaders, Parent Delegation, and Classloader Leaks
cards.summary:
Class loading is how the JVM turns .class files into runtime Class objects. A ClassLoader is responsible for finding a class by name, reading its bytecode, and defining the class in the JVM. The key invariant is that a class is identified by both its fully qualified name and its defining classloader — two classes with the same name loaded by different classloaders are entirely different types, and casting an instance of one to the other throws ClassCastException even though the names match. This is the mechanism that makes servlet containers, Spring Boot fat jars, OSGi, and every plugin system possible.

There are three standard classloaders in Java 9+. Bootstrap is the primitive one: it loads the core JDK classes (java.lang.*, java.util.*, and other modules in the java.base module). It is implemented in native code and returns null from getClassLoader() when you ask a core class for its classloader. Platform (formerly Extension, renamed in Java 9 with the module system) loads JDK modules outside java.base — sql, xml, crypto, and so on. Application (also called System) loads the application classpath: the classes in your fat jar, the classes on the classpath, and any directories or JARs the application was launched with. Every user code class is normally loaded by the Application classloader. Custom classloaders (URLClassLoader, or a subclass you write) extend this chain and are used by containers, plugin systems, and build tools.

The parent delegation model is the loading protocol. When a classloader is asked for a class, it first delegates to its parent, and the parent delegates to its parent, up to Bootstrap. If Bootstrap finds the class, it returns it; only if no ancestor can find the class does the original loader try to load it itself. This is what prevents a user-defined java.lang.String from shadowing the real one — a malicious or accidental String class on the classpath is never loaded, because Bootstrap finds the real java.lang.String first. Parent delegation is the default and should normally not be overridden, but containers sometimes do (Tomcat's WebappClassLoader delegates in the reverse order for webapp classes, so two webapps can have different versions of the same library in the same JVM).

Class unloading is the classloader leak problem. A Class object is unloaded only when its defining classloader is garbage-collectable — that is, when there are no live references to the classloader, no live instances of its classes, no live Class objects, and no live threads with that classloader as context. In a long-running application server, a webapp's classloader can be retained by a single reference: a ThreadLocal set by the webapp but held by a pooled thread (container thread pools outlive the webapp), a JDBC driver registered in DriverManager (which holds a static reference to the webapp's class), a static field in a library cached by the container, or a thread started by the webapp that is still running. The symptom is Metaspace growth on every redeploy — the old classloaders cannot be collected, and their classes stay in Metaspace forever. The fixes are: clean up ThreadLocals in @PreDestroy, deregister JDBC drivers and MBeans, stop all threads the webapp started, and use a classloader-leak-prevention library (or Tomcat's leak prevention) if the framework is out of your control.

Dynamic proxies are a heavy user of class loading. A JDK dynamic proxy (java.lang.reflect.Proxy.newProxyInstance) generates a new class at runtime, one per (interface set, classloader) pair. That class is loaded by the same classloader as the interfaces, so it is unloaded when that classloader is unloaded (hence the same leak rules apply). CGLIB (used by Spring for subclass proxies) generates a subclass of the target class with bytecode manipulation, loaded by a classloader that can see the target class. Both mechanisms are also the reason that a Metaspace leak can be caused by an in-memory proxy cache that grows without bound — a good reason to keep proxy classes per (target, classloader) rather than per instance, and to avoid creating dynamic proxies in a hot loop.

The interview-quality answer names the three standard classloaders (Bootstrap, Platform, Application), explains parent delegation and why it prevents shadowing, explains class identity as (name, classloader) and its consequences (ClassCastException, container isolation), describes classloader leaks (ThreadLocal, JDBC driver, static references, running threads) and their Metaspace symptom, and ties dynamic proxies to class loading. That demonstrates you understand class loading as the foundation of containers and frameworks, not just as 'the thing that loads classes'.
bullets: Class identity is (fully qualified name + defining classloader) — two classes with the same name loaded by different classloaders are different types and cannot be cast.
Standard classloaders: Bootstrap (java.base, native), Platform (other JDK modules), Application/System (classpath and fat jar).
Parent delegation: every classloader asks its parent first, up to Bootstrap — this is why user code cannot shadow java.lang.String.
Class unloading requires the defining classloader to be garbage-collectable: no live instances, no live Class objects, no live threads with that classloader.

Classloader leaks retain the classloader and all its classes in Metaspace — common culprits are ThreadLocal on pooled threads, JDBC drivers registered in DriverManager, static references in cached libraries, and running threads.
Dynamic proxies (JDK, CGLIB) generate classes at runtime, loaded by a specific classloader — they are both a user of class loading and a potential Metaspace leak if cached without bound.
Diagnose Metaspace growth with jcmd VM.metaspace and MAT/YourKit classloader views — look for retained classloaders.
cards.code:
The three standard classloaders (Java 9+)

  Bootstrap    native, loads java.base (java.lang.*, java.util.*, ...)
  Platform     loads other JDK modules (java.sql, java.xml, java.crypto, ...)
               was Extension before Java 9
  Application  loads application classpath, fat jar contents
               (System classloader)

Parent delegation

  ClassLoader.loadClass(name):
    if parent != null: try parent.loadClass(name)
    else:              try Bootstrap (native)
    if not found:      findClass(name)   -- this loader's own search

  -> user-defined java.lang.String never wins: Bootstrap has it

Class identity and container isolation

  Same class name, different classloader:
    Class<?> a = loaderA.loadClass("com.example.Foo");
    Class<?> b = loaderB.loadClass("com.example.Foo");
    a == b            -> false (different classes)
    Object o = a.newInstance();
    b.cast(o)         -> ClassCastException (same name, different type)

  This is how Tomcat gives each webapp its own Spring version in one JVM.

Classloader leak (webapp redeploy)

  Webapp stops, but its classloader stays reachable ->
    Metaspace grows on every redeploy ->
    OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace after enough cycles

  Common leaks:
    - ThreadLocal<X> set on a container thread, not removed
        -> container thread lives forever -> retains webapp classloader
    - JDBC driver registered in java.sql.DriverManager
        -> DriverManager holds a static reference to the driver class
    - MBean registered in the platform MBeanServer
    - Static field in a shared library (e.g. caching framework)
        -> static -> webapp class -> webapp classloader
    - Thread started by the webapp still running after stop

  Fixes:
    - @PreDestroy / ServletContextListener.contextDestroyed to clean up
    - driver.deregister: DriverManager.deregisterDriver(driver)
    - unregister MBeans: MBeanServer.unregisterMBean(name)
    - stop all threads the webapp started
    - classloader-leak-prevention libraries for common offenders

Dynamic proxies and classloading

  // JDK proxy: generated class implements the interfaces
  //   loaded by the same classloader as the interfaces
  Foo proxy = (Foo) Proxy.newProxyInstance(
      Foo.class.getClassLoader(),
      new Class<?>[] { Foo.class },
      handler);

  // CGLIB proxy: generated subclass of the target class
  //   loaded by a classloader that can see the target class
  Foo proxy = (Foo) Enhancer.create(Foo.class, methodInterceptor);

  // Both are Metaspace consumers:
  //   cache proxies per (target, classloader), not per instance
  //   avoid creating proxies in hot loops

Diagnose Metaspace

  jcmd <pid> VM.metaspace
  -> shows committed/used/capacity per classloader

  jmap -clstats <pid>
  -> classloader statistics: how many classes each loader defined

  MAT / YourKit: 'Class Loader Explorer' -> find the retained classloaders
  and their GC roots

cards.title: Object Allocation and Reference Types: TLAB, Scalar Replacement, and Strong/Soft/Weak/Phantom
cards.summary:
Object allocation in Java is faster than many developers assume, and the JVM achieves this with a handful of techniques that interviewers like to probe. The first is bump-the-pointer: within a region of free space, allocation is just moving a pointer forward by the object size (plus alignment padding). There is no free-list search, no metadata traversal — just a pointer bump. The second is the Thread-Local Allocation Buffer (TLAB): because a shared bump pointer would need synchronization on every allocation, each thread gets its own small chunk of Eden (typically 1 to a few percent of Eden) and allocates from it without any lock. When the TLAB is exhausted, the thread requests a new one, which does need a brief synchronization — but that happens once per TLAB, not once per object. The third is zeroing: the JVM must zero new memory before use (Java guarantees field defaults), and this is done by the OS (zero-fill-on-demand pages) or by the allocator in bulk, not per field. These three together make new Object() in Java roughly as cheap as a stack allocation in C — a few nanoseconds, not a malloc call.

An object's memory layout is also worth knowing. Every object has a header: a mark word (a bit-packed field used for hash code, GC age, locking state) and a klass pointer (a reference to its Class metadata in Metaspace). The header is typically 12 bytes on 64-bit HotSpot (8-byte mark word + 4-byte compressed class pointer with -XX:+UseCompressedOops), and the object is padded to an 8-byte boundary. Instance fields follow the header, ordered by the JVM to minimize padding (longs and doubles first, then ints and floats, then shorts and chars, then bytes and booleans, then references — with references grouped together for compressed oops). A tiny object like new Object() is 16 bytes; a new Integer(42) is 16 bytes too; a String is 40-plus. These numbers come up in heap dump analysis and in back-of-the-envelope memory sizing.

Escape analysis and scalar replacement (covered in the JIT card) can eliminate allocations entirely for objects that do not escape their method or thread. For objects that do escape, allocation is real but cheap thanks to TLAB. The combination explains why Java allocation rates in the millions per second are normal, and why premature optimization to avoid small allocations is usually wrong — the JIT and the allocator together handle it. What matters for performance is retention, not allocation: objects that live a long time force GC work, while short-lived objects die in Eden cheaply.

Reference types are the JVM's mechanism for controlling how strongly an object is held. A strong reference (the default: Foo f = new Foo()) keeps the object alive as long as the reference is reachable. A SoftReference keeps the object alive but allows the GC to clear it under memory pressure — the classic use case is a cache that can shrink when heap is tight. The JVM clears soft references only when memory is low, so an application that holds only soft references will not OOM easily, but a cache built on soft references is a cache that silently shrinks at the worst possible moment. A WeakReference is cleared as soon as the object is only weakly reachable — WeakHashMap uses this to build a map whose entries disappear when their keys are no longer strongly referenced elsewhere. Weak references are the standard tool for canonicalizing maps and for observer registries that should not keep listeners alive. A PhantomReference is enqueued after the object is collected, allowing cleanup code to run (a mechanism for post-mortem cleanup, now largely superseded by Cleaner). Each reference type can be registered with a ReferenceQueue, which is how the program learns that the referenced object has been cleared or collected.

The discipline around reference types is: use them where a cache or an association should not prevent garbage collection, and never rely on SoftReference for correctness (the JVM may clear soft references at any time, so a soft cache must always have a reload path). Weak references are also a source of bugs when the value holds a strong reference to the key (a WeakHashMap<Key, Value> where Value has a field pointing back to Key keeps the key alive forever — the classic WeakHashMap self-reference trap). Phantom references are mostly used by libraries (DirectByteBuffer's Cleaner, Netty's leak detector) and rarely by application code, because Cleaner is simpler and safer for the same purpose.

The interview-quality answer explains bump-the-pointer and TLAB (fast allocation, per-thread, brief sync on TLAB refill), describes the object header and layout (mark word, klass pointer, field ordering, 8-byte padding), mentions escape analysis and scalar replacement as the elimination path for non-escaping objects, and covers the four reference types with their use cases (strong = default, soft = memory-pressure cache, weak = canonicalization / non-retaining references, phantom = post-mortem cleanup via ReferenceQueue / Cleaner). That demonstrates you understand allocation and memory retention as distinct concerns, which is the mental model behind most JVM performance work.
bullets: Allocation is fast: bump-the-pointer within free space, TLAB for lock-free per-thread allocation, bulk zeroing by the OS/allocator — no malloc-style free-list search.
Every object has a header: mark word (hash, GC age, lock state) and klass pointer (Class metadata); the object is padded to an 8-byte boundary; fields are reordered to minimize padding.
Escape analysis + scalar replacement can eliminate allocations entirely for objects that do not escape the method or thread — allocation in source does not always mean allocation on the heap.
Retention matters more than allocation: short-lived objects die cheaply in Eden; long-lived objects cause GC work. Optimize retention, not raw allocation count.

Strong reference (default) keeps the object alive; SoftReference can be cleared under memory pressure (caches); WeakReference is cleared as soon as only weakly reachable (WeakHashMap, canonical maps); PhantomReference is enqueued after collection for cleanup.
A WeakHashMap value that strongly references its key keeps the key alive forever — the classic self-reference trap.
ReferenceQueue lets the program learn when a reference is cleared or collected; Cleaner (java.lang.ref.Cleaner, Java 9+) supersedes PhantomReference for most cleanup use cases.

cards.title: GC Algorithms & Collectors Deep Dive: Serial, Parallel, G1, ZGC, and Shenandoah
cards.summary:
Every JVM garbage collector balances three competing goals: throughput (percentage of CPU spent running application code rather than GC), latency (duration of Stop-The-World pauses), and memory footprint (metadata and headroom required by the collector). All modern HotSpot collectors are tracing collectors: they start from GC Roots—active local variables and parameters on thread stacks, static fields of loaded classes, active JNI references, and monitor/synchronization locks—and trace the live object graph using tri-color marking (White = unvisited/candidate for collection, Gray = visited but children not yet scanned, Black = visited with all children scanned). Once live objects are identified, generational collectors exploit the Weak Generational Hypothesis (most objects die young, often within milliseconds in Eden) by copying survivors to a fresh region rather than sweeping in place. Copying compacts memory automatically, leaving zero fragmentation and preserving fast bump-the-pointer allocation.

Serial GC (-XX:+UseSerialGC) uses a single GC thread and pauses all application threads at a safepoint for both Young and Old collections. Because it has tiny metadata overhead and zero thread-coordination cost, it is actually the right choice for tiny single-core containers (< 100 MB–256 MB heap) or short-lived CLI tools. Parallel GC (-XX:+UseParallelGC, the default in Java 8) uses multiple GC threads during STW pauses to finish collection as fast as possible. It delivers the highest raw throughput for batch/ETL jobs, but its Old Gen Full GC pause scales linearly with heap size—a 16 GB heap can freeze for seconds.

G1 GC (-XX:+UseG1GC, default since Java 9) replaces rigid contiguous Young/Old spaces with ~2,048 equal-sized regions (1 MB to 32 MB each) dynamically assigned as Eden, Survivor, Old, or Humongous (any object larger than 50% of a region). To avoid scanning the entire Old Gen during a Young GC, G1 maintains a Card Table (512-byte memory chunks) and per-region Remembered Sets (RSets) updated by write barriers whenever an Old object points to a Young object. G1 runs in distinct phases: (1) Young-Only Evacuation (STW, copies Eden/Survivors); (2) Initial Mark (piggybacked on a Young GC, STW); (3) Concurrent Marking (runs alongside app threads to rank Old regions by garbage density); (4) Remark & Cleanup (short STW); and (5) Mixed GC (evacuates all Young regions plus the 'Garbage First' Old regions that fit inside -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis, default 200ms). Two classic G1 production traps: setting -Xmn/-XX:NewSize explicitly (which prevents G1 from shrinking Young Gen to meet your pause target) and frequent Humongous allocations (> 50% region size), which go straight to Old Gen, fragment regions, and trigger an Evacuation Failure ('to-space exhausted')—falling back to a slow Full GC.

ZGC (-XX:+UseZGC) and Shenandoah (-XX:+UseShenandoahGC) break the link between heap size and pause time, keeping STW pauses under 1 millisecond even on multi-terabyte heaps. Classic collectors must freeze the world while relocating objects so application threads never read a stale memory address. ZGC solves this concurrently using colored pointers (storing GC state metadata in unused upper bits of 64-bit references) and load barriers (a few CPU instructions executed when reading an object reference from the heap: if the pointer's color shows the object was moved, the barrier reads the forwarding table and self-heals the reference on the fly). Shenandoah uses a similar concurrent compaction model with Brooks forwarding pointers and load/store barriers. In Java 21+, Generational ZGC (-XX:+UseZGC -XX:+ZGenerational) separates Young and Old regions so short-lived objects are collected cheaply without scanning the whole heap—drastically reducing the allocation-stall risk where app threads outpace the concurrent collector. The trade-off for ZGC/Shenandoah is ~5-15% CPU overhead from barriers and needing extra heap headroom (~20-30%) so concurrent relocation finishes before the heap fills up.

In interviews, never recite 20 obscure GC flags. State the workload-driven rule: use Parallel GC for offline batch throughput, G1 GC for balanced microservices (tune only -Xmx and -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis, and bump -XX:G1HeapRegionSize if Humongous objects appear), and Generational ZGC for strict sub-10ms p99 services or huge heaps—and always inspect -Xlog:gc* before touching any flag.
bullets: Tri-color marking from GC Roots (stack locals, statics, JNI handles) + Weak Generational Hypothesis (most objects die in Eden).
Serial GC: single-threaded STW, lowest footprint—best for tiny single-core containers. Parallel GC: multi-threaded STW, max throughput for batch jobs.
G1 GC (default Java 9+): ~2,048 dynamic regions + Card Tables/RSets to avoid full-heap scans; targets MaxGCPauseMillis (200ms default).
G1 traps: never hardcode -Xmn (breaks pause-time auto-sizing), and watch for Humongous allocations (> 50% region size) causing Evacuation Failures.
ZGC & Shenandoah: sub-millisecond STW pauses independent of heap size via concurrent relocation + load barriers (colored pointers in ZGC).
Generational ZGC (Java 21+, -XX:+ZGenerational) collects Young objects separately, cutting CPU/headroom overhead and preventing allocation stalls.
Tuning rule: size heap cleanly, pick the collector for your SLA (throughput vs latency), and read -Xlog:gc* logs before adding flags.
cards.code:
Collector Trade-Off Matrix

  Collector       Flag                           STW Pause       Throughput   Best For
  --------------  -----------------------------  --------------  -----------  -----------------------------
  Serial          -XX:+UseSerialGC               10s-100s ms     Low          <256 MB heap, 1 CPU core
  Parallel        -XX:+UseParallelGC             100ms - 2s+     Highest      Batch / ETL / offline compute
  G1 (default)    -XX:+UseG1GC                   10 - 200 ms     High         General microservices
  Gen ZGC (21+)   -XX:+UseZGC -XX:+ZGenerational < 1 ms (flat)   High (-5%)   Strict p99 APIs, huge heaps
  Shenandoah      -XX:+UseShenandoahGC           < 1 - 5 ms      High (-5%)   Low-latency (OpenJDK/RedHat)

G1 Remembered Set (RSet) & Card Table
  Old Region [Card 512B] --write barrier--> marks card dirty if Old obj points to Young obj
  Young GC only scans dirty cards in RSets, NOT the entire Old Gen!

G1 Humongous Allocation Trap
  4 GB Heap -> 2 MB Region Size -> Any array > 1 MB (50%) = Humongous Object
  Fix: -XX:G1HeapRegionSize=4m (or 8m) + check allocation flame graphs

Modern Unified GC Logging (Java 9+)
  -Xlog:gc*:file=/var/log/gc.log:time,uptime,level,tags:filecount=5,filesize=20m

cards.title: JNI & Foreign Function API (Project Panama): Native Interop, Pinning, and Safety
cards.summary:
Java Native Interface (JNI) is the bridge that lets JVM bytecode call native C/C++ libraries (.so, .dll, .dylib) and lets native code inspect or manipulate Java objects. In production, JNI powers workloads that pure Java either cannot express or cannot run fast enough: OS-specific syscalls not in the JDK, hardware-accelerated cryptography and TLS (Netty's `netty-tcnative` wrapping BoringSSL/OpenSSL), embedded storage engines (RocksDB in Kafka Streams/Flink), compression (Zstd, LZ4), and GPU/SIMD machine learning runtimes (ONNX, TensorFlow, PyTorch).

The biggest risk of JNI is that it completely bypasses the JVM's memory-safety sandbox. Native C/C++ code does not throw `NullPointerException` or `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`—a buffer overflow, use-after-free, or dereferenced null pointer causes a `SIGSEGV` segmentation fault that kills the entire JVM process instantly with an `hs_err_pid.log` crash file, bypassing every `try/catch` block. Even without crashes, JNI leaks are invisible to Java heap dumps because `malloc()` memory lives off-heap in native RSS; tracking them requires `-XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary` (`jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory`) or OS tools like `valgrind`/`jemalloc` profiling.

Performance in JNI is governed by three hidden costs that frequently surprise engineers. First, call-boundary overhead: every JNI call forces the JVM to transition thread state from `_thread_in_Java` to `_thread_in_native`, spill CPU registers, marshal arguments, and block JIT inlining across the boundary. Calling a tiny native function (like a 10-line math helper) inside a tight loop is routinely slower than pure Java because the JIT cannot inline or optimize across the JNI wall. Second, GC pinning and critical sections: when native code needs access to a Java `byte[]` via `GetByteArrayElements`, the JVM must either copy the entire array into C memory (O(n) allocation + copy cost) or pin the memory. If you use `GetPrimitiveArrayCritical` to get a raw pointer without copying, the JVM suppresses GC relocation (or pins the G1 region—region pinning was improved in Java 22 G1, JEP 423, but older JDKs stall GC globally), which can delay safepoints and spike p99 latency across completely unrelated threads! Third, JNI lookups (`FindClass`, `GetMethodID`) are slow string-based reflective lookups if not cached.

Project Panama—finalized in Java 22 as the **Foreign Function & Memory (FFM) API** (JEP 454)—modernizes native interop and solves most of JNI's pain points in pure Java. Instead of writing C header files (`javah`), C glue wrappers, and platform-specific builds, FFM lets you load a shared library and bind C functions directly in Java using `Linker.nativeLinker()` and `MethodHandle` (`downcallHandle`), which the JIT understands and optimizes far better than JNI. For off-heap memory, FFM replaces raw unsafe pointers and brittle `DirectByteBuffer` cleaners with `MemorySegment` and `Arena`. An `Arena` (`Arena.ofConfined()` for single-thread, `Arena.ofShared()` for multi-thread) gives deterministic, scoped deallocation via `try-with-resources`, automatic bounds checking on every read/write, and immediate use-after-free protection (accessing a segment after its `Arena` closes throws `IllegalStateException` in Java rather than silently corrupting memory or segfaulting).

In interviews, frame the decision clearly: avoid JNI/FFM for chatty, fine-grained calls (JIT pure Java wins); use it only for coarse-grained native engines (RocksDB, OpenSSL, codecs, BLAS/SIMD); prefer FFM API over JNI on Java 22+ for safety, deterministic `Arena` cleanup, and zero C glue code; and always watch out for `GetPrimitiveArrayCritical` stalling GC/safepoints on older JDKs.
bullets: JNI runs outside the JVM sandbox: a C/C++ segfault (SIGSEGV) crashes the entire JVM immediately—no try/catch can catch it.
JNI overhead: JIT cannot inline across the JNI boundary, thread-state transitions add fixed cost, and FindClass/GetMethodID must be cached.

GC Pinning Trap: GetPrimitiveArrayCritical hands C a raw Java array pointer by suppressing/pinning GC—stalling safepoints and spiking p99 latency across all threads (mitigated partially by G1 region pinning in Java 22+).
Off-heap JNI leaks don't appear in heap dumps—diagnose with Native Memory Tracking (NMT) and process RSS monitoring.

Project Panama / FFM API (Java 22+): pure-Java native calls via Linker + MethodHandle (no C glue code) and safe off-heap memory via MemorySegment + Arena (bounds-checked, deterministic free via try-with-resources).
Rule of thumb: only cross the native boundary for coarse-grained work (crypto, RocksDB, codecs, ML/GPU)—never per-item in a tight loop.

cards.title: JVM Diagnostics: jcmd, jstack, jstat, jmap, JFR, async-profiler, and Heap Dumps
cards.summary:
When a production Java service freezes, burns 100% CPU, or climbs steadily toward an OOMKill, guessing from application logs rarely works. Senior backend interviews test whether you know which diagnostic tool answers which symptom—and critically, which tools are safe to run on live traffic versus which ones freeze the JVM.

First, know `jcmd <pid>`: since Java 7+, `jcmd` is the unified diagnostic CLI that replaces older standalone tools (`jstack`, `jmap`, `jinfo`). Running `jcmd <pid> help` lists every command supported by that running JVM. For hung requests, thread leaks, or high CPU, take **3 thread dumps 5 seconds apart** using `jcmd <pid> Thread.print` (or `jstack <pid>`). Comparing 3 snapshots separates transient waits from real deadlocks: threads stuck in `BLOCKED` waiting on the exact same monitor lock ID indicate contention or deadlocks (the output includes a `Found one Java-level deadlock` section at the bottom), while threads stuck in `RUNNABLE` on the exact same stack frame across all 3 dumps point to an infinite loop or catastrophic regex backtracking.

Second, beware of **safepoint bias** in traditional CPU profilers. Tools like `jstack` or VisualVM sampler can only inspect thread stacks when threads reach a JVM safepoint. If a hot method is running an unrolled loop or tight math without frequent safepoint checks, the sampler waits until the method exits to a safepoint—blaming the *wrong* method in your profile! **async-profiler** solves this by using OS `perf_events` + JVM `AsyncGetCallTrace` to sample threads asynchronously at any instruction without waiting for safepoints, producing accurate CPU and allocation **flame graphs** (wide flat plateaus at the top = where CPU/allocations actually burn). **Java Flight Recorder (JFR)** (`jcmd <pid> JFR.start duration=60s settings=profile filename=/tmp/rec.jfr`) is built directly into OpenJDK/HotSpot with < 1-2% overhead, capturing GC pauses, lock contention (`jdk.JavaMonitorEnter`), thread allocations (`jdk.ObjectAllocationInNewTLAB`), and JIT deoptimizations continuously in production.

Third, for memory leaks and GC pressure, start safely with `jstat -gcutil <pid> 1000`. Every 1 second, it prints live percentages for Survivor (`S0`, `S1`), Eden (`E`), Old Gen (`O`), Metaspace (`M`), Young GC count/time (`YGC`/`YGCT`), and Full GC count/time (`FGC`/`FGCT`) with virtually zero overhead. If Old Gen (`O`) creeps toward 99% and never drops after Full GCs, you have a memory leak (unbounded cache, static collection, or unclosed listener). Next, run `jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram` (or `jmap -histo <pid>`—avoid `:live` on busy prod pods because `:live` forces a Full GC!) to see which class has millions of instances.

Finally, capturing a **Heap Dump** (`jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump /tmp/heap.hprof`) writes the entire live heap to disk and pauses the JVM during the dump. Never run this blindly on a 16–32 GB production pod still taking load balancer traffic—the STW pause will trigger HTTP 504s and Kubernetes liveness-probe restarts. Instead, either drain the pod out of service first, or configure `-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/var/log/dumps/` so the JVM dumps automatically on crash. Open the `.hprof` in **Eclipse MAT**: skip the raw Histogram first and open the **Dominator Tree**—it sorts objects by **Retained Heap** (how much total memory would be freed if that single object were GC'd), then run *Path to GC Roots (exclude weak/soft refs)* to pinpoint the exact static map or thread holding the leak.
bullets: jcmd <pid> is the modern unified CLI (Thread.print, GC.class_histogram, GC.heap_dump, VM.native_memory, JFR.start).
Thread dumps (3x, 5s apart): BLOCKED on same monitor = lock contention/deadlock; RUNNABLE on same line = infinite loop/CPU spin.
Safepoint bias: jstack/VisualVM only sample at safepoints and misreport CPU hotspots; async-profiler (OS perf_events) avoids safepoint bias and generates flame graphs.
JFR (Java Flight Recorder): built-in, < 1-2% overhead in production; records GC pauses, lock contention, TLAB allocations, and JIT deoptimizations.
jstat -gcutil <pid> 1000: zero-risk live GC monitor. Watch Old Gen (O) after Full GCs—if it stays near 100%, you have a retention leak.
Heap dump safety: GC.heap_dump and jmap -histo:live trigger STW pauses—drain traffic first or use -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError.
Eclipse MAT triage: check Dominator Tree (Retained Heap, not just Shallow Heap) -> 'Path to GC Roots' to find what is holding the leak.
cards.code:
# 1. Live GC health every 1s (safe in prod)
jstat -gcutil <pid> 1000
#  S0     S1     E      O      M     YGC   YGCT    FGC   FGCT
#  0.00  42.1  68.4   98.7   91.2   412   3.812   14   18.420  <-- O=98.7% + FGC climbing = LEAK

# 2. Thread dumps (take 3x, 5s apart) & JFR recording (<2% overhead)
jcmd <pid> Thread.print > /tmp/tdump1.txt
jcmd <pid> JFR.start name=prod settings=profile duration=60s filename=/tmp/app.jfr

# 3. async-profiler CPU + Allocation flame graphs (no safepoint bias)
./asprof -d 30 -e cpu -f /tmp/cpu-flame.html <pid>
./asprof -d 30 -e alloc -f /tmp/alloc-flame.html <pid>

# 4. Class histogram & Heap Dump (drain pod traffic first!)
jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram | head -n 25
jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump /tmp/heap.hprof

# 5. Off-heap / Native memory check (needs -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary)
jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary

quizzes.question: A developer overrides equals() on a User class to compare by email but forgets to override hashCode(), then adds 100 users to a HashSet and two of them share the same email. What happens at insertion?
options: Both are stored because HashSet compares by reference and sees them as different objects
Only the first is stored because HashSet falls back to equals() when hashes collide
Both are stored because HashSet falls back to identity hashCode() from Object, so 'equal' users hash to different buckets and both get inserted
The second is rejected with an IllegalStateException
quizzes.explanation: HashSet uses a two-stage lookup: hashCode() finds the bucket, equals() finds the entry within it. Without overriding hashCode(), both users inherit Object's identity-based hashCode and hash to different buckets, so equals() is never consulted. Both are inserted, silently violating the Set's 'no duplicates' guarantee. Option B is wrong because with different hashCodes, equals is never even called.

quizzes.question: Given `Thread t = new Thread(() -> process()); t.run();`, what happens?
options: A new OS thread is created and process() runs on it
process() runs synchronously on the caller's thread; no new thread is created
t enters RUNNABLE state and process() runs asynchronously
The JVM throws IllegalThreadStateException
quizzes.explanation: run() is an ordinary method — calling it directly executes the task body on the calling thread, synchronously. Only start() asks the JVM to allocate a new OS thread and then invoke run() on it. The code compiles and runs without error, which is why this bug reaches production.

quizzes.question: You create a ThreadPoolExecutor with corePoolSize=10, maximumPoolSize=100, and a default LinkedBlockingQueue<>(). Under sustained load, active threads stay at 10 and the queue grows without limit. Why?
options: The pool forgot to set keepAliveTime, so extra threads time out
LinkedBlockingQueue's default constructor uses Integer.MAX_VALUE capacity, so the queue is never 'full' and maximumPoolSize is never triggered
ThreadPoolExecutor always caps at corePoolSize regardless of configuration
The rejection handler silently discards tasks, masking thread creation
quizzes.explanation: The task flow is: core threads → enqueue → only if queue is full and active < max, spawn more. With an unbounded queue, the enqueue step never fails, so max is never reached. This is why Executors.newFixedThreadPool (which uses exactly this unbounded queue) is unsafe for production — memory grows until OOM.

quizzes.question: A user-facing HTTP service submits jobs to Executors.newFixedThreadPool(10) with an unbounded queue. During a spike, 500k jobs queue up and the service runs out of memory. What is the correct fix?
options: Increase the pool size to 500,000 so all jobs run immediately
Replace with Executors.newCachedThreadPool so threads scale with load
Construct a ThreadPoolExecutor with a bounded ArrayBlockingQueue and an explicit CallerRunsPolicy for backpressure, plus timeouts on submission
Use ForkJoinPool.commonPool() for the jobs
quizzes.explanation: The root cause is the unbounded queue absorbing load until memory dies. A bounded queue plus CallerRunsPolicy gives natural backpressure — the submitting thread executes the task itself, slowing submission. Increasing pool size just delays the same failure; newCachedThreadPool replaces an unbounded queue with unbounded thread creation (thread-explosion OOM); ForkJoinPool.commonPool is shared and CPU-sized, which is even worse for IO jobs.

quizzes.question: A CompletableFuture pipeline has multiple thenApplyAsync stages, no exceptionally/handle/whenComplete attached anywhere, and one of the async stages throws a RuntimeException. What does the caller (who never calls get or join on the result) observe?
options: The exception propagates to the main thread and crashes the JVM
The exception is logged automatically by the JVM
Nothing — the CompletableFuture completes exceptionally and, without a handler attached downstream, the exception is silently swallowed
The pipeline automatically retries the failed stage
quizzes.explanation: CompletableFuture does not print or propagate exceptions. If no exceptionally, handle, or whenComplete is attached and the caller never inspects the future via get/join, the exception is lost — a classic production bug. Always attach a handler or ensure the result is awaited somewhere.

quizzes.question: A User class implements compareTo to sort by email, but equals() compares by id. You add two users with the same email but different ids to a TreeSet. What is the result?
options: Both are stored because equals() determines uniqueness
Only the first is stored — TreeSet uses compareTo (returns 0) to detect duplicates, silently dropping the second
TreeSet throws a ClassCastException at insertion
TreeSet falls back to hashCode() and stores both
quizzes.explanation: TreeSet is a red-black tree that uses compareTo/compare to place elements and to detect duplicates. When compareTo returns 0, the element is treated as a duplicate and not added — even though equals() would return false. This is why the contract requires compareTo/compare to be consistent with equals.

quizzes.question: What is the result of `String a = "hello"; String b = new String("hello"); System.out.println(a == b);`?
options: true — the compiler interns both strings to the same pool object
false — a is interned in the pool, b is a fresh heap object; == compares references
true — String overrides == to compare content
Compile error — you cannot compare Strings with ==
quizzes.explanation: String literals like "hello" are interned into the JVM's string pool at compile/class-load time and reference the same instance across the codebase. new String("hello") explicitly allocates a new object outside the pool. == compares references, so they are not equal. a.equals(b) returns true because content matches. You cannot override ==, so option C is wrong.

quizzes.question: A developer builds a 10,000-character log line with `String s = ""; for (int i = 0; i < 10_000; i++) s += "x";` and it takes seconds. Why?
options: String concatenation always uses the String pool, which is slow under load
Each += allocates a new immutable String and copies all previous characters — O(n²) total work
The JIT compiler does not optimize String operations, so the loop runs in the interpreter
Concatenation triggers a Full GC on every iteration
quizzes.explanation: String is immutable: s += "x" is equivalent to s = new StringBuilder().append(s).append("x").toString() (roughly). Each iteration creates a new String of growing length and copies the entire previous content, so total work is 1+2+3+...+n = O(n²). Use StringBuilder to accumulate in a mutable buffer.

quizzes.question: A developer says 'Spring is a library that I call to create objects.' Why is this an inaccurate description of Spring's IoC container?
options: Spring is a compiler plugin, not a library or container
IoC inverts control — the container owns creation, wiring, and lifecycle of your beans; your code declares what it needs rather than calling a factory
Spring is only a collection of utility classes and has no container
Spring only works with databases, not with general objects
quizzes.explanation: The defining principle of IoC is that control is inverted: instead of your code calling constructors and wiring dependencies, a container manages object creation, dependency resolution, lifecycle callbacks, and proxying. Spring's ApplicationContext is that container. Spring does ship utility libraries, but its core value is the container that owns your beans.

quizzes.question: Two beans of type PaymentClient exist — StripePaymentClient and PaypalPaymentClient — and OrderService has @Autowired PaymentClient client with no @Qualifier or @Primary. What does Spring do at startup?
options: Picks the bean whose name is alphabetically first
Picks the bean whose name matches the field name 'client' if -parameters is enabled; otherwise throws NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException
Silently injects null and continues
Always picks the bean declared last in the container
quizzes.explanation: The resolution chain is: unique type → @Qualifier → @Primary → bean-name fallback (requires -parameters to preserve parameter names; enabled by default in Spring Boot) → error. If the field name 'client' does not match either bean name and no qualifier/primary exists, Spring throws NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException at startup. It never silently injects null for a required dependency.

quizzes.question: A class has @Transactional on a public method, but when it calls another @Transactional method on itself (this.otherMethod()), no transaction is started. Why?
options: Spring does not support transactions on public methods
The AOP proxy is bypassed on self-invocation — the internal call goes directly to the target instance, not through the proxy
The @Transactional annotation must be repeated on every method call site
Spring Boot disables @Transactional by default
quizzes.explanation: Spring's @Transactional is implemented via a BeanPostProcessor that wraps the bean in a proxy during postProcessAfterInitialization. External callers hit the proxy, which starts the transaction, then invokes the target. Self-invocation (this.otherMethod()) bypasses the proxy entirely and calls the raw method — no transaction is started. The fix is to extract the second method into another bean, use @Transactional on the outer method only, or use TransactionTemplate.

quizzes.question: Which statement about @Service and @Component is most accurate?
options: They register beans with different lifetimes — @Service is always singleton, @Component can be prototype
@Service is functionally identical to @Component at runtime; the difference is semantic, signaling business logic to readers and tools
@Service is required for @Transactional to work
@Component is only for controllers, @Service is for repositories
quizzes.explanation: @Service is meta-annotated with @Component and produces identical bean registration behavior. Its value is documentation and tooling. Only @Repository has additional runtime behavior (persistence exception translation). Only @Controller affects MVC handler mapping. @Transactional works on any Spring bean, not just @Service-annotated classes.

quizzes.question: A service class uses field injection (@Autowired PaymentClient client). In a unit test that does new OrderService(), the client field is null and calls throw NullPointerException. Why?
options: Field injection is deprecated and does not work in production
Field injection is performed by Spring via reflection after construction; without a Spring context, the field is never set
PaymentClient must be annotated with @Primary
Field injection requires the field to be static
quizzes.explanation: Field injection is a container feature — Spring uses reflection to set the field during bean population. A plain new OrderService() creates the object but never populates fields, so the field stays null. Constructor injection avoids this because the test passes dependencies explicitly. This is one of the standard arguments for preferring constructor injection.

quizzes.question: Bean A has a constructor that takes Bean B, and Bean B has a constructor that takes Bean A. Both are @Service. What happens at startup, and why?
options: Spring resolves it via the three-level cache — the cycle is broken automatically
Spring throws BeanCurrentlyInCreationException because constructor injection cannot satisfy a cycle; the three-level cache only works for field/setter injection
Spring injects null for one of the parameters and warns in logs
Spring retries construction until the cycle resolves
quizzes.explanation: To construct A you need a fully constructed B; to construct B you need a fully constructed A. Neither can be created first, so Spring fails fast with BeanCurrentlyInCreationException. The three-level singleton cache only works when a bean can be instantiated without its dependencies (no-arg constructor) and have them populated afterward via field or setter — that is exactly what constructor injection forbids.

quizzes.question: Why does Spring's singleton cache have three levels (singletonObjects, earlySingletonObjects, singletonFactories) instead of just two?
options: Three levels are required by the Java Memory Model for visibility of shared state
The singletonFactories level can decide at exposure time whether to hand out the raw bean or an AOP proxy, so cyclic beans still see the proxied version (e.g. @Transactional works)
Three levels improve cache lookup performance by a factor of three
The third level exists only for backwards compatibility with Spring 2.x
quizzes.explanation: During a cycle, an early reference to a partially constructed bean must be exposed so other beans can hold it. If that bean is proxied (due to @Transactional, @Async, etc.), the early reference must be the proxy — otherwise the other bean holds the raw instance and AOP silently bypasses. singletonFactories holds an ObjectFactory that can produce the proxy on demand, giving Spring the ability to wrap the reference before exposure. earlySingletonObjects caches the exposed result so repeated lookups are consistent.

quizzes.question: A service has @Transactional on a public method, and a call to that method from outside the class correctly starts a transaction. But when the same method calls another @Transactional method on the same class (this.other()), no new transaction is started. Why?
options: Spring requires @Transactional to be on a final method to open a new transaction
Self-invocation goes directly to the raw target instance, bypassing the proxy that would otherwise start the transaction
Spring disables transactions on methods called internally for safety
Constructor injection prevents self-invocation transactions
quizzes.explanation: Spring's @Transactional is installed via an AOP proxy that external callers hit. A self-call (this.other()) executes on the target instance directly, never touching the proxy, so the interceptor that would start the transaction is never invoked. The fixes are: extract the second method into another bean, use TransactionTemplate, or AspectJ load-time weaving. Option A is the opposite of the truth — final methods cannot be proxied and their @Transactional is silently ignored.

quizzes.question: A @Service class has no interfaces and a @Transactional method marked final. External calls reach the method without errors, but no transaction appears in the logs. What is the most likely cause?
options: Spring does not support transactions on classes without interfaces
CGLIB cannot override final methods, so the proxy does not intercept the call — @Transactional is silently ignored
The class needs a @Repository annotation to enable transactions
Final methods require @Transactional(propagation = MANDATORY)
quizzes.explanation: Without an interface, Spring uses CGLIB, which generates a subclass and overrides methods. Final methods cannot be overridden, so the interception point does not exist and @Transactional has no effect. Spring does not warn you — the annotation is a no-op on a final method. Transactions work fine without interfaces when methods are non-final. Neither @Repository nor propagation affects this.

quizzes.question: Inside @Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false), method jdbc() calls ds() directly to build a JdbcTemplate. Compared to the default proxyBeanMethods=true, what happens?
options: Nothing changes — @Bean methods always return the same singleton
ds() is called as a plain Java method with the proxy disabled, so a new DataSource is created every time jdbc() runs, causing duplicate connection pools
Spring throws a compile error because @Bean methods cannot call each other in lite mode
The DataSource bean is registered twice with different names
quizzes.explanation: With proxyBeanMethods=false, Spring does not create the CGLIB subclass that intercepts @Bean method calls, so ds() runs as ordinary Java code and builds a fresh DataSource each time. Only the DataSource returned by Spring's own invocation is registered as a bean; the one created inside jdbc() is a duplicate that lives outside the container. The fix is to inject DataSource as a parameter instead of calling ds().

quizzes.question: Which BeanPostProcessor actually installs @Transactional proxies around beans?
options: AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor
CommonAnnotationBeanPostProcessor
AbstractAutoProxyCreator (and its subclasses like InfrastructureAdvisorAutoProxyCreator)
ConfigurationClassPostProcessor
quizzes.explanation: AbstractAutoProxyCreator and its infrastructure variants are BeanPostProcessors whose postProcessAfterInitialization checks each bean for matching advisors (from @Transactional, @Cacheable, @Async, @PreAuthorize, etc.) and returns an AOP proxy wrapping the original. AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor handles @Autowired/@Value injection; CommonAnnotationBeanPostProcessor invokes @PostConstruct/@PreDestroy; ConfigurationClassPostProcessor is a BeanFactoryPostProcessor that parses @Configuration classes — it runs before any bean is instantiated.

quizzes.question: During startup you see 'Bean myService is not eligible for getting processed by all BeanPostProcessors (for example: not eligible for auto-proxying)'. What is the practical consequence?
options: The bean will not be created and startup will fail
myService was created too early — before the auto-proxy-creator BPP was ready — so @Transactional/@Async on its methods will silently not apply
The bean is automatically switched to prototype scope
The bean is registered twice in the container
quizzes.explanation: BPPs themselves (and their dependencies) are instantiated before the rest of the beans. If myService is created during that early phase — because a BPP depends on it, or a BFPP instantiates it — the auto-proxy BPP has not yet been registered and myService never gets wrapped. Startup does not fail; the bug is silent. The fix is to remove the early dependency (usually use ObjectProvider<MyService> inside the BPP instead of direct injection).

quizzes.title: What Is Spring Boot and Why Does It Exist on Top of Spring?
quizzes.summary:
Spring Framework, for all its power, is painful to start a project with. Setting up a web app in vanilla Spring requires: an XML file or a @Configuration class for the DispatcherServlet, a servlet container (Tomcat) downloaded and configured separately, a Jackson ObjectMapper configured correctly, a DataSource bean wired to a database driver, a transaction manager, a connection pool, plus manually curated dependency versions in Maven or Gradle. The problem is not that any one step is hard — it is that every new Spring project requires all of them, and every version mismatch between Spring 5.3.x, Jackson 2.13.x, Hibernate 5.6.x, and Tomcat 9 is a debugging session waiting to happen.

Spring Boot's core thesis is Convention over Configuration: pick sensible defaults for common choices, let the developer override only what they care about, and make the whole thing runnable as a single jar. Concretely, Spring Boot contributes four things on top of Spring: (1) Starters — curated dependency bundles (spring-boot-starter-web pulls Spring MVC, Jackson, Tomcat, and validation, all version-compatible); (2) Auto-configuration — Spring Boot inspects what is on the classpath and configures beans automatically (if H2 is on the classpath and no DataSource bean exists, Boot creates an in-memory one); (3) An embedded server — Tomcat, Jetty, or Undertow is packaged inside the jar, so `java -jar app.jar` is a runnable web server with no external install; (4) Actuator — production features like health checks, metrics, and environment inspection out of the box.

The distinction people get wrong: Spring Boot is NOT a replacement for Spring. It is Spring — the same ApplicationContext, the same @Service, @Autowired, @Transactional, the same AOP, the same bean lifecycle. Spring Boot adds a launcher (@SpringBootApplication), a dependency management layer, a classpath-driven auto-configuration mechanism, and production defaults. If you are debugging a @Transactional issue in a Spring Boot app, you are using Spring's @Transactional — Boot does not change how it works. If you are debugging circular dependencies, you are using Spring's bean lifecycle — Boot only sets allow-circular-references=false by default.

A good analogy: vanilla Spring is a fully stocked professional kitchen where you must organize every utensil yourself; Spring Boot is the same kitchen pre-arranged with a default layout, common ingredients stocked, and a recipe book open on the counter — you can rearrange anything, but the default setup gets you cooking in five minutes. The kitchen is the same; the arrangement is different.

The interview-relevant mental model: @SpringBootApplication on a main class is a composed annotation of @SpringBootConfiguration (a @Configuration class), @EnableAutoConfiguration (turn on classpath-driven bean provisioning), and @ComponentScan (scan the current package and below). When main() calls SpringApplication.run(...), Boot builds an ApplicationContext, runs auto-configuration, starts the embedded server, and fires ApplicationReadyEvent. Everything else — starters, actuators, embedded Tomcat — is a layer on that context. If you understand the context, you understand the app; if you understand only the annotations, you are memorizing.
bullets: Spring Boot is Spring + convention over configuration; same IoC container, same annotations, same AOP.
Four contributions on top of Spring: starters (curated deps), auto-configuration (classpath-driven beans), embedded server, Actuator.
@SpringBootApplication = @SpringBootConfiguration + @EnableAutoConfiguration + @ComponentScan.
The embedded server means java -jar app.jar is a fully self-contained web application — no external Tomcat.
If you are debugging a bean or a transaction in Spring Boot, you are debugging Spring — Boot does not change that behavior.

quizzes.title: What Happens Inside Spring Boot During Startup: Step-by-Step Sequence
quizzes.summary:
When you call SpringApplication.run(Application.class, args), Spring Boot executes a well-defined sequence that lasts from 'JVM started main' to 'ApplicationReadyEvent fired and the port is listening'. Understanding this sequence is what lets you debug slow startups, order-of-initialization bugs, and 'why did my bean get created before that other bean?' problems.

The sequence, in order: (1) SpringApplication constructs — it inspects the classpath to guess the application type (SERVLET, REACTIVE, or NONE), discovers listeners via spring.factories / META-INF/spring.factories, and detects the main class. (2) The application starts an Environment — property sources (system properties, environment variables, application.yml, application-{profile}.yml, command-line args) are loaded in priority order. (3) The banner is printed. (4) ApplicationContext is created — AnnotationConfigServletWebServerApplicationContext for a typical Spring MVC app. (5) ApplicationContextInitializers run — user-supplied hooks that can modify the context before beans are loaded. (6) Environment-prepared listeners fire. (7) The context is refreshed: this is the big one. It triggers ConfigurationClassPostProcessor (parses @Configuration classes, discovers @ComponentScan targets, evaluates @Conditional, registers @Bean definitions from auto-configuration), then instantiates all singletons in dependency order, runs BeanPostProcessors (which install @Autowired, @PostConstruct, AOP proxies), and finally starts the embedded web server. (8) ContextRefreshedEvent fires. (9) ApplicationRunner and CommandLineRunner beans run — with @Order determining sequence. (10) ApplicationReadyEvent fires; the app is now serving traffic.

The most common startup failure modes map to these phases. Missing bean errors (NoSuchBeanDefinitionException) happen during step 7 when bean instantiation runs. Port-in-use errors (WebServerException: Unable to start embedded Tomcat) happen during the server-start sub-phase of step 7 — after all beans have been created. Configuration exceptions (invalid properties, failed @ConfigurationProperties binding) surface during step 7's bean instantiation, especially for beans that fail-fast. ApplicationRunner exceptions run AFTER the web server is up — if one throws, the app has already started listening and will only begin shutting down because of the error.

The banner is a nice diagnostic marker: if you see the banner but no 'Tomcat started on port 8080', you know you failed during context refresh. If you see 'Tomcat started' but nothing serving, the issue is probably downstream (ApplicationRunner throwing, then triggering shutdown) or a filter chain misconfiguration.

Two startup-tuning facts matter in production. First, lazy initialization (spring.main.lazy-initialization=true, or @Lazy per bean) defers non-critical bean creation until first use — startups go from 30s to 3s in large apps, at the cost of first-request latency spikes and delayed failure detection. Second, startup failures are much easier to diagnose with debug logging (logging.level.root=DEBUG or --debug on the command line): Boot prints an auto-configuration report ('Positive matches', 'Negative matches', 'Exclusions') that lists exactly which conditions failed and why.

An interview answer that names the phases in order, knows the difference between 'context refresh' and 'web server start', and explains why ApplicationRunner runs after the port is open, is a stronger answer than any list of annotations.
bullets: Order: construct SpringApplication → load Environment → create context → refresh context (parse @Configuration, run BPPs, instantiate beans) → start embedded server → ApplicationRunner → ApplicationReadyEvent.
Environment is built from property sources in priority order: command-line > env vars > application-{profile} > application.yml > defaults.
Context refresh is where most failures happen: bean instantiation, auto-configuration, AOP wrapping, and the web server start all occur here.
ApplicationRunner/CommandLineRunner run AFTER the server is listening — exceptions here trigger shutdown of an already-started app.
spring.main.lazy-initialization=true trades startup speed for first-request latency and delayed failure detection.
--debug prints an auto-configuration report listing positive and negative condition matches — best tool for 'why was this bean not created?'
quizzes.code:
SpringApplication.run(Application.class, args)

1. SpringApplication construct
   - guess application type (SERVLET / REACTIVE / NONE)
   - load listeners from META-INF/spring.factories
   - dedupe and reorder listeners

2. Environment prepared
   - property sources loaded in priority order
   - active profiles resolved

3. Banner printed

4. ApplicationContext created
   (AnnotationConfigServletWebServerApplicationContext)

5. ApplicationContextInitializers run

6. context refresh() -- THE BIG ONE
   a. ConfigurationClassPostProcessor
      - parse @Configuration classes
      - resolve @ComponentScan
      - evaluate @Conditional on auto-configs
      - register @Bean definitions
   b. BeanFactoryPostProcessors (placeholder resolution, etc.)
   c. Instantiate singletons in dependency order
   d. BeanPostProcessors per bean (@Autowired, @PostConstruct, AOP)
   e. Start embedded web server (Tomcat)

7. ContextRefreshedEvent fired

8. ApplicationRunner / CommandLineRunner run (with @Order)

9. ApplicationReadyEvent fired -> app is live

quizzes.title: Auto-Configuration Internals: @Conditional, spring.factories, and How a DataSource Appears
quizzes.summary:
Auto-configuration is the magic that makes Spring Boot feel instant: add spring-boot-starter-data-jpa to pom.xml, declare a few properties, and a fully configured DataSource, EntityManagerFactory, and transaction manager appear. The mechanism is not magic; it is a set of @Configuration classes that are conditionally loaded based on what is on the classpath, what beans already exist, and what properties are set. Understanding the mechanism is what turns 'why is my custom DataSource ignored?' into a five-minute diagnosis.

@EnableAutoConfiguration (composed into @SpringBootApplication) triggers AutoConfigurationImportSelector, which reads class names from META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports (Spring Boot 2.7+; older versions used META-INF/spring.factories). These are the auto-configuration classes shipped with Boot and any third-party starter. The list is huge (over a hundred for a typical app) but most classes do not produce any beans because their @Conditional checks fail.

Conditions are the gatekeepers. @ConditionalOnClass(DataSource.class) — only applies if the class is on the classpath. @ConditionalOnMissingBean(DataSource.class) — only applies if you have NOT already defined a DataSource. @ConditionalOnProperty(name="spring.datasource.url") — only applies if the property is set. @ConditionalOnBean(DataSource.class) — only applies if a DataSource exists (used for dependent configs, like entityManagerFactory which requires a DataSource). Together these form a boolean expression: 'activate this auto-config only when the environment supports it and the developer has not overridden it.'

Take the DataSource example. DataSourceAutoConfiguration has @ConditionalOnClass({ DataSource.class, EmbeddedDatabaseType.class }) — the JDBC API must be present (because spring-jdbc is on the classpath). Inside, several nested configurations apply conditionally: EmbeddedDataSourceConfiguration activates only if no spring.datasource.url is set and an embedded DB driver (H2, HSQLDB, Derby) is on the classpath; PooledDataSourceConfiguration activates only if spring.datasource.url is set or an embedded DB driver exists. HikariDataSource is the default pool when HikariCP is on the classpath (which spring-boot-starter-jdbc brings). If you define your own DataSource bean, @ConditionalOnMissingBean back-off kicks in and Boot's auto-config steps aside — this is the ordering contract you rely on to override any auto-configured bean.

Ordering matters when one auto-config depends on another. @AutoConfigureAfter(DataSourceAutoConfiguration.class) on JpaAutoConfiguration ensures JPA config is evaluated after the DataSource config is registered. This is how Boot avoids a chicken-and-egg situation where the entity manager is configured before its DataSource exists.

The debugging tool is --debug or logging.level.org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure=DEBUG. Boot prints a ConditionEvaluationReport with 'Positive matches' (which auto-configs ran and why) and 'Negative matches' (which did not and why). If your custom Configuration is being ignored, the report tells you whether the auto-config's @ConditionalOnMissingBean actually saw your bean, or whether your bean was registered too late.

The interview-grade mental model: auto-configuration is a large library of @Configuration classes, each guarded by conditions, loaded from a classpath index (AutoConfiguration.imports), applied in a deterministic order, and designed to back off the moment you define your own bean. Everything else — starters, spring.factories, condition reports — is machinery around that core idea.
bullets: @EnableAutoConfiguration reads AutoConfiguration.imports (formerly spring.factories) to discover candidate auto-config classes.
Conditions decide applicability: @ConditionalOnClass, @ConditionalOnMissingBean, @ConditionalOnProperty, @ConditionalOnBean.
Every auto-config is designed to back off when the developer defines their own bean of the same type — this is why overriding works.
@AutoConfigureAfter / @AutoConfigureBefore enforce ordering between dependent auto-configs (e.g., JPA after DataSource).
--debug prints a ConditionEvaluationReport: 'Positive matches' = ran, 'Negative matches' = skipped and why.
DataSourceAutoConfiguration: activates on DataSource.class + spring-jdbc; EmbeddedDataSourceConfiguration for in-memory, PooledDataSourceConfiguration for real URLs, HikariCP as default pool.

quizzes.title: Starters and BOM: Why You Rarely Specify Versions in a Spring Boot pom.xml
quizzes.summary:
Two mechanisms make dependency management in Spring Boot almost invisible: starters and the Bill of Materials (BOM). A starter is a POM-only dependency (no classes) that aggregates a curated set of libraries. The BOM is a POM that declares <dependencyManagement> entries for dozens of libraries with specific versions, so all children inherit those versions without repeating them. Together, starters give you the right libraries and the BOM gives you the right versions — and they are tested as a set, so you do not hit 'Jackson 2.15 does not work with Spring MVC 6.0.3' surprises.

spring-boot-starter is the base — Spring core, logging (Logback + SLF4J), autoconfigure, and the Spring Boot launcher. spring-boot-starter-web adds Spring MVC, Jackson, Tomcat (embedded), and validation. spring-boot-starter-data-jpa adds Spring Data JPA, Hibernate, HikariCP, and spring-jdbc. spring-boot-starter-security adds Spring Security plus its filter chain. spring-boot-starter-test pulls in JUnit 5, AssertJ, Mockito, Hamcrest, JSONAssert, and Spring Test — with scope test. Each starter is a curated bundle the Spring team has verified to work together.

The parent POM does the version management. Every Spring Boot app has either <parent>spring-boot-starter-parent</parent> (simplest) or imports spring-boot-dependencies via <dependencyManagement><scope>import</scope></dependencyManagement>. Either way, when you declare spring-boot-starter-web without a <version>, Maven consults the BOM's dependencyManagement and inserts the version automatically. If you explicitly specify a version, you override the BOM — usually a mistake.

The <parent> variant does more than the BOM import. spring-boot-starter-parent is itself a parent POM that configures the compiler plugin (Java version defaults), resource filtering for application.properties placeholders, surefire for tests, and repackage for executable jars. If you cannot inherit from the parent (multi-module builds, corporate parents), use <scope>import</scope> to get the BOM but expect to configure plugins yourself.

Starters are not magic — they are just well-designed dependency graphs. Removing a transitive dependency a starter brings in (for example, excluding Tomcat to use Jetty) is normal: <exclusions> on the starter, then add spring-boot-starter-jetty. Overriding a starter's transitive version (say, a newer Jackson) is possible but risky — you lose the version compatibility guarantee the Spring team tested.

Maven or Gradle? Spring Boot works with both.
