In Gradle, apply the io.spring.dependency-management plugin to get the same BOM behavior, or use Spring Boot's newer convention of a platform BOM (implementation platform(org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-dependencies:3.x.y)). Either way, the principle is the same: declare the starter without a version and let the BOM resolve it.

An interview-worthy summary: starters = curated bundles; BOM = version catalog applied via dependencyManagement; together they eliminate the 'what version of Jackson goes with Spring 6?' question. If you override versions, do it deliberately and re-run the full test suite — you are opting out of the compatibility guarantee the Spring team verified for that release.
bullets: A starter is a POM-only artifact that aggregates curated dependencies (spring-boot-starter-web = Spring MVC + Jackson + Tomcat + validation).
The BOM (spring-boot-dependencies) declares <dependencyManagement> versions so children omit <version> and inherit tested combinations.
<parent>spring-boot-starter-parent</parent> gives both the BOM and plugin configuration (compiler, surefire, repackage).
Without parent inheritance, use <dependencyManagement><scope>import</scope> to bring in the BOM — you must configure plugins yourself.
Overriding a transitive version (e.g., newer Jackson) opts you out of the version-compatibility guarantee — do it only with a full test run.
Excluding a transitive dep (e.g., exclude Tomcat, add spring-boot-starter-jetty) is standard and safe.
quizzes.code:
<!-- Standard: inherit parent -> BOM + plugins configured -->
<parent>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
    <version>3.2.0</version>
</parent>

<dependencies>
    <!-- no version needed -- BOM supplies it -->
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
    </dependency>
</dependencies>

<!-- Corporate parent: import the BOM instead -->
<dependencyManagement>
    <dependencies>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-dependencies</artifactId>
            <version>3.2.0</version>
            <type>pom</type>
            <scope>import</scope>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>
</dependencyManagement>

<!-- Swap Tomcat for Jetty -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
    <exclusions>
        <exclusion>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-tomcat</artifactId>
        </exclusion>
    </exclusions>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-jetty</artifactId>
</dependency>

quizzes.title: Configuration Precedence and Profiles: Where Does a Property Value Actually Come From?
quizzes.summary:
Spring Boot reads properties from over a dozen sources, and when the same key exists in multiple sources, the one with the highest precedence wins. This is powerful but also the source of 'my change to application.yml had no effect' bugs — someone set an environment variable with the same name, and env vars beat file config.

The precedence order (highest to lowest, simplified but practical): (1) Devtools global settings (~/.config/spring-boot); (2) @TestPropertySource on a test; (3) command-line arguments (--server.port=8081); (4) SPRING_APPLICATION_JSON env var; (5) ServletConfig / ServletContext init parameters; (6) JNDI attributes; (7) System.getProperties() (Java system properties, -Dkey=value); (8) OS environment variables (SERVER_PORT); (9) application-{profile}.yml outside the jar; (10) application-{profile}.yml inside the jar; (11) application.yml outside the jar; (12) application.yml inside the jar; (13) @PropertySource on a @Configuration; (14) SpringApplication.setDefaultProperties. Memorizing the whole list is less important than remembering the two rules: command-line and env vars always beat file config, and {profile} files beat non-profile files at the same location.

The OS environment variable behavior is where most confusion lives. If application.yml has server.port: 8080, but the container also exports SERVER_PORT=9090, then 9090 wins. Boot's relaxed binding maps SERVER_PORT to server.port, so any UPPER_SNAKE_CASE env var overrides the property of the same lowercase.dotted name. This is normally desirable in containers (you set config via env vars, not files), but it becomes a trap when a leftover env var from a CI job silently overrides a recent file change.

Profiles are named sets of configuration you activate via spring.profiles.active. Files named application-{profile}.yml override application.yml for the same location. You can activate multiple profiles at once (comma-separated) and Boot merges them left-to-right — the rightmost profile wins for conflicting keys (after the base). Common patterns: application-dev.yml for local, application-prod.yml for production, and profile-specific beans annotated with @Profile("prod") that only instantiate in that profile. Since Spring Boot 2.4, profile groups let you activate a named group (spring.profiles.group.production=prod-db,prod-metrics) so one flag turns on multiple profiles.

Practical debugging: the Actuator /actuator/env endpoint (when exposed) lists every property with its source and precedence — the fastest way to find 'where is this value coming from?'. If you cannot enable Actuator, an EnvironmentAware bean can print the property source list at startup for the same purpose. For any property you care about, always ask: which of the twelve sources has it, and does anything higher-precedence override it?

An interview-quality answer names the general rule (command line > env vars > profile files > base files) rather than reciting all twelve, gives the SERVER_PORT example, and mentions @Profile / profile groups and Actuator's env endpoint as the practical tools. That shows you understand configuration as a precedence system, not as scattered @Value lookups.
bullets: Command-line args and env vars beat all file config; profile files beat non-profile files at the same location.
SERVER_PORT env var overrides server.port from application.yml — relaxed binding maps UPPER_SNAKE_CASE to dot.case automatically.
spring.profiles.active activates profiles; application-{profile}.yml overrides application.yml; multiple profiles merge left-to-right with the rightmost winning.
Profile groups (spring.profiles.group.production=prod-db,prod-metrics) let one flag activate several profiles.
@Profile("prod") on a @Bean or @Configuration makes it conditional on the active profile.
Actuator /actuator/env shows every property with its source and precedence — the fastest 'where does this value come from?' tool.
quizzes.code:
# Layered config
# application.yml              (base, lowest in-jar priority)
server.port: 8080
spring.datasource.url: jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/app

# application-prod.yml         (overrides base in prod)
spring.datasource.url: jdbc:postgresql://db.prod:5432/app
spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size: 30

# Run with:
java -jar app.jar --spring.profiles.active=prod --server.port=9090
# effective server.port: 9090     (command line wins)
# effective datasource.url: prod  (profile file wins over base)

# Container override
#   docker run -e SERVER_PORT=7070 -e SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod app
#   SERVER_PORT overrides server.port from any file

# Profile group -- one switch, multiple profiles
# spring.profiles.group.production=prod-db,prod-metrics
# java -jar app.jar --spring.profiles.active=production

# Inspect everything live
# GET /actuator/env    -> every property + source + precedence

// Conditional bean by profile
@Configuration
@Profile("prod")
class ProdConfig {
    @Bean DataSource dataSource() { ... }
}

quizzes.title: @ConfigurationProperties vs @Value: Type Safety, Relaxed Binding, and When to Use Each
bullets: @Value injects one scalar; @ConfigurationProperties binds an entire prefix tree to a POJO.
@ConfigurationProperties gives relaxed binding (kebab, camel, snake, env-var forms all match the same field), type conversion (Duration, DataSize, enums), JSR-380 validation, and IDE metadata.
@Value does no validation, no relaxed binding, no autocomplete, and fails cryptically when a required property is missing.
@ConfigurationProperties class must become a bean — @Component, @ConfigurationPropertiesScan, or @EnableConfigurationProperties.
Rule of thumb: @Value for one-off scalars, @ConfigurationProperties for anything with 3+ related fields, nesting, or validation.

quizzes.title: @Transactional Internals and the Six Silent Failures
quizzes.summary:
@Transactional is the most misused annotation in the Spring ecosystem. It is a thin, easy-to-write annotation that looks like it 'just works', but its semantics are governed by proxies, propagation rules, and rollback contracts — and it fails silently in six common ways that ship to production and cause data corruption or phantom transactions.

How it actually works. @Transactional is implemented by a BeanPostProcessor (AbstractAutoProxyCreator via InfrastructureAdvisorAutoProxyCreator) that wraps the finished bean in a proxy (JDK dynamic proxy if it implements interfaces, CGLIB otherwise). External callers hit the proxy, which starts a transaction (or joins one), invokes the target method, commits if it returns normally, and rolls back if it throws. This is why self-invocation (this.someMethod()) bypasses @Transactional — the internal call skips the proxy. This is also why final methods break — CGLIB cannot override them.

Propagation controls what happens when a transactional method calls another. REQUIRED (default) joins the existing transaction if one exists, otherwise starts a new one. REQUIRES_NEW always suspends the current transaction and starts a fresh one — useful when you need to persist audit logs even if the outer transaction rolls back. NESTED creates a savepoint inside the current transaction; it rolls back to the savepoint, not the whole transaction. MANDATORY requires an existing transaction or throws. NEVER forbids one. SUPPORTS uses one if present, else runs non-transactionally. NOT_SUPPORTED suspends any existing transaction. Most bugs live in REQUIRES_NEW (people forget it commits independently) and NESTED (savepoints need database support).

Isolation levels map to the database's own: READ_COMMITTED (default), READ_UNCOMMITTED, REPEATABLE_READ, SERIALIZABLE. Setting anything stricter than the database default has real cost — locks, retries, deadlocks — so choose deliberately, not by habit.

The six silent failures:

1. Self-invocation. this.method() bypasses the proxy. Calls inside the same class do not start a new transaction. The fix is to move the inner method to another bean, use TransactionTemplate, or use AspectJ load-time weaving.

2. Checked exceptions do not roll back. @Transactional only rolls back on RuntimeException and Error by default. If your method throws a checked exception (IOException, a custom Exception), the transaction commits. Fix: @Transactional(rollbackFor = Exception.class), or throw an unchecked exception, or handle and rethrow wrapped.

3. Final methods and final classes cannot be proxied by CGLIB. @Transactional on a final method is silently ignored — no transaction starts, no warning. Fix: remove final, extract into an interface (JDK proxy handles it), or use AspectJ.

4. Private methods are not proxied. Spring's proxy-based AOP only intercepts public methods (and protected for CGLIB, but the common contract is public). @Transactional on a private method does nothing. Fix: make the method public or restructure.

5. Wrong proxy target in injection. If you @Autowired the concrete class but Spring produced a JDK proxy of the interface, injection fails at startup with BeanNotOfRequiredTypeException. Fix: inject the interface, or force proxyTargetClass=true.

6. readOnly=true on a method that writes. readOnly is a hint to Hibernate to skip dirty-checking and to the JDBC driver to mark the connection read-only. If the method writes, the write is either silently ignored or fails when the driver enforces read-only. Fix: remove readOnly on write methods; use it only for genuine reads.

Additional common pitfalls worth knowing: long transactions holding database locks across network calls to downstream services (never do IO inside a transaction); @Transactional on @Async methods (async executes on a different thread with a different transaction context — the transaction often does not propagate as expected); and nested @Transactional where the inner REQUIRES_NEW bean is actually the same bean invoked via self-invocation, so REQUIRES_NEW silently does nothing.

An interview answer that names the proxy model, the six failure modes, and the REQUIRED vs REQUIRES_NEW distinction is far stronger than 'it makes methods transactional'. Bonus points for mentioning TransactionTemplate (imperative, no proxy, no self-invocation risk) as the escape hatch when @Transactional's proxy model gets in the way.
bullets: @Transactional uses a runtime AOP proxy (JDK or CGLIB) — external callers hit the proxy, which manages begin/commit/rollback.
Six silent failures: self-invocation, checked exceptions, final methods/classes, private methods, wrong injection type, readOnly on writes.
Rollback default: only RuntimeException and Error. Use rollbackFor = Exception.class for checked exceptions.
Propagation: REQUIRED (join or create), REQUIRES_NEW (suspend outer, always new), NESTED (savepoint), MANDATORY, NEVER, SUPPORTS, NOT_SUPPORTED.
Never do network IO inside a transaction — long-held locks cause cascading timeouts.
TransactionTemplate is the imperative escape hatch — no proxy, no self-invocation trap.

quizzes.title: Actuator: Health, Metrics, Env, and the Endpoints That Make Spring Boot Production-Ready
quizzes.summary:
Actuator is the module that gives a running Spring Boot app an HTTP interface for introspection and operations. Add spring-boot-starter-actuator and Boot exposes a set of endpoints under /actuator by default: /actuator/health (are you up?), /actuator/info (build and git metadata), /actuator/metrics (JVM and application metrics), and a few others, depending on what is on the classpath. The full set of possible endpoints includes env, beans, configprops, mappings, loggers, threaddump, heapdump, httptrace, scheduledtasks, and prometheus — but most are disabled by default because they can leak sensitive data.

/actuator/health is the endpoint Kubernetes readiness and liveness probes talk to. It aggregates multiple HealthIndicators (database reachable, disk space, Redis ping, Kafka broker reachable) into an overall status: UP, DOWN, OUT_OF_SERVICE, UNKNOWN. You can write custom HealthIndicators by implementing the interface and registering them as beans, and you can control what is shown to unauthenticated users with management.endpoint.health.show-details (default never; use when_authorized to reveal DB details only to authenticated callers).

/actuator/metrics exposes Micrometer meters — JVM memory, GC pauses, HTTP request timings, thread pool stats, DataSource pool utilization, and any custom counters or timers you register. Meter names follow Micrometer conventions (http.server.requests, jvm.memory.used, hikaricp.connections.active). The /actuator/prometheus endpoint (when the micrometer-registry-prometheus dependency is present) exports these in Prometheus text format, ready to be scraped.

/actuator/env lists every property with its source and precedence — the single best tool for 'where is this value coming from?' debugging. /actuator/configprops shows the bound @ConfigurationProperties beans. /actuator/beans shows every bean in the context with its type and dependencies. /actuator/mappings shows all HTTP routes. /actuator/threaddump dumps thread stacks (great for hanging requests). /actuator/heapdump produces a .hprof file you can open in a profiler — be careful with this in production, it can be hundreds of MB.

Security is critical. By default, most endpoints are disabled. Even health and info should generally not be exposed on the public internet — Kubernetes probes work fine on an internal port. The recommended production setup: management.server.port=8081 puts Actuator on a separate internal port, unreachable from the outside; secure it with Spring Security on that port; enable only the endpoints you need (management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,info,prometheus); and put health behind authentication with management.endpoint.health.show-details=when_authorized.

Custom endpoints are easy: annotate a class with @Endpoint(id = "features") and @ReadOperation methods for GET-like reads, @WriteOperation for POST-like writes. Custom health indicators: implement HealthIndicator and register the bean — Boot's aggregate picks it up automatically.

An interview answer that names health, metrics, env, and loggers specifically (with the security warning) shows real production experience. An answer that only says 'it exposes endpoints' is superficial.
bullets: Actuator exposes operational endpoints under /actuator: health, info, metrics, env, beans, configprops, loggers, threaddump, heapdump.
/actuator/health aggregates multiple HealthIndicators (DB, disk, Redis, custom) into UP/DOWN — used by Kubernetes probes.
/actuator/metrics exposes Micrometer meters; /actuator/prometheus exports them for scraping.
/actuator/env shows property sources and precedence — best tool for config debugging.
Security: most endpoints disabled by default; put Actuator on a separate port (management.server.port) and expose only what you need (exposure.include).
Custom: @Endpoint for operations, HealthIndicator for health checks.

quizzes.title: Embedded Server and Graceful Shutdown: How java -jar Actually Serves HTTP
quizzes.summary:
In classic Java web deployments, your application was a WAR file dropped into a pre-installed Tomcat, and the server lived outside your build. Spring Boot flips this: the application IS the server. spring-boot-starter-web brings spring-boot-starter-tomcat, which brings the Tomcat embed jar, and Spring Boot creates a Tomcat instance programmatically inside the JVM. When you run java -jar app.jar, your main method runs, the context refreshes, and around step 7e of the startup sequence Boot instantiates Tomcat, binds the port, deploys the DispatcherServlet, and starts accepting requests. There is no external install, no war file, no container — one JVM, one jar, one server.

The default is Tomcat, but Jetty and Undertow are drop-in swaps: exclude spring-boot-starter-tomcat, add spring-boot-starter-jetty or spring-boot-starter-undertow. Jetty is often chosen for lower memory and better support of long-lived connections like WebSockets; Undertow has the smallest footprint and is optimized for very high concurrency. Configuration is uniform via server.* properties regardless of choice: server.port, server.servlet.context-path, server.tomcat.max-threads, server.undertow.io-threads.

server.tomcat.max-threads (default 200) is the maximum number of worker threads — if it saturates, new requests queue in the OS accept backlog or are rejected depending on the OS. This is different from the HikariCP connection pool size; if max-threads is 200 but the DB pool is 10, 190 threads will block on connection acquisition, which is where many production latency incidents originate. Sizing those two together (threads ≈ pool × expectedIOwaitRatio) is a real engineering decision, not a checkbox.

Graceful shutdown is the property that separates a toy app from a production app. When a pod receives SIGTERM (Kubernetes rolling update, deploy), the default behavior in Spring Boot pre-2.3 was to kill the JVM immediately — in-flight requests get 500 errors and clients see broken responses. With server.shutdown=graceful (since Boot 2.3, default in 3.x is still immediate unless enabled), Boot stops accepting new requests on the connector, waits up to spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase (default 30s) for in-flight requests to finish, then proceeds to close the context and run @PreDestroy / DisposableBean / custom destroy-method on beans. Kubernetes should set terminationGracePeriodSeconds greater than the timeout so the pod does not get SIGKILLed mid-drain.

Graceful shutdown is a chain: stop accept connector → wait for in-flight requests → stop the servlet container → publish ContextClosedEvent → run @PreDestroy on beans → run DisposableBean.destroy → run custom destroy-method → close the JVM. If you have background executors or message listeners (Kafka, Rabbit, SQS pollers), they must be stopped during shutdown too — that is what @PreDestroy and SmartLifecycle implementations are for. Kafka consumers should stop their pollers, commit offsets cleanly, and leave the consumer group so partitions reassign without a rebalance storm. Getting this right is the difference between a deploy that loses zero in-flight requests and one that drops a small percentage on every rollout.

An interview answer that explains (1) the server is inside the JVM, not external, (2) Tomcat is the default but Jetty/Undertow are drop-in swaps, (3) graceful shutdown is opt-in and needs Kubernetes terminationGracePeriodSeconds coordination, and (4) background processors must be stopped in @PreDestroy, is a complete answer.
bullets: Spring Boot embeds the server (Tomcat default) inside the JVM; the app jar is the web server, no external Tomcat install.
Jetty and Undertow are drop-in alternatives via starter swap; same server.* properties apply.
server.tomcat.max-threads (default 200) is worker-thread limit; mismatch with DB pool size causes connection-acquire latency spikes.
server.shutdown=graceful stops accepting new requests, drains in-flight up to spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase, then destroys beans.
Kubernetes terminationGracePeriodSeconds must exceed the shutdown timeout, or the pod is SIGKILLed mid-drain.
Background processors (Kafka, Rabbit, executors) must be stopped in @PreDestroy / SmartLifecycle for clean shutdown.

quizzes.question: A team migrates from RabbitMQ to Kafka but keeps designing topics with a single partition 'to guarantee ordering' and sets retention to 1 hour 'to clean up after ourselves'. What is the core mistake?
options: Kafka cannot support single-partition topics

They are applying queue habits to a log — Kafka ordering is per-partition, and retention is a storage policy independent of consumption; single-partition topics cap parallelism and short retention destroys replay
Kafka requires at least three partitions per topic
Retention must always be infinite in Kafka
quizzes.explanation: A single partition gives total order but caps consumer-group parallelism at one consumer and is a capacity bottleneck. Kafka retention is about how much history remains on disk, not about deleting after consumption — short retention eliminates replay, which is Kafka's core differentiator from a queue. The correct design uses key-based partitioning (per-key order, parallel across keys) and retention sized to replay requirements.

quizzes.question: A topic has 4 partitions and a consumer group has 6 consumers. What happens to the extra 2 consumers?
options: They share partitions with the existing consumers, splitting the load
They sit idle — within a consumer group, each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer, so only 4 consumers can be active
Kafka automatically increases the partition count to match the consumer count
The group rebalances and evicts the extra consumers
quizzes.explanation: Kafka's consumer-group assignment guarantees that each partition is owned by exactly one consumer at a time. With 4 partitions, at most 4 consumers in the group can be active; the remaining 2 are assigned no partitions and sit idle until a partition is freed (consumer leaves, crashes, or the topic is expanded). Adding consumers beyond the partition count does not increase parallelism.

quizzes.question: A developer says 'the producer writes to the Kafka cluster and the consumer reads from the cluster.' Why is this imprecise in a way that matters for debugging?
options: Producers write to ZooKeeper and consumers read from brokers

Both producers and consumers talk to specific partition leaders on specific brokers; followers replicate but do not serve client requests, so a 'leader not available' error is a broker-specific failure, not a cluster-wide one
Consumers write to the cluster and producers read from it
Kafka clients always connect to every broker simultaneously
quizzes.explanation: Kafka clients communicate with partition leaders, not with the cluster as an abstract entity. Each partition has one leader broker; producers send to that leader, and consumers fetch from that leader. Followers replicate in the background and are not read from under normal conditions. This matters for debugging: a leader election, a broker that is overloaded, or a network partition between a client and a specific broker produces errors scoped to those partitions, not to the whole topic.

quizzes.question: Three downstream services — analytics, fraud detection, and billing — all need to react to the same 'order_placed' events. Which approach best fits Kafka's model?
options: Create three separate queues and have the order service publish three copies
Use one topic with three independent consumer groups — each group reads the full stream at its own pace with its own offsets
Use a single consumer group with three consumers, one per service
Kafka cannot fan out one event to multiple services
quizzes.explanation: Kafka fan-out is natively achieved with multiple consumer groups on the same topic. Each group maintains independent committed offsets, so analytics, fraud, and billing each read the entire stream without interfering. A single consumer group with three consumers would divide partitions among them, meaning each event goes to only one service — that is queue semantics, not fan-out. Publishing three copies creates coupling and duplication.

quizzes.question: A high-throughput pipeline uses acks=all and idempotence, but throughput is lower than expected. Which producer tuning change is most likely to improve throughput without sacrificing durability?
options: Switch acks to 0
Increase linger.ms (e.g., to 10–20 ms) and batch.size (e.g., to 64 KB), and enable compression (lz4 or zstd)
Disable idempotence
Reduce max.in.flight.requests.per.connection to 1
quizzes.explanation: With acks=all and idempotence, durability is fixed; the remaining throughput levers are batching and compression. A larger linger.ms lets batches fill, a larger batch.size allows more records per request, and compression reduces network I/O and broker disk usage. acks=0 and disabling idempotence sacrifice durability. Reducing max.in.flight to 1 serializes requests and hurts throughput further.

quizzes.question: What exactly does the idempotent producer protect against, and what does it NOT protect against?
options: It protects against duplicate records caused by producer retries within one producer session; it does not protect against duplicates across producer restarts or consumer-side reprocessing
It guarantees exactly-once end-to-end across producers and consumers
It protects against message loss but not duplication
It requires ZooKeeper to track producer sequence numbers
quizzes.explanation: The idempotent producer assigns a Producer ID and per-partition sequence numbers; the broker deduplicates retries within that session. A producer restart gets a new PID, so cross-session deduplication requires transactions (exactly-once semantics). Consumer-side duplicates from at-least-once processing are a separate problem solved by idempotent consumers, not by the producer.

quizzes.question: A consumer uses auto-commit, polls records 100–199, auto-commit fires and commits offset 200, then the consumer crashes while processing record 150. What happens on restart?
options: The consumer resumes from offset 150 and reprocesses 150–199
The consumer resumes from offset 200, and records 150–199 are lost — this is at-most-once behavior
The broker replays 150–199 automatically because the crash was detected
The consumer enters a rebalance loop until the missing records are recovered
quizzes.explanation: Auto-commit commits the latest offset returned by poll(), not the last processed offset. Once offset 200 is committed, restarting seeks to 200, skipping any records between 150 and 199 that were polled but not processed. This is the classic auto-commit data-loss scenario. Manual commit after processing is required for at-least-once semantics.

quizzes.question: A consumer processing a batch of 500 records takes 7 minutes, exceeding max.poll.interval.ms (default 5 minutes). What is the consequence?
options: Kafka buffers the extra time and no action is taken
The consumer is considered dead, a rebalance fires, its partitions are reassigned, and another consumer reprocesses the same records — causing duplicates
The consumer commits offsets automatically and continues
The broker increases max.poll.interval.ms dynamically
quizzes.explanation: max.poll.interval.ms is the maximum allowed time between poll() calls. If processing exceeds it, the group coordinator removes the consumer from the group, triggering a rebalance and reassigning its partitions. The new owner starts from the last committed offset, which may be behind the slow consumer's actual position — so the same records are processed again. The fixes are to reduce max.poll.records, process asynchronously while polling, or increase the interval if long processing is legitimate.

quizzes.question: A topic has 3 partitions and a consumer group has 5 consumers. Two consumers sit idle. A developer proposes increasing the partition count to 5 to use all consumers. What is the consequence for messages already in the topic?
options: No consequence — existing messages are automatically redistributed
The key-to-partition mapping changes for keys whose murmur2 hash maps to the new partitions, so messages with the same key may no longer land in the same partition, breaking per-key ordering
Kafka refuses to add partitions to a topic that already has data
All existing offsets are invalidated and consumers must start from offset 0
quizzes.explanation: Increasing partition count changes the modulo divisor in murmur2(key) % numPartitions. Keys that previously mapped to partition 0 may now map to partition 3 or 4. Existing messages stay where they are, but future messages with the same key may go to a different partition — so per-key order across the repartitioning boundary is no longer guaranteed. Adding partitions is safe for throughput but not for key-based ordering unless the partitioner is designed to be stable across count changes.

quizzes.question: A consumer receives a higher generation ID than it expected in a heartbeat response. What should it do, and why?
options: Ignore it and keep processing — generation IDs are informational only
Stop fetching, commit its current offsets (with the old generation, which the coordinator may reject), and send a JoinGroupRequest to rejoin the group
Immediately shut down the JVM to avoid committing stale offsets
Increase session.timeout.ms and continue
quizzes.explanation: A higher generation ID means a rebalance has been triggered and this consumer's membership is stale. It must stop fetching, attempt to commit what it has processed, and rejoin via JoinGroupRequest. The coordinator rejects commits from an older generation to prevent a zombie consumer from overwriting offsets that a new owner is already advancing. Shutting down the JVM is excessive; ignoring the generation leads to rejected commits and duplicate or lost work.

quizzes.question: A topic has replication.factor=3, min.insync.replicas=2, acks=all, and unclean.leader.election.enable=false. Two brokers become unreachable, leaving one replica. What happens to producer writes?
options: Writes succeed with acks=1 behavior because one replica is still alive
Writes fail — the ISR is below min.insync.replicas, so the leader rejects acks=all writes rather than accept non-durable data
Kafka automatically lowers min.insync.replicas to 1
The remaining broker becomes leader and writes succeed with acks=all
quizzes.explanation: With min.insync.replicas=2, acks=all writes require at least two replicas to acknowledge. When only one replica remains, the ISR is below the minimum and the leader rejects the write — Kafka prefers to fail rather than silently degrade to acks=1 and risk data loss. Kafka does not auto-lower min.insync.replicas; that would defeat the durability guarantee.

quizzes.question: Consumers cannot read records beyond the high watermark even though the leader's log end offset is higher. Why?
options: The high watermark is a performance optimization that limits read bandwidth
Records beyond the high watermark have not been replicated to all ISR members; reading them could expose data that would be lost if the leader failed before replication
The high watermark is the retention boundary — older records are deleted past it
Consumers can read past the high watermark if they set isolation.level=read_uncommitted
quizzes.explanation: The high watermark is the highest offset replicated to every in-sync replica. Records between the high watermark and the leader's log end offset exist only on the leader (and possibly some followers), so if the leader failed, those records could disappear. Kafka hides them from consumers to preserve the durability guarantee. isolation.level=read_uncommitted controls visibility of aborted transactional records, not the high watermark boundary.

quizzes.question: A team wants exactly-once processing from a Kafka topic to an external PostgreSQL database. They enable Kafka transactions on the producer. What is still missing?
options: Nothing — Kafka transactions guarantee exactly-once to any downstream system

Kafka's exactly-once guarantee is internal to Kafka; writes to PostgreSQL are outside the transaction, so the database write must be made idempotent (e.g., upsert or inbox table) to prevent duplicates on retry
They must set isolation.level=read_uncommitted on the consumer
They must increase max.in.flight.requests.per.connection to 10
quizzes.explanation: Kafka transactions make the Kafka-side writes and offset commits atomic, but PostgreSQL is a separate system that is not part of the Kafka transaction. If the consumer commits the Kafka transaction and then the PostgreSQL write fails, or vice versa, the two systems diverge. The external write must be idempotent (upsert, unique constraint, inbox table) to close the gap. read_uncommitted would make things worse (it exposes aborted records); increasing in-flight requests does not address the boundary.

quizzes.question: A consumer uses manual commit. It processes a payment record (charging the customer via an external API), then crashes before commitSync() succeeds. On restart, the record is redelivered and the customer is charged twice. What is the correct fix?
options: Switch to auto-commit so the offset is committed before the external call
Use an idempotency key with the payment provider so the retry returns the original result instead of charging again, and store the key in a dedup table alongside the local state
Increase session.timeout.ms so the crash is not detected
Disable retries on the producer
quizzes.explanation: The crash happened after the side effect but before the offset commit — the classic dual-write gap. Auto-commit would commit before processing and lose payments instead of duplicating them, which is worse. Increasing session timeout does not prevent the crash or the redelivery. The correct fix is idempotency at the external system (Stripe-style Idempotency-Key) plus a local dedup record so retries are safe.

quizzes.question: A consumer uses enable.auto.commit=true. It polls records 100–199, auto-commit fires and commits 200, then crashes while processing record 150. What happens on restart, and what is the failure class?
options: It resumes from 150 and reprocesses — at-least-once
It resumes from 200 and records 150–199 are lost — at-most-once
It resumes from 100 and reprocesses everything — at-least-once
The broker automatically replays 150–199
quizzes.explanation: Auto-commit commits the latest offset returned by poll(), not the last processed offset. Once offset 200 is committed, restarting seeks to 200 and skips records 150–199 that were polled but never processed. This is at-most-once behavior — data loss. The fix is enable.auto.commit=false and commit only after processing succeeds.

quizzes.question: An order service publishes events with key=orderId to a 6-partition topic. A new order-123 event is produced and then a second order-123 event follows. Which statement is guaranteed?
options: Both events land on the same partition and are consumed in production order by any consumer group
The events may land on different partitions because the partitioner is not deterministic
Both land on the same partition only if they are produced by the same producer instance
Ordering is guaranteed globally across all partitions
quizzes.explanation: Key-based partitioning (murmur2(key) % partitions) is deterministic, so both events land on the same partition as long as the partition count does not change. However, Kafka's ordering guarantee for same-key messages is stated for a single producer: if two different producer instances send order-123 events, the broker may interleave them depending on timing. With a single producer, order is preserved. Global ordering across partitions is never guaranteed.

quizzes.question: A producer sends null-key records to a topic with 6 partitions. A consumer expects to see the records in the same order they were sent. What is wrong with this expectation?
options: Null-key records are rejected by Kafka
Null-key records use a sticky partitioner and have no ordering guarantee — consecutive records can land on different partitions and be processed out of order
Null-key records always go to partition 0, so order is guaranteed
Null-key records are replicated more slowly, causing reordering
quizzes.explanation: With a null key, the producer uses the sticky partitioner: it fills one partition's batch before switching to another. There is no deterministic mapping, and records can be distributed across partitions with no cross-partition order. If ordering matters, the producer must supply a key (e.g., entity ID) so all related records land in the same partition.

quizzes.question: A developer uses topic-partition-offset as the idempotency key for a consumer that writes to an external database. After a cluster failover and replay, duplicate records appear despite the dedup logic. Why?
options: Kafka does not support idempotency keys in record headers
Topic-partition-offset is not stable across replays and cluster moves — the same logical message gets a new offset after failover, so the dedup key changes and the duplicate is not recognized
The external database does not support unique constraints
Consumer idempotency requires enable.idempotence=true on the producer
quizzes.explanation: Offsets are positional and change when data is replayed, retained/compacted, or mirrored to another cluster. The same logical event can have a different topic-partition-offset after failover, so using that triple as the dedup key fails to recognize the redelivered copy. The key must be generated at the origin (eventId UUID or business key) and carried in the record so it survives redelivery.

quizzes.question: What exactly does the idempotent producer (enable.idempotence=true) protect against, and where does its guarantee stop?
options: It guarantees exactly-once end-to-end from producer to consumer and external databases
It deduplicates producer retries within a single producer session using PID + per-partition sequence numbers; it does not survive producer restarts and does not make consumers idempotent
It prevents duplicate messages across all producers in the cluster
It requires ZooKeeper to track producer sequence numbers
quizzes.explanation: The idempotent producer assigns a Producer ID (PID) per producer session and a sequence number per partition. The broker drops duplicate (PID, partition, sequence) batches within that session. A producer restart gets a new PID, so cross-session exactly-once requires transactions. Consumer-side duplicates from at-least-once processing require application-level idempotency (dedup table or idempotency keys) — enable.idempotence does nothing for that.

quizzes.question: A team needs to reprocess six months of historical events after fixing a bug in a downstream analytics service. They currently use RabbitMQ with messages deleted after acknowledgment. What is the most appropriate course of action?
options: Reset RabbitMQ offsets to replay the messages

RabbitMQ deletes messages after acknowledgment and has no replay — the team must either introduce Kafka (or another durable log) for the events that need replay, or add external archival storage and a replay pipeline
Enable RabbitMQ's built-in replay feature
Switch to SQS FIFO, which retains messages for replay
quizzes.explanation: Replay after consumption is the defining differentiator of Kafka's log model. RabbitMQ deletes messages after ack, and SQS also deletes after ack — neither supports replaying history. The architectural fix is to use a durable log (Kafka) for event streams that require replay, or to archive events externally and build a replay mechanism. Options A and C assume features that do not exist; option D is false.

quizzes.question: You are designing a task queue for image thumbnail generation inside AWS. Each job must be processed exactly once by a worker, and there is no need to replay history. The team has limited operational capacity. Which choice is most defensible?
options: Kafka with acks=all and transactions — it guarantees exactly-once
RabbitMQ with quorum queues and manual ack — complex routing and per-message ack
SQS FIFO with a deduplication ID and a DLQ — managed queue, ordering within message groups, no infrastructure to operate
A PostgreSQL table polled every second for pending jobs
quizzes.explanation: The requirements are task-queue semantics, exactly-once-per-job (via FIFO dedup), no replay, AWS-native, and low operational overhead. SQS FIFO fits all of these: it is managed, supports deduplication, provides ordering within a message group, and has a DLQ. Kafka's transactions guarantee exactly-once within Kafka but add significant operational complexity and are overkill for a task queue with no replay requirement. RabbitMQ is viable but requires operating a cluster. A PostgreSQL polling table is a valid small-scale option but has contention and scaling limits; SQS is the pragmatic choice here.

quizzes.question: A topic stores user profile updates with key=userId and value=profileJSON. Consumers need the current profile for each user, not the full history of changes. The topic is growing unbounded because retention is set to 30 days. What is the most appropriate fix?
options: Reduce log.retention.ms to 1 hour so old profiles are deleted
Set cleanup.policy=compact so only the latest record per userId is retained, optionally combined with delete to bound storage
Switch the key to a random UUID so records distribute evenly
Increase replication.factor to 5 to reduce storage per broker
quizzes.explanation: The topic is a changelog: consumers need current state per key, not history. Compaction (cleanup.policy=compact) retains at least the latest record per key and discards older duplicates — exactly the right semantics. A short retention window would delete profiles that have not been updated recently, causing consumers to lose state. Random keys destroy per-user ordering and make compaction meaningless. Replication factor affects durability, not retention semantics.

quizzes.question: A producer with transactional.id='payment-0' is paused by a long GC. A new instance starts with the same transactional.id and begins processing. The old instance wakes up and tries to commit its transaction. What happens?
options: Both transactions commit and downstream sees duplicates
The old instance's commit is rejected with ProducerFencedException because the Transaction Coordinator incremented the epoch; only the latest producer for a transactional.id can commit
Kafka blocks the new instance until the old one commits
The old instance silently succeeds because transactional.id is just a label
quizzes.explanation: This is the zombie fencing mechanism. When a new producer initializes with the same transactional.id, the coordinator increments the epoch. Any commit from an older epoch — the zombie — is rejected with ProducerFencedException. This ensures that only one producer instance can commit transactions for a given transactional.id at a time, preventing duplicate or conflicting writes.

quizzes.question: A team enables Kafka transactions on the producer but forgets to set isolation.level=read_committed on the consumer. What do downstream consumers observe?
options: Only committed records — the default isolation level is read_committed
Records from aborted transactions and transaction control markers (BEGIN, COMMIT, ABORT), because the default isolation.level is read_uncommitted
A startup error because transactional topics require read_committed
No records at all — transactional topics are invisible without read_committed
quizzes.explanation: The consumer default is read_uncommitted, which exposes all records in the log — including those from aborted transactions and the transaction markers. Setting read_committed makes the consumer wait for the transaction outcome and only return records from committed transactions. This is the consumer-side half of EOS that candidates often omit.

quizzes.question: You need to continuously copy changes from a PostgreSQL table into a Kafka topic, with offset tracking and retries, without writing producer code. Which tool fits best?
options: Kafka Streams with a KStream source
Kafka Connect with a JDBC source connector
A custom consumer that polls PostgreSQL and calls producer.send()
ksqlDB with a CREATE SOURCE TABLE statement
quizzes.explanation: This is an integration problem, not a processing problem. Kafka Connect's JDBC source connector handles connection management, offset tracking (via the connect-offsets topic), retries, and scaling through tasks. Writing a custom producer is reinventing Connect poorly. Kafka Streams processes data already in Kafka; it is not an ingestion framework. ksqlDB can read from external sources in some configurations, but Connect is the standard, configuration-driven tool for this job.

quizzes.question: A Kafka Streams application performs a stateful aggregation (count of orders per customer). Where is the state stored, and how does it survive a restart?
options: In Kafka topic partitions directly — no local storage is used
In a local state store (RocksDB by default) backed by a compacted changelog topic; on restart, state is restored by replaying the changelog
In ZooKeeper, which Streams uses as a state backend
In the Streams application's heap only — state is lost on restart unless manually persisted
quizzes.explanation: Stateful Streams operations use local state stores for performance, backed by changelog topics for durability. Every update to the state store is also written to the changelog topic (compacted). When a Streams instance restarts or a task migrates, it replays the changelog to rebuild the local store before processing resumes. ZooKeeper is not a Streams state backend, and heap-only state would be lost on restart.

quizzes.question: A producer team adds a new required field to an Avro schema without a default value. The Schema Registry is set to BACKWARD compatibility. What happens?
options: The schema registers successfully and consumers break at runtime
The Registry rejects the registration because BACKWARD compatibility requires that new consumers can read old data — adding a required field without a default violates this
The Registry automatically makes the field optional
BACKWARD compatibility only applies to Protobuf, not Avro
quizzes.explanation: BACKWARD compatibility means a consumer using the new schema can read data written with the old schema. Adding a required field without a default breaks this: old data does not contain the field, and the new consumer has no value to use. The Registry rejects the change at registration time — this is the enforcement point that prevents runtime breakage. The producer must add a default value or use a union type to make the field optional.

quizzes.question: Consumer lag is 500,000 records and the consumer processes 2,000 records/second. The freshness SLO requires data to be no more than 60 seconds old. Is the consumer meeting the SLO, and what is the first thing you check?
options: Yes — 500,000 records is a small number
No — lag_time = 500,000 / 2,000 = 250 seconds, far above the 60-second SLO; first check whether all partitions are balanced and whether any consumer thread is stuck
Yes — lag in records is irrelevant; only bytes matter
No — the only fix is to increase partition count immediately
quizzes.explanation: Raw lag counts are meaningless without conversion to time. 500,000 / 2,000 = 250 seconds behind — well beyond a 60-second SLO. The first diagnostic step is partition-level inspection: is the lag evenly distributed, or is one partition (hot key or stuck thread) dominating? Increasing partitions is a capacity fix, but it does not address a stuck consumer or a skewed key. Diagnosis comes before remediation.

quizzes.question: A topic has 3 partitions. During a flash sale, producer throughput spikes 10x, and one partition receives 80% of the messages while the other two are nearly idle. What is the most likely cause?
options: The partition count is too low and should be increased to 30
The producer is using a low-cardinality key (e.g., isFlashSale=true) so almost all messages hash to the same partition — use a high-cardinality key or key salting
Kafka automatically rebalances partitions when one is overloaded
The consumer group has too many members
quizzes.explanation: Partition skew is almost always a key distribution problem. A low-cardinality key routes most messages to the same partition, leaving others idle and creating a hotspot. The fix is a high-cardinality key (user_id, order_id) or key salting for skewed natural keys. Adding partitions without fixing the key does not help — the skewed key still hashes to one partition. Kafka does not automatically rebalance partition data.

quizzes.question: A team implements a classic Singleton for a config registry with a private constructor and a static instance field. A security audit finds they can create a second instance using reflection (setAccessible(true) + newInstance). Which implementation would have prevented this?
options: Eager static final initialization — it is thread-safe
Enum singleton — the JLS guarantees one instance and reflection cannot create a second enum constant
Double-checked locking with volatile
Holder idiom with a private static nested class
quizzes.explanation: The enum singleton is the only implementation the JLS itself protects against reflection — Constructor.newInstance() throws IllegalArgumentException when the target is an enum. Eager, DCL, and holder all use a private constructor that reflection can bypass with setAccessible(true). Serialization is also handled by enum (readResolve is not needed). This is why Joshua Bloch recommends enum as the default for singletons.

quizzes.question: A Spring Boot service stores the current request's user ID in a static field of a @Service class, and users intermittently see other users' data. What is the root cause?
options: The @Service scope should be changed to prototype
@Service beans are singletons by default, so a static (or instance) mutable field is shared across all concurrent requests — request state leaks between users
Spring Boot requires @RequestScope on the class
The field should be volatile
quizzes.explanation: Spring's default bean scope is singleton — one instance shared by all threads handling all requests. A field that stores per-request state on that instance (or a static field on the class) is shared state, so request A's user ID is visible to request B. Adding volatile only fixes visibility, not the leak. The correct design is to pass the user ID as a parameter, use @RequestScope, or store it in a ThreadLocal that is cleared in a finally block.

quizzes.question: You are choosing between Factory Method and Abstract Factory. The requirement is: choose at startup between a Stripe stack (payment, refund, and webhook handler — all Stripe-aware) or a PayPal stack (the same three, PayPal-aware). Which pattern fits?
options: Factory Method — one creation method is enough
Abstract Factory — you have a family of three related products that must be compatible, and one factory per family guarantees it
Builder — assemble each product step by step
Singleton — only one payment provider can exist
quizzes.explanation: The requirement is a family of related products (payment + refund + webhook) that must come from the same provider to be compatible. Abstract Factory models exactly this: a PaymentFactory interface with three creation methods, and a StripeFactory / PayPalFactory implementation each producing all three. Factory Method would only work if there were one product. Builder assembles one complex object; it does not enforce family compatibility. Singleton is orthogonal.

quizzes.question: A team writes a Builder for HttpClient. In build(), they do not validate that the required url field is set, and the HttpClient constructor accepts null. A NullPointerException appears later when a caller invokes send(). What should be fixed?
options: Move validation into each builder setter so it fails at the earliest opportunity
Validate required fields in build() and throw a descriptive IllegalArgumentException naming the missing field — this is the last opportunity to catch the problem at construction
Add null checks in every method of HttpClient
Use Optional for url
quizzes.explanation: build() is the correct place to validate because it is the single exit point of the builder and the last moment before construction. It gives a clear error ('url is required') at the call site, which is far better than a downstream NPE. Validating in every setter is possible but is noisy (setters are called in any order) and does not handle cross-field invariants. Null checks scattered in every method are a symptom, not a fix. Optional is a signaling tool, not a validation mechanism.

quizzes.question: You must integrate a legacy SOAP payment library that exposes chargeRupees(long paise) returning XML, into your application which uses a clean PaymentClient.charge(BigDecimal) returning a Receipt object. Which pattern fits, and why?
options: Decorator — wrap PaymentClient to add XML handling
Adapter — PaymentClient's interface is different from LegacyPay's, so you need to translate one interface into the other
Proxy — control access to LegacyPay
Facade — simplify LegacyPay behind one method
quizzes.explanation: The two interfaces are genuinely different — one takes BigDecimal and returns Receipt, the other takes paise and returns XML. Adapter is exactly 'convert interface A into interface B'. Decorator keeps the interface and adds behavior, which is wrong here because the interfaces differ. Proxy controls access, also wrong. Facade simplifies a subsystem, but the goal here is interface translation, not simplification.

quizzes.question: You have an InputStream and want optional buffering, gzip decompression, and progress reporting in any combination. Inheritance would produce 2^3 = 8 subclasses; the decorator approach produces 3 wrappers that can be stacked. What is the key structural rule that makes decorators work?
options: Each decorator must extend the concrete class it decorates
Each decorator must implement the same interface as the component it wraps, and delegate calls to the wrapped instance — this allows arbitrary stacking while keeping the client unaware
Decorators must not call the wrapped object, only add their own behavior
Decorators must be singletons for performance
quizzes.explanation: A decorator implements the component interface (so it looks like a component to the client) and holds a reference to another component (so it can delegate). This allows a decorator to wrap either a concrete component or another decorator, giving arbitrary stacking with no combinatorial subclass explosion. Extending the concrete class (option A) prevents wrapping other decorators. Not delegating (option C) is impossible — you would lose the wrapped behavior. Singletons (option D) are unrelated.

quizzes.question: A code review shows `new BufferedInputStream(new GZIPInputStream(new FileInputStream(f)))` and the team's intent is to 'decompress the file and use it as a buffer'. Is this the right order?
options: Yes — Buffered wraps the stream to add buffering on top of decompressed bytes

The order should be `new GZIPInputStream(new BufferedInputStream(new FileInputStream(f)))` — buffering should be at the byte-source level (before decompression) to avoid tiny reads from disk, and decompression should be at the top
BufferedInputStream and GZIPInputStream cannot be stacked
The order does not matter — the JDK detects it
quizzes.explanation: Decorator order matters. GZIPInputStream reads compressed bytes from its source in small chunks. If BufferedInputStream wraps FileInputStream at the bottom, the gzip decoder reads from a buffer (fast). If the buffering is on top of GZIPInputStream, the gzip decoder reads directly from the file — tiny, unbuffered reads — and buffering only helps callers reading decompressed data. The standard idiom is `new GZIPInputStream(new BufferedInputStream(new FileInputStream(f)))`. The JDK does not auto-detect or reorder decorators.

quizzes.question: A team replaces slf4j with a direct dependency on log4j2 in every module, so they can use log4j2-specific features. What architectural property did they lose?
options: Thread safety — log4j2 is not thread-safe
The ability to swap the logging implementation at deployment time — a facade (slf4j) lets you pick the backend binding without changing application code
Transaction support — log4j2 does not support transactions
The ability to log at ERROR level
quizzes.explanation: SLF4J is a facade: application code depends only on the org.slf4j.Logger interface, and the actual backend (logback, log4j2, JUL) is chosen by the binding on the classpath at deployment. Coupling every module to log4j2 classes means switching backends later requires editing every module. Logging is not transactional, and log level support is orthogonal — those are distractors.

quizzes.question: A service annotates a method with @Cacheable. The first call queries the database and caches the result; the second call returns the cached value without ever invoking the target method. Which pattern is this, and why?
options: Decorator — it wraps the method and always calls it, then caches the result
Proxy — it controls access to the real method and may not call it at all when the cache hits
Adapter — it adapts the method's return type
Observer — it notifies the cache on each call
quizzes.explanation: The distinguishing test between Proxy and Decorator is 'is the real object always called?' With @Cacheable, the proxy checks the cache first and short-circuits on a hit — the target method is never invoked. That is the defining behavior of a Proxy (controlling access), not a Decorator (which always delegates and adds behavior around the call). This is why Spring's @Cacheable is a proxy-based annotation: the proxy decides whether to invoke the target.

quizzes.question: A @Transactional method calls another @Transactional method on the same class via this.other(). The inner method's transaction annotation is silently ignored. Which property of the proxy pattern explains this?
options: Proxies cannot work with self-invocation by design — the pattern requires a separate class
The proxy intercepts external calls; this.other() bypasses the proxy and goes directly to the raw target, so the inner @Transactional is never seen
Spring disables nested transactions for safety
The inner method must be declared public for @Transactional to work
quizzes.explanation: Spring's @Transactional is implemented via a proxy (JDK or CGLIB) that external callers hit. The proxy wraps the transaction logic around the method. A self-invocation (this.other()) executes on the raw target instance — it never touches the proxy, so the transaction interceptor never fires. This is a direct consequence of how the Proxy pattern works: the proxy is only in the call path when the caller holds a proxy reference. The fixes are to move the inner method to another bean, use TransactionTemplate, or use AspectJ load-time weaving.

quizzes.question: A file-tree client computes total size by checking `if (node instanceof Directory) { recurse } else { add file.size() }` at every level. A code reviewer suggests refactoring to Composite. What is the concrete benefit?
options: The tree becomes faster because instanceof checks are expensive
The client is replaced by a single recursive call — both File and Directory implement a common size() method, so the client no longer branches on type at every level
The refactor eliminates the need for recursion
Composite enforces file-system permissions
quizzes.explanation: Composite's value is making leaves and containers interchangeable through a common interface. The client calls node.size() once; the Directory implementation sums its children's size() calls recursively, and each File returns its own size. This eliminates the instanceof branching at every level of the walk, which is the concrete source of bugs (missing branches, wrong aggregation). Composite does not eliminate recursion — the Directory implementation still recurses — and performance is not the point. Permissions are unrelated.

quizzes.question: You have a compression module with a single GZIP implementation and no plan to add another. A colleague proposes introducing a CompressionStrategy interface 'for extensibility'. What is the correct assessment?
options: This is required by the Open/Closed Principle

This is premature abstraction — with only one implementation and no realistic second, the interface is indirection without benefit; introduce it when the second algorithm actually arrives or when tests need a fake
Strategy always pays off because it decouples client from implementation
Compression must use Strategy because it is an algorithmic concern
quizzes.explanation: The Strategy pattern's cost is an extra interface, extra classes, and client awareness of the strategy. That cost only pays off when there are two or more real variations, or when the algorithm varies by input and the choice is made at runtime. Adding the pattern for a hypothetical future is premature abstraction — a common GoF over-application. The right move is to write GZIP directly, and refactor to Strategy when a second algorithm is genuinely needed (test-driven refactoring, not speculation). Open/Closed is about allowing extension without breaking callers — it does not mandate introducing extension points before they are needed.

quizzes.question: A long-running service registers listeners on an application-wide event bus but never unregisters them. After a week of traffic, memory usage grows steadily and heap dumps show thousands of stale listener instances. What is the cause and fix?
options: Garbage collection is disabled for listener classes

The event bus holds strong references to registered listeners, so the subject prevents garbage collection of listeners whose owning request or session has ended — unregister in @PreDestroy, use WeakReference, or use a lifecycle-aware event framework
Listeners must be singletons to avoid the leak
The leak is caused by @Async on the listeners
quizzes.explanation: Observer's classic production bug is unregistering. If the subject holds a strong reference to each observer, the observer (and everything it references) cannot be collected even after its natural lifecycle ends. In long-lived subjects — a static event bus, a singleton publisher — the leak accumulates. The fixes are @PreDestroy (or finally) to unregister, WeakReference so the subject does not prevent collection, or a framework that ties observer registration to bean lifecycle (Spring's ApplicationListener beans are automatically managed). @Async is orthogonal — it affects delivery but not reference lifetime.

quizzes.question: A service publishes an event inside a @Transactional method, and a listener writes to an audit table outside the transaction. Occasionally the audit row is written for an order that ultimately rolls back. What is the correct fix?
options: Use @Async on the listener so it runs after the request returns
Use @TransactionalEventListener (Spring Boot 3) so the listener fires only after the transaction commits — an audit row is never written for a rolled-back order
Move the audit write into the same transaction
Remove the event and call the audit service directly
quizzes.explanation: Publishing an event inside a transaction but consuming it outside creates a dual-write gap — the audit writes for orders that later roll back, or (conversely) misses audit rows for orders that commit but whose listener fails. @TransactionalEventListener is designed for this: it defers the listener until after the commit phase, so it only runs for events whose transaction succeeded. @Async changes thread, not visibility of the transaction. Moving the write into the same transaction works but couples the audit to the order's transaction (often undesirable — audit should survive order rollback in some designs). Removing the event defeats the decoupling.

quizzes.question: A team wants to implement undo/redo in a text editor. They consider (A) calling each edit operation's inverse directly from an undo stack, and (B) implementing each edit as a Command with execute() and undo(). What is the architectural advantage of B?
options: Commands are always faster than direct calls

Commands capture the state needed to undo, so the undo logic is encapsulated with the edit that produced it — the editor does not need to know how to invert each operation, and new operations can be added without editing the undo manager
Commands eliminate the need for an undo stack
Commands are required by the Observer pattern
quizzes.explanation: The Command pattern's advantage is encapsulation of the request plus its inverse. Each command knows how to undo its own effect because it stored the necessary state at execute time (previous content, position, deleted bytes). The UndoStack is generic — it just pops and calls undo() — so adding a new command type does not touch the undo machinery. Without Command, the undo stack becomes a switch statement over operation types, and every new operation edits it. Performance is not the motivation, and UndoStack is exactly what Command uses.

quizzes.question: A distributed job system needs to persist user-initiated background tasks so they survive restarts and can be retried or reordered. Which pattern most naturally fits this requirement, and why?
options: Observer — jobs notify the scheduler when they complete
Strategy — the scheduler swaps algorithms per job
Command — jobs are objects with execute(), so they can be serialized, persisted, queued, retried, and reordered without changing the invoker
Adapter — jobs adapt different APIs
quizzes.explanation: Command packages a request as a first-class object. That is what enables persistence: the command can be serialized, stored in a database, retrieved on restart, and re-executed. It also enables retry (execute again), queueing (multiple commands in an ordered structure), and reordering (commands are independent objects). Without Command, a background task is a method call with a receiver — it cannot survive a restart because the caller's stack is gone. Observer is about notifications, Strategy is about algorithm selection, Adapter is about interface translation — none of them gives you a persistable unit of work.

quizzes.question: A base class defines importFile() that calls read(), parse(), validate(), write(), logSummary() in order. A subclass overrides importFile() to skip validate(). What went wrong with the Template Method pattern?
options: Nothing — subclasses are supposed to override the template method when their workflow differs

The template method was not declared final (or otherwise protected from being overridden), so a subclass could change the algorithm's structure — the fix is to make importFile() final and allow only the step methods to vary
validate() should have been abstract
The base class should not call logSummary()
quizzes.explanation: The whole point of Template Method is that the base class controls the flow and subclasses vary the steps — the template method itself must not be overridable. Making it final (or at least sealed to the intent) enforces this. If a subclass can override the template method, the pattern has no guarantee, and behavior varies in unpredictable ways that the base class cannot test or reason about.

quizzes.question: A team has three importers (CSV, JSON, XML) that each duplicate the read → validate → write → log flow, differing only in the parse step. Which pattern is the natural fit, and why?
options: Strategy — inject the parse algorithm at runtime
Template Method — the flow is fixed across variations, so put it in a base class and let subclasses override parse()
Observer — the importer notifies listeners on each row
Facade — hide the read/validate/write subsystem
quizzes.explanation: The tell between Template Method and Strategy is whether the algorithm's structure is fixed while only steps vary. Here the flow (read → validate → write → log) is identical across CSV, JSON, and XML; only parse() differs. That is exactly Template Method — put the flow in the base class once, override parse() in each subclass. Strategy would be appropriate if the entire import algorithm varied (e.g., 'sync vs async', 'strict vs lenient') — but Strategy would still leave the shared flow duplicated. Observer and Facade solve unrelated problems.

quizzes.question: An Order class has a big method with `switch(state)` blocks in pay(), ship(), deliver(), cancel(). Every new state requires editing every method. Which pattern and refactor solves the problem, and what is the distinguishing test vs Strategy?
options: Strategy — inject the state as a strategy at runtime

State — extract each state into a class implementing its legal operations, and each state transitions the Order to the next state on success; State differs from Strategy because the state objects trigger transitions internally, not the client
Observer — the Order notifies observers on state changes
Factory — create the correct state class based on input
quizzes.explanation: The problem is conditional explosion over a state matrix — the exact motivation for State. Each state becomes a class implementing pay/ship/deliver/cancel with only the legal operations; on success it calls order.setState(next). The distinguishing question from Strategy is 'who changes the reference?' — in State, the state objects transition internally; in Strategy, the client selects the algorithm externally. Observer solves event notification, not state-dependent behavior. Factory is a creation pattern, not a behavior pattern.

quizzes.question: A new LoggingFilter is added to a Spring Security filter chain but it never calls chain.doFilter(request, response). What is the effect, and why is this the classic Chain-of-Responsibility bug?
options: The filter is skipped — Spring detects the missing call and moves to the next filter
The request is dropped — every subsequent filter (including authentication and the controller) is skipped because the chain only advances when the current handler calls proceed
The filter runs twice
Spring throws a NullPointerException at startup
quizzes.explanation: In a chain of responsibility, each handler must explicitly pass control forward by calling the chain's proceed method (chain.doFilter for servlet filters). If it returns without doing so, the request is treated as handled — the response as-is is sent, and every downstream filter and the controller are skipped. Spring does not auto-detect the missing call. This is the classic failure mode of Chain of Responsibility and is why integration tests for the whole chain (not just individual filters) are essential.

quizzes.question: A team describes their request pipeline as 'Chain of Responsibility' — auth, rate limit, validation, logging, business handler — where each handler can short-circuit OR pass through, and multiple handlers act on the same request. Which variant are they using, and is this the classic GoF version?
options: Pure Chain of Responsibility — exactly one handler acts, as the GoF describes
Impure Chain of Responsibility (middleware style) — multiple handlers act and pass through, short-circuiting only on failure; the pure GoF variant guarantees exactly one handler
Decorator — this is just stacking decorators
Observer — each handler observes the request
quizzes.explanation: The pure GoF Chain of Responsibility guarantees that exactly one handler processes the request. The middleware variant, which dominates in practice (servlet filters, Spring Security, gRPC interceptors), lets multiple handlers act and pass through, and only short-circuits on failure. Naming the variant explicitly is a strong interview signal — it shows you understand the pattern beyond the textbook definition. Decorator wraps a specific target and always delegates; Observer is about event notification, not pipeline control.

quizzes.question: A for-each loop over an ArrayList calls list.remove(item) inside the loop. The next iteration throws ConcurrentModificationException even though only one thread is running. Why?
options: ArrayList is not thread-safe, so single-threaded removal also fails

The ArrayList's fail-fast iterator checks a modCount field on next(); list.remove() changes modCount, so the iterator detects structural modification and throws — the fix is iterator.remove(), removeIf(), or iterating a snapshot
ConcurrentModificationException is only thrown when the collection is larger than 1000 elements
The loop must be replaced with a stream to avoid the exception
quizzes.explanation: The name is misleading — ConcurrentModificationException also fires in single-threaded code. Every java.util collection's iterator is fail-fast: it reads a modCount on creation and checks it on each next(). list.remove(item) increments modCount, so the next() call detects a structural change and throws. The fix is iterator.remove() (updates both collection and modCount atomically), Collection.removeIf(predicate), or iterating over a copy (new ArrayList<>(list)). Thread-safety is orthogonal — the bug is structural modification during iteration, not concurrency.

quizzes.question: A compiler team needs to add operations (type-check, code-gen, optimize, pretty-print) to an AST whose node types (Add, Mul, Number) are stable but whose operations grow every release. Which pattern fits, and what is the trade-off?
options: Strategy — inject the operation at runtime
Visitor — add an accept(Visitor) method to each node, define operations as Visitor implementations; adding an operation is one new class, but adding a new element type breaks every Visitor
Observer — nodes notify visitors on visit
Decorator — wrap nodes with additional behavior
quizzes.explanation: This is the canonical Visitor use case: stable element hierarchy, growing operations. Each node adds accept(visitor) → visitor.visitConcrete(this); each operation is a Visitor implementation. Adding a new operation (e.g., depth calculation) is a new Visitor class with no edits to the nodes. The trade-off is the asymmetric cost: adding a new node type forces every existing Visitor to add a new method. For sealed hierarchies in Java 21, pattern matching is often cleaner — but Visitor remains the right tool when visitors are supplied by external code or when the operation set is expected to grow without touching the nodes.

quizzes.question: What does 'double dispatch' mean in the Visitor pattern?
options: The visitor is called twice — once for the element and once for its children

The call dispatches on two types in sequence: first element.accept(visitor) selects the accept() override based on the concrete element type, then the accept implementation calls visitor.visitConcrete(this) which selects the visit method based on the concrete visitor type
The visitor and the element both extend the same base class
Both the visitor and the element must be final classes
quizzes.explanation: Java's normal method dispatch is single: the concrete type of the receiver selects the method. Visitor needs two types (element type AND visitor type) to select the right behavior, so it does it in two steps. First, element.accept(visitor) uses virtual dispatch on element's runtime class. Then accept() calls visitor.visitConcrete(this) — the argument's compile-time type is the concrete element class, so the correct overload on the visitor is selected. That two-step process is 'double dispatch'. It is not calling anything twice or requiring final classes.

quizzes.question: An editor implements undo by storing the full document state on every keystroke. After a few minutes of typing, memory spikes because 50,000 snapshots are queued. Which pattern-level fix addresses the root cause?
options: Use Observer to notify the undo stack only on important edits

Combine patterns: use Command for fine-grained keystroke undo (each command stores its inverse) and Memento for coarse checkpoints (e.g., every 100 edits or before a dangerous operation) — the trade-off is snapshot cost vs undo granularity
Use Strategy for the undo algorithm
Compress each snapshot with gzip before storing
quizzes.explanation: The Memento pattern's trade-off is snapshot memory cost. Full-document snapshots per keystroke do not scale. The pragmatic answer used by real editors is a hybrid: Command pattern for fine-grained undo (each command stores just its inverse — the inserted characters and position), plus Memento for coarse checkpoints (a full snapshot before risky operations, or every N edits). Compression helps but does not fix the O(N²) growth. Observer and Strategy do not address the memory problem — they change notification or algorithm selection, not the amount of state stored.

quizzes.question: Ten services need to react to OrderPlaced events. Currently each producer calls each consumer directly, and adding a new consumer requires editing every producer. Which pattern fits, and what is the risk?
options: Observer — each consumer registers as an observer on the producer

Mediator — introduce an event bus (e.g., ApplicationEventPublisher, Kafka, RabbitMQ) that routes events; producers publish once, consumers subscribe; the risk is the mediator becoming a God Object if coordination logic accumulates
Adapter — adapt each producer to each consumer's interface
Decorator — wrap producers with consumers
